A NOTE TO THE READER

About this book & suggested learning methodology

A chapterwise companion for understanding, practising and revising Class 9 mathematics.

Mathematics becomes easier to revise when ideas are organised, examples are worked through carefully and practice follows understanding. These notes bring the fourteen chapters together in one chapterwise resource, following the sequence used in the supplied Ganita Manjari manuscript.

What you will find in the chapters

01
At-a-glance summaries: Compact tables or formula summaries that bring the central ideas of a chapter into one place.
02
Key ideas and reminders: Short explanations, important observations and cautions that help clarify common points of confusion.
03
Worked examples: Illustrative problems with solutions arranged in a clear, step-by-step sequence.
04
Chapter-end practice: Questions that let you check recall, apply concepts and attempt more challenging problems.
05
Solutions and answers: A back-of-chapter answer section for checking your work after attempting the questions.
A SUGGESTED STUDY ROUTINE
Read the summary first, study the key ideas, attempt each worked example before reading its solution, and then complete the chapter-end questions without looking at the answers.

Use these notes as a companion to active study, not as a replacement for understanding the textbook concepts or showing your own mathematical reasoning.

A PRACTICAL APPROACH

How to use this book for maximum retention

A repeatable routine for each chapter.

01
Preview the chapter: Begin with the chapter-at-a-glance table or formula summary. Identify the ideas and relationships you need to remember.
02
Read actively: Work through each section in order. Pause at key ideas and cautions; rewrite a rule in your own words when needed.
03
Attempt before revealing: Cover the solution to each worked example. Try the question independently, then compare your steps with the printed solution.
04
Practise independently: Complete the chapter-end questions without referring to the worked examples. Mark questions that need another attempt.
05
Check and revisit: Use the solutions at the back to check your answers. Return to the relevant section for any step or concept that remains unclear.

For Digital & Kindle Readers:

Use the reader navigation menu to move between chapters. Because digital books reflow to fit the reader's screen and font settings, use the table of contents and chapter links to locate a section.

Before you move to the next chapter

□  Can I explain the main idea in my own words? □  Can I solve a similar example without help?
□  Have I checked signs, calculations and units? □  Have I revisited the questions I got wrong?

CHAPTER 1
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

These notes revise Chapter 1 (The Use of Coordinates), Chapter 2 (Introduction to Linear Polynomials) and Chapter 3 (The World of Numbers) Chapter 4 (Exploring Algebraic Identities) Chapter 5 (Circles) and Chapter 6 (Measuring Space: Perimeter and Area) and Chapter 7 (The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability) and Chapter 8 (Exploring Sequences and Progressions) Chapter 9 (Propositions and their Converses) and Chapter 10 (How Quantities Combine: Understanding Data) and Chapter 11 (The World of Algorithms) and Chapter 12 (Quadrilaterals) and Chapter 13 (Two Variables, One Line) and Chapter 14 (Surface Area and Volume) in the order of your NCERT textbook. Each section begins with a boxed summary you can recall in half a minute, followed by the key points and solved examples, with every solution written one step to a line. Cover the solution and try each example first. Finish with the chapter-end questions, and check them against the answers at the back.

The chapter at a glance

Idea Statement
Ordered pair ( x , y ) with x first. ( a , b ) and ( b , a ) are different points unless a = b .
Axes, origin Perpendicular lines X ′ O X and Y ′ O Y meeting at O (0, 0) .
Abscissa, ordinate x is the distance from the y -axis; y is the distance from the x -axis.
Points on axes ( k , 0) on the x -axis; (0, k ) on the y -axis. In no quadrant.
Quadrants I (+, +) , II (−, +) , III (−, −) , IV (+, −) .
Distance √(( x 2 − x 1 ) 2 + ( y 2 − y 1 ) 2 ) . From the origin: √( x 2 + y 2 ) .
Reflection x -axis ( x , − y ) ; y -axis (− x , y ) ; origin (− x , − y ) . Lengths unchanged.
Midpoint (( x 1 + x 2 )/2, ( y 1 + y 2 )/2) . End point: x 2 = 2 x M − x 1 , y 2 = 2 y M − y 1 .
Trisection One-third and two-thirds of the change in x and in y from A .
Collinear Longest distance = sum of the other two, or equal steepness.

Chapter 1: Orienting Yourself 1.1 History in Brief Ganita Manjari · Class 9
1.1

History in Brief

Period Contribution
c. 2600 BCE Sindhu–Sarasvatī cities are laid out on regular grids.
c. 800 BCE Baudhāyana’s Śulba Sūtras: grid layouts and the theorem behind the distance formula.
c. 4th century BCE Ujjayinī taken as the prime meridian (0° longitude); Ptolemy (c. 150 CE) calls it “Ozine”.
499 CE Āryabhaṭa uses sines to fix positions of celestial bodies.
628 CE Brahmagupta treats zero and negative numbers as numbers; this makes four quadrants possible.
1637 CE Descartes: a point of a plane is fixed by two perpendicular distances from two axes.
1.2

Locating Points on a Map

Key Idea
A position on a flat surface is an ordered pair ( x , y ) : x is the horizontal distance and y the vertical distance from the starting point O (0, 0) . The order matters.

A map drawn to a scale such as 1 cm : 1 foot makes one map unit stand for one real unit.

A floor map is two-dimensional: it shows length and breadth only. Height (of a window or a table top) is a third direction and cannot be marked.

Points on the bottom wall have y = 0; points on the left wall have x = 0.

Two points on one wall are separated by the difference of the coordinate that changes.

In a city grid, (4, 3) and (3, 4) are different crossings.

Example 1
A room has corners O(0, 0), A(16, 0), B(16, 9), C(0, 9). A door runs from D1(9, 0) to R1(11.5, 0). Find the room size, the distance of the door from the left wall, and the door width.
Solution. Length OA = 16 ft and breadth OC = 9 ft, so the room is 16 ft by 9 ft.
D1 has x = 9, so the door starts 9 ft from the left wall
y = 0, so it is on the bottom wall.
Width = 11.5 − 9 = 2.5 ft.
Example 2
Point A is 3 units right and 5 units up from the origin. Write A. Is a point 5 right and 3 up the same point?
Solution. Horizontal distance first: A = (3, 5).
The other point is (5, 3).
The pairs differ, so the points differ: order matters.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 8 of 215
Chapter 1: Orienting Yourself 1.3 The Cartesian Plane Ganita Manjari · Class 9
1.3

The Cartesian Plane

Key Idea
For P ( x , y ) : abscissa = x = distance from the y -axis; ordinate = y = distance from the x -axis. The sign shows the side. x -axis points: ( k , 0) . y -axis points: (0, k ) . Origin: (0, 0) .

A number line is one-dimensional; two perpendicular number lines give the two-dimensional plane.

Right of O and above O are positive; left and below are negative.

Watch out: (0, 6) is on the y-axis. It is the y-value that is 0 on the x-axis.

Example 3
State the axis and distance from the origin of B(4.5, 0), E(−2.9, 0), H(0, 4), G(0, −4.5).
Solution. B and E have y = 0: on the x-axis, 4.5 units right and 2.9 units left of O.
H and G have x = 0: on the y-axis, 4 units above and 4.5 units below O.
Example 4
For P(−3, 7) name the abscissa and ordinate and find the distance of P from each axis.
Solution. Abscissa −3, ordinate 7.
Distance from the y-axis = |−3| = 3
from the x-axis = |7| = 7.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 9 of 215
Chapter 1: Orienting Yourself 1.4 Quadrants Ganita Manjari · Class 9
1.4

Quadrants

Quadrant Position Signs of ( x , y ) Example
I upper right (+, +) (3, 4)
II upper left (−, +) (−5, 3)
III lower left (−, −) (−3, −4)
IV lower right (+, −) (3, −5)
Key Idea
Quadrants are numbered anticlockwise from the upper right. Points on the axes belong to no quadrant.

The line parallel to the y-axis through x = c contains the points (c, y); the line parallel to the x-axis through y = c contains (x, c).

Without negative numbers only Quadrant I and the positive parts of the axes could be described.

Watch out: (0, −5) is on the negative y-axis, not in Quadrant III.

Example 5
In which quadrant does (−3, 4) lie?
Solution. x < 0: left of the y-axis.
y > 0: above the x-axis.
So Quadrant II.
Example 6
W has x-coordinate −5. H lies on the line through W parallel to the y-axis. Find H and its possible quadrants.
Solution. That line keeps x fixed, so H = (−5, y).
y > 0: Quadrant II.
y < 0: Quadrant III.
y = 0: on the x-axis, no quadrant.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 10 of 215
Chapter 1: Orienting Yourself 1.5 Distance Between Two Points Ganita Manjari · Class 9
1.5

Distance Between Two Points

Same y (horizontal): distance = |x2 − x1|. Same x (vertical): distance = |y2 − y1|.

Slanted: draw the right triangle whose legs are |x2 − x1| and |y2 − y1|. The Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem, (hypotenuse)² = sum of the squares of the legs, gives the formula below.

Key Idea
Distance of P ( x , y ) from the origin: √( x 2 + y 2 ) . The differences are squared, so the order of the points does not matter. Watch out: square before adding. The distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6) is √(3 2 + 4 2 ) = 5 , not √7 .
Figure Test using distances
Isosceles triangle Two sides equal
Equilateral triangle Three sides equal
Right triangle (longest side)² = sum of the squares of the other two
Rhombus Four sides equal
Rectangle Opposite sides equal and diagonals equal
Square Four sides equal and diagonals equal

Circles. P is inside, on or outside a circle (centre O, radius r) when OP < r, OP = r or OP > r. Two circles with centres d apart and radii r1, r2 cross at two points if |r1 − r2| < d < r1 + r2, and touch if d = r1 + r2.

Example 7
Find the distance between P(−2, 3) and Q(4, 11).
Solution. x2 − x1 = 6
y2 − y1 = 8.
PQ = √(62 + 82)
= √100
= 10 units.
Example 8
Show that A(0, 0), B(6, 0), C(0, 8) form a right triangle.
Solution. AB = 6 (horizontal), AC = 8 (vertical), BC = √(62 + 82) = 10.
AB2 + AC2 = 36 + 64
= 100
= BC2, so the angle at A is a right angle.
Example 9
Show that (1, 0), (0, 1), (−1, 0), (0, −1) are the vertices of a square and find its area.
Solution. Each side is √(12 + 12) = √2, so all four sides are equal.
Both diagonals are 2 (from (1, 0) to (−1, 0) and from (0, 1) to (0, −1)), so the diagonals are equal.
It is a square.
Area = (√2)² = 2 square units.

Chapter 1: Orienting Yourself 1.6 Reflections Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 10
Show that A(6, 8), B(−8, 6), C(0, −10) lie on a circle centred at O. Is D(5, 5) inside or outside? Is E(9, −8)?
Solution. OA = √(36 + 64)
= 10
OB = √(64 + 36)
= 10
OC = 10.
So all lie on the circle of radius 10.
OD = √50 < 10: inside.
OE = √(81 + 64)
= √145 > 10: outside.
Example 11
Circle 1 has centre (0, 0) and radius 3; circle 2 has centre (6, 8) and radius 7. Do they cross, touch or miss?
Solution. d = √(62 + 82)
= 10 and r1 + r2 = 10.
d = r1 + r2, so the circles touch at exactly one point.
1.6

Reflections

Reflection in Rule Example: (3, −5)
the x -axis ( x , y ) → ( x , − y ) (3, 5)
the y -axis ( x , y ) → (− x , y ) (−3, −5)
the origin ( x , y ) → (− x , − y ) (−3, 5)
Key Idea
A point and its image are equally far from the mirror line. A reflection keeps all lengths (an isometry ), so the image is congruent to the figure.

The axis you reflect in keeps its own coordinate: the x-axis keeps x, the y-axis keeps y.

Reflecting in the x-axis and then the y-axis (either order) is the same as reflecting in the origin.

Example 12
Reflect A(3, 4), D(7, 1), M(9, 6) in the y-axis and check that AD is unchanged.
Solution. Keep y, change the sign of x: A′(−3, 4), D′(−7, 1), M′(−9, 6).
A′D′ = √(42 + 32)
= 5
= AD.
Example 13
A point is 5 units from the y-axis and 3 units from the x-axis and lies in Quadrant III. Find it, and its reflection in the origin.
Solution. In Quadrant III both coordinates are negative: (−5, −3).
Reflection in the origin: (5, 3).
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 12 of 215
Chapter 1: Orienting Yourself 1.7 The Midpoint of a Segment Ganita Manjari · Class 9
1.7

The Midpoint of a Segment

Key Idea
The midpoint has the average of the x -values and of the y -values. Divide by 2. To find the other end, use the reversed formula:

Trisection: one step = (change in x)/3 and (change in y)/3. P is one step from A, Q is two steps. Check: P is the midpoint of AQ.

Triangle from its midpoints: add the equal-vertex pairs. If D, E, F are the midpoints of AB, BC, CA, then xA + xB = 2xD and so on; add all three sums, halve to get xA + xB + xC, then subtract each pair to find the third vertex.

Example 14
Find the midpoint of (2, −5) and (6, 9).
Solution. ((2 + 6)/2, (−5 + 9)/2) = (4, 2).
Example 15
M(2, −3) is the midpoint of A(−1, 4) and B. Find B.
Solution. x = 2(2) − (−1)
= 5 and y = 2(−3) − 4 = −10.
B = (5, −10).
Example 16
Find the points that trisect AB, where A(−3, 2) and B(9, −7).
Solution. Change in x = 12, so one step = 4.
Change in y = −9, so one step = −3.
P = (−3 + 4, 2 − 3)
= (1, −1) and Q = (1 + 4, −1 − 3) = (5, −4).
Example 17
The midpoints of AB, BC, CA are D(2, 3), E(4, 5), F(1, 6). Find A, B, C.
Solution. x: xA + xB = 4
xB + xC = 8
xC + xA = 2.
Sum = 7.
So xC = 7 − 4 = 3, xA = 7 − 8 = −1, xB = 7 − 2 = 5.
y: sums 6, 10, 12, total 14.
So yC = 8, yA = 4, yB = 2.
A(−1, 4)
B(5, 2)
C(3, 8).
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 13 of 215
Chapter 1: Orienting Yourself 1.8 Collinear Points Ganita Manjari · Class 9
1.8

Collinear Points

Key Idea
Three points are collinear if they lie on one straight line. Test without plotting, in either of two ways.

Distances: the longest of AB, BC, CA equals the sum of the other two.

Steepness (slope): the steepness of AB equals the steepness of BC.

Caution
Equal lengths prove nothing. For A (0, 0) , B (3, 4) , C (6, 0) we get A B = B C = 5 , but A B + B C = 10 ≠ A C = 6 , so the points are not collinear.
Example 18
Are A(−2, −3), B(0, 1), C(3, 7) collinear?
Solution. AB = √(4 + 16)
= 2√5
BC = √(9 + 36)
= 3√5
AC = √(25 + 100)
= 5√5.
AB + BC = 5√5
= AC, so they are collinear.
(Steepness of AB = 4/2 = 2 and of BC = 6/3 = 2.)
Example 19
Are (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 4) collinear?
Solution. Steepness of the first pair = 1
of the second pair = (4 − 2)/(3 − 2) = 2.
1 ≠ 2, so they are not collinear.

CHAPTER 2
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

Introduction to Linear Polynomials

The chapter at a glance

Idea Statement
Polynomial, degree One variable, non-negative whole-number powers. Degree = highest power: 0 constant, 1 linear, 2 quadratic, 3 cubic.
Value at x = k Replace x by k and simplify: P ( k ) .
Linear polynomial a x + b , a ≠ 0 . Zero: x = − b / a .
Function machine f ( x ) = a x + b : multiply the input by a , then add b .
Linear pattern Constant difference d . n -th term = d n + c , with c = first term − d .
Growth and decay y = b + a t : a > 0 growth, a < 0 decay. b = starting value.
Master relation y = a x + b : a = slope (rate), b = y-intercept (initial value).
From two data points a = ( y 2 − y 1 )/( x 2 − x 1 ) , then b = y 1 − a x 1 .
Graph Straight line. y-intercept (0, b ) ; x-intercept (− b / a , 0) . y = a x passes through the origin.
Parallel lines Same a , different b .
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 21 of 215
Chapter 2: Linear Polynomials 2.1 Polynomials and Their Degree Ganita Manjari · Class 9
2.1

Polynomials and Their Degree

Key Idea
An algebraic expression joins numbers and letters ( variables ) with + , − , × , ÷ . In 4 x + 5 y + 3 the terms are 4 x , 5 y and 3; the coefficients are 4 and 5; the constant is 3. A univariate polynomial has one variable with non-negative whole-number powers. Its degree is the highest power of the variable.
Degree Name Example
0 Constant P ( x ) = 8 , written 8 x 0
1 Linear P ( z ) = 3 z + 7
2 Quadratic P ( x ) = x 2 + 5 x + 1
3 Cubic P ( y ) = 5 y 3 + y 2 + 2 y − 1

A missing term has coefficient 0: in 4z3 + 5z2 − 11 the coefficient of z is 0.

The sign belongs to the coefficient: in x4 − 3x3 the coefficient of x3 is −3.

Example 1
Find the degree and name of (i) 2x2 − 5x + 3 (ii) y3 + 2y − 1 (iii) −9 (iv) 4z − 3.
Solution. (i) Highest power 2: degree 2, quadratic.
(ii) Highest power 3: degree 3, cubic.
(iii) −9 = −9x0: degree 0, constant.
(iv) Highest power 1: degree 1, linear.
Example 2
In x4 − 3x3 + 6x2 − 2x + 7 write the coefficients of x3 and x2 and the constant term.
Solution. Coefficient of x3 is −3, of x2 is 6, and the constant term is 7.
Example 3
Write the coefficient of z and the constant term of 4z3 + 5z2 − 11.
Solution. There is no z term, so 4z3 + 5z2 + 0z − 11: coefficient of z is 0.
The constant term is −11.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 22 of 215
Chapter 2: Linear Polynomials 2.2 Linear Polynomials as Functions Ganita Manjari · Class 9
2.2

Linear Polynomials as Functions

Key Idea
A linear polynomial has degree 1: a x + b with a ≠ 0 . Each extra unit of x changes the value by the same fixed amount a . As a function , f ( x ) = a x + b is an input–output machine: multiply the input by a , then add b .

The value of P(x) at x = k is P(k): replace x by k.

A linear polynomial has exactly one zero: ax + b = 0 gives x = −b/a.

Word problems: let a letter stand for the unknown, write an equation from the story, solve it, then check it against the story.

Example 4
Find the value of 5x − 3 at x = 0, −1 and 2.
Solution. x = 0: 5(0) − 3 = −3.
x = −1: 5(−1) − 3 = −8.
x = 2: 5(2) − 3 = 7.
Example 5
Find the zero of 4x − 10.
Solution. Set 4x − 10 = 0: x = 10/4 = 5/2.
Check: 4(5/2) − 10 = 0.
Example 6
Salil’s mother is three times as old as Salil. In 5 years their ages add up to 70. Find their present ages.
Solution. Salil’s age x
his mother’s 3x.
In 5 years: (x + 5) + (3x + 5) = 70, so 4x = 60 and x = 15.
Salil is 15 and his mother is 45.
Example 7
Two integers are in the ratio 2 : 5 and differ by 63. Find them.
Solution. Let them be 2x and 5x: 5x − 2x = 63, so x = 21.
The integers are 42 and 105.
Example 8
Ruby has ₹2 and ₹5 coins worth ₹88. She has three times as many ₹2 coins as ₹5 coins. How many of each?
Solution. ₹5 coins: x
₹2 coins: 3x.
5x + 2(3x) = 88, so 11x = 88 and x = 8.
She has 8 five-rupee coins and 24 two-rupee coins.
Example 9
A rectangle has perimeter 24 cm and length 3 cm more than twice its width. Find its sides.
Solution. Width w, length 2w + 3.
Half the perimeter: (2w + 3) + w = 12, so w = 3.
Length = 9 cm.
The sides are 9 cm and 3 cm.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 23 of 215
Chapter 2: Linear Polynomials 2.3 Linear Patterns Ganita Manjari · Class 9
2.3

Linear Patterns

Key Idea
In a linear pattern the difference between consecutive terms is a constant d . The n -th term is a linear polynomial in n : d n + c , where c = first term − d .
Stage n 1 2 3 4 n
Tiles 1 3 5 7 2 n − 1

Find d, then c, then check the rule with n = 1 and n = 2.

Increasing pattern: d > 0. Decreasing pattern: d < 0, for example 120 − 9n.

Example 10
Find the rule for 5, 8, 11, 14, …
Solution. d = 8 − 5
= 3 and c = 5 − 3 = 2, so the n-th term is 3n + 2.
Check: n = 1 gives 5
n = 4 gives 14.
Example 11
A bank account starts with ₹500 and ₹150 is added each month. Write the amount after n months.
Solution. Start 500, plus 150 each month: 500 + 150n.
Example 12
A rally has 120 members and 9 leave every hour. Write the number remaining after n hours.
Solution. 120 − 9n.
Example 13
A 500-page book is read at 20 pages a day. How many pages are left after 15 days?
Solution. L(n) = 500 − 20n, so L(15) = 500 − 300 = 200 pages.
Example 14
A box is 7 cm long and 11 cm broad. Write its volume in terms of the height h and find it for h = 9.
Solution. Base area = 7 × 11 = 77 cm², so V(h) = 77h, a linear pattern.
V(9) = 693 cm³.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 24 of 215
Chapter 2: Linear Polynomials 2.4 Linear Growth and Linear Decay Ganita Manjari · Class 9
2.4

Linear Growth and Linear Decay

Key Idea
A quantity that changes by a fixed amount in equal intervals follows y = b + a t . If a > 0 it is linear growth ; if a < 0 it is linear decay . a is the rate of change and b the starting value.

When a decaying quantity runs out, solve b + at = 0.

Always state the unit of the rate: “per month”, “per day”, “per year”.

Example 15
A plant is 1.75 ft tall and grows 0.5 ft every month. Write its height after t months and find it after 7 months.
Solution. h(t) = 1.75 + 0.5t: linear growth.
h(7) = 1.75 + 3.5
= 5.25 ft.
Example 16
A phone costing ₹10,000 loses ₹800 of value each year. Find its value after 3 years.
Solution. v(t) = 10000 − 800t: linear decay.
v(3) = 10000 − 2400
= ₹7{,}600.
Example 17
A village has 750 people and 50 are added each year. Find the population after 6 years.
Solution. P(t) = 750 + 50t: linear growth.
P(6) = 750 + 300
= 1050.
Example 18
A prepaid balance of ₹600 falls by ₹15 a day. When does it reach zero?
Solution. b(x) = 600 − 15x: linear decay.
600 − 15x = 0 gives x = 40 days.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 25 of 215
Chapter 2: Linear Polynomials 2.5 The Master Relation y = ax + b Ganita Manjari · Class 9
2.5

The Master Relation y = ax + b

Key Idea
Every linear relation between x and y can be written y = a x + b . a is the slope , the change in y per unit change in x . b is the y-intercept , the value of y when x = 0 .

Two data points fix the relation. Write y1 = ax1 + b and y2 = ax2 + b, subtract to get a, then substitute to get b.

Check the answer with the second data point.

Example 19
A learning platform bills ₹400 for 10 modules and ₹500 for 14 modules. Find the relation y = ax + b.
Solution. 10a + b = 400 and 14a + b = 500.
Subtract: 4a = 100, so a = 25.
10(25) + b = 400 gives b = 150.
So y = 25x + 150.
Check: 25(14) + 150 = 500.
Example 20
A gym court costs ₹800 for 10 hours and ₹1100 for 15 hours. Find the relation.
Solution. 5a = 300, so a = 60.
10(60) + b = 800 gives b = 200.
So y = 60x + 200.
Example 21
Water freezes at 0°C = 32°F and boils at 100°C = 212°F. Express °C in terms of °F as C = aF + b.
Solution. 0 = 32a + b and 100 = 212a + b.
Subtract: 100 = 180a, so a = 5/9.
b = −32 × 5/9
= −160/9.
So C = (5/9)(F − 32).
Check: F = 212 gives (5/9)(180) = 100.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 26 of 215
Chapter 2: Linear Polynomials 2.6 Graphs and Slopes Ganita Manjari · Class 9
2.6

Graphs and Slopes

Key Idea
The graph of y = a x + b is a straight line . Two points are enough to draw it.

y-intercept: the line cuts the y-axis at (0, b).

x-intercept: put y = 0. The line cuts the x-axis at (−b/a, 0), the zero of ax + b.

Slope: a > 0 rises from left to right; a < 0 falls; a larger |a| is steeper. When b = 0 the line y = ax passes through the origin.

Parallel lines have the same a and different b.

Example 22
Write the slope and y-intercept of (i) y = 5 − 2x (ii) 3y = 9x + 6 (iii) 4y = 2x − 8.
Solution. (i) y = −2x + 5: slope −2, y-intercept 5.
(ii) y = 3x + 2: slope 3, y-intercept 2.
(iii) y = (1/2)x − 2: slope 1/2, y-intercept −2.
Example 23
Find the line p(x) = ax + b through (1, 5) and (3, 11). Where does it cut the axes?
Solution. Slope a = (11 − 5)/(3 − 1) = 3.
From 5 = 3(1) + b: b = 2.
So p(x) = 3x + 2.
y-intercept (0, 2). x-intercept: 3x + 2 = 0 gives x = −2/3, so (−2/3, 0).
Example 24
p(x) passes through (2, 3) and (6, 11). Find q(x), parallel to it, through (4, −1).
Solution. Slope of p: (11 − 3)/(6 − 2) = 2, and 3 = 2(2) + b gives p(x) = 2x − 1.
q has slope 2: −1 = 2(4) + d, so d = −9 and q(x) = 2x − 9.
Example 25
Show that every line y = ax + a with a > 0 passes through one common point.
Solution. ax + a = a(x + 1)
= 0 gives x = −1 whatever a is.
Every such line passes through (−1, 0).

Chapter 3: The World of Numbers Overview & Key Ideas Ganita Manjari · Class 9
CHAPTER 3
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

The World of Numbers

The chapter at a glance

Idea Statement
Natural numbers N {1, 2, 3, …} , born from one-to-one correspondence.
Zero a − a = 0 ; a + 0 = a ; a − 0 = a ; a × 0 = 0 .
Integers Z {…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …} . Positive: fortune (dhana). Negative: debt (ṛiṇa).
Sign rules (+)(+) = + , (−)(−) = + , (+)(−) = − .
Rational numbers Q p / q with p , q integers and q ≠ 0 . Every integer n = n /1 . Lowest terms: gcd ( p , q ) = 1 .
Density Between rationals a and b lies their average ( a + b )/2 . Distance between them: | a − b | .
Irrational numbers Cannot be written as p / q : for example √2, √3, π. Proved by contradiction.
Real numbers R Rational and irrational numbers together: every point of the number line.
Decimals Rational: terminating or repeating. Irrational: non-terminating and non-repeating.
Terminating test In lowest terms p / q terminates when q = 2 m × 5 n .
Repeating to p / q Multiply by 10 k ( k = length of the repeating block) and subtract.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 33 of 215
Chapter 3: The World of Numbers 3.1 Counting and Natural Numbers Ganita Manjari · Class 9
3.1

Counting and Natural Numbers

Key Idea
One-to-one correspondence matches each object of one collection with exactly one object of another, such as one pebble for each returning cow. This gave the natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, 4, …} .

Lebombo bone (~35,000 years ago): 29 deliberate notches, probably a lunar-phase tally.

Ishango bone (~20,000 BCE, near the Nile): columns of marks grouping the primes 11, 13, 17, 19 and doublings.

Lothal and Harappa: standard cubic weights and measures supported long-distance trade.

Vedic and Buddhist texts named large powers of 10: up to 1012 (parārdha) and, in the Lalitavistara, up to 1053 (tallakṣaṇa).

Example 1
A merchant in Lothal exchanges 2 bags of spices for 15 copper ingots. How many ingots will he get for 12 bags?
Solution. Rate of exchange = 15/2 ingots per bag.
Ingots for 12 bags = 12 × 15/2.
= 6 × 15.
= 90.
He receives 90 copper ingots.
Example 2
At the same rate, how many bags of spices buy 60 ingots?
Solution. Bags needed = 60 ÷ 15/2.
= 60 × 2/15.
= 8.
So 8 bags of spices buy 60 ingots.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 34 of 215
Chapter 3: The World of Numbers 3.2 Zero: Śhūnya Ganita Manjari · Class 9
3.2

Zero: Śhūnya

Key Idea
Brahmagupta (628 CE) defined zero as a − a = 0 and gave its rules: a + 0 = a , a − 0 = a , a × 0 = 0 .

Babylonians and Mayans used a blank or a mark as a placeholder; Indian mathematicians treated zero as a number that can be added, subtracted and multiplied.

The Bakhśhālī manuscript (early centuries CE) shows the earliest zero as a solid dot, the bindu.

Śhūnyatā, the philosophical idea of emptiness, helped Āryabhaṭa and Brahmagupta accept zero.

Example 3
Evaluate (9 + 0) − 0 + 4 × 0 using the rules for zero.
Solution. 9 + 0 = 9.
9 − 0 = 9.
4 × 0 = 0.
So the value is 9 + 0 = 9.
Example 4
Show that 12 − 12 = 0 and find 0 × (−8).
Solution. By definition, a − a = 0 with a = 12.
So 12 − 12 = 0.
By the rule a × 0 = 0, 0 × (−8) = 0.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 35 of 215
Chapter 3: The World of Numbers 3.3 Integers: Fortunes and Debts Ganita Manjari · Class 9
3.3

Integers: Fortunes and Debts

Key Idea
The integers are Z = {…, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …} . Positive integers are fortunes (dhana, moves right of zero); negative integers are debts (ṛiṇa, moves left of zero).
Product Sign Example
positive × positive positive 3 × 4 = 12
negative × negative positive (−3) × (−4) = 12
positive × negative negative 3 × (−4) = −12

Why (−)(−) = +: a negative is a debt; taking away 4 debts of ₹3 leaves you ₹12 richer, so (−3) × (−4) = +12.

Use brackets around a negative number inside an expression, and add or subtract signed numbers carefully.

Example 5
A trader borrows ₹850, then earns a profit of ₹1200, then suffers a loss of ₹450. Find his final standing.
Solution. Debt = −850, profit = +1200, loss = −450.
Net standing = (−850) + 1200 + (−450).
= 1200 − 850 − 450.
= 1200 − 1300.
= −100.
His final standing is a debt of ₹100.
Example 6
Evaluate (−5) × (−8) − 12.
Solution. (−5) × (−8) = 40.
40 − 12 = 28.
Example 7
A diver at 12 m below the surface rises 5 m and then dives 9 m. Find the final depth.
Solution. Start: −12.
After rising 5 m: −12 + 5 = −7.
After diving 9 m: −7 − 9 = −16.
The diver is 16 m below the surface.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 36 of 215
Chapter 3: The World of Numbers 3.4 Rational Numbers and Density Ganita Manjari · Class 9
3.4

Rational Numbers and Density

Key Idea
A rational number is p / q with p , q integers and q ≠ 0 . The set is Q . Division by zero has no meaning, so q = 0 is not allowed.

Every integer is rational: n = n/1.

A rational number has many forms: −1/3 = −2/6 = −10/30. The standard form is lowest terms, with gcd(p, q) = 1.

Absolute value |x| is the distance of x from 0 on the number line. The distance between a and b is |a − b|.

Density: between any two rational numbers there is always another, namely their average. So there are infinitely many in between.

Example 8
Find three rational numbers between 1 and 3/2.
Solution. First average: m1 = (1 + 3/2)/2.
= (5/2)/2.
= 5/4.
Average of 1 and 5/4: m2 = (1 + 5/4)/2.
= (9/4)/2.
= 9/8.
Average of 5/4 and 3/2: m3 = (5/4 + 6/4)/2.
= (11/4)/2.
= 11/8.
Three rational numbers are 9/8, 5/4 and 11/8.
Example 9
Write −18/24 in lowest terms.
Solution. gcd(18, 24) = 6.
−18/24 = −(18 ÷ 6)/(24 ÷ 6).
= −3/4.
Example 10
Find the distance between −3/2 and 5/4 on the number line.
Solution. Distance = |−3/2 − 5/4|.
= |−6/4 − 5/4|.
= |−11/4|.
= 11/4.
Example 11
Find a rational number between 2/3 and 3/4.
Solution. Write with a common denominator: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12.
Average = (8/12 + 9/12)/2.
= (17/12)/2.
= 17/24.

Chapter 3: The World of Numbers 3.5 Irrational Numbers Ganita Manjari · Class 9
3.5

Irrational Numbers

Key Idea
A number that cannot be written as p / q is irrational . Around 800 BCE Baudhāyana met one: the diagonal of a unit square, d 2 = 1 2 + 1 2 = 2 , so d = √2 .

Proof by contradiction: assume the opposite, reach an impossible conclusion, and so reject the assumption.

Āryabhaṭa (499 CE) gave the approximation π ≈ 3927/1250 = 3.1416 and called it āsanna, “approximate”.

Mādhava (14th century, Kerala) found an infinite series for π, since an irrational number needs an unending process:

Example 12
Prove that √2 is irrational.
Solution. Assume √2 is rational.
Then √2 = p/q with p, q integers, q ≠ 0, and gcd(p, q) = 1.
Squaring: 2 = p2/q2.
So p2 = 2q2.
Hence p2 is even, so p is even.
Let p = 2k.
Then (2k)2 = 2q2.
4k2 = 2q2.
q2 = 2k2.
Hence q2 is even, so q is even.
So p and q are both even and share the factor 2.
This contradicts gcd(p, q) = 1.
Therefore √2 is irrational.
Example 13
Show that 3 + √2 is irrational.
Solution. Assume 3 + √2 = r, where r is rational.
Then √2 = r − 3.
r − 3 is rational, being a difference of rational numbers.
So √2 is rational.
This contradicts the fact that √2 is irrational.
Therefore 3 + √2 is irrational.
Example 14
Locate √2 on the number line.
Solution. Mark O at 0 and A at 1.
At A draw AB ⊥ OA with AB = 1.
Join OB.
OB2 = 12 + 12
= 2.
So OB = √2.
With centre O and radius OB draw an arc to cut the number line at P.
P represents √2 ≈ 1.414.

Example 15
Say whether each is rational or irrational: 0.25, √16, √7, 22/7, π, 0.101001000…
Solution. 0.25 = 1/4: rational.
√16 = 4: rational.
√7: 7 is not a perfect square, so irrational.
22/7 is a fraction of integers: rational.
π: irrational.

0.101001000… never terminates and never repeats: irrational.

3.6

Real Numbers and Decimals

Key Idea
The real numbers R are the rational and irrational numbers together: they fill the whole number line.
Type Decimal form Example
Rational Terminating or repeating block 3/8 = 0.375; 1/7 =
Irrational Non-terminating and non-repeating √2 = 1.41421356…; π = 3.14159265…

Terminating test: write p/q in lowest terms. The decimal terminates exactly when q = 2m × 5n (no other prime factors).

Cyclic number: 1/7 = . Multiplying 142857 by 1 to 6 only rotates its digits, for example 142857 × 2 = 285714.

Repeating to fraction: let x be the decimal; multiply by 10k where k is the number of repeating digits; subtract to remove the repeating part.

Example 16
Without dividing, say whether 7/20 and 5/12 have terminating decimals.
Solution. 7/20 is in lowest terms and 20 = 22 × 5.
Only 2 and 5 occur, so 7/20 terminates.
7/20 = 35/100.
= 0.35.
5/12 is in lowest terms and 12 = 22 × 3.
The prime factor 3 occurs, so 5/12 does not terminate: it repeats.

Solution. Let x = 0.6666….
Then 10x = 6.6666….
Subtract: 10x − x = 6.6666… − 0.6666….
9x = 6.
x = 6/9.
x = 2/3.

Solution. Let x = 0.1666….
10x = 1.6666….
100x = 16.6666….
Subtract: 100x − 10x = 16.6666… − 1.6666….
90x = 15.
x = 15/90.
x = 1/6.

Chapter 4: Algebraic Identities 4.1 Identities and Equations Ganita Manjari · Class 9
4.1

Identities and Equations

Key Idea
An algebraic identity is an equality that is true for every value of its variables. An equation is true only for particular values of the variable.

Equation: x2 − 1 = 24 holds only for x = 5 and x = −5.

Identity: (a + b)2 = a2 + 2ab + b2 holds for all values of a and b: positive, negative, zero or rational.

Identities can be read both ways: expand when you multiply, factorise when you reverse.

Example 1
Take the consecutive squares 16, 25, 36. Add the smallest and largest and subtract twice the middle one.
Solution. Smallest + largest = 16 + 36 = 52.
Twice the middle = 2 × 25 = 50.
Result = 52 − 50 = 2.
The same happens for 1, 4, 9 and for 9, 16, 25.
We prove it for all cases in Section 4.3.
Example 2
Is x2 − 1 = 24 an identity?
Solution. Solve: x2 = 25.
So x = 5 or x = −5.
Try x = 0: LHS = −1 ≠ 24.
It fails for most values, so it is an equation, not an identity.

4.2

The Square of a Sum

Key Idea
( a + b ) 2 = a 2 + 2 a b + b 2

Area of the big square = (a + b)2.

The same area = a2 + ab + ab + b2 = a2 + 2ab + b2.

Mental squares: split a number into a round number and a small one.

Example 3
Expand (5x + 2y)2.
Solution. Take a = 5x and b = 2y.
a2 = (5x)2
= 25x2.
2ab = 2(5x)(2y)
= 20xy.
b2 = (2y)2
= 4y2.
(5x + 2y)2 = 25x2 + 20xy + 4y2.
Example 4
Find 432 using an identity.
Solution. Write 43 = 40 + 3.
432 = (40 + 3)2.
= 402 + 2(40)(3) + 32.
= 1600 + 240 + 9.
= 1849.
Example 5
Find 1022.
Solution. 102 = 100 + 2.
1022 = 1002 + 2(100)(2) + 22.
= 10000 + 400 + 4.
= 10404.

4.3

The Square of a Difference and Factorisation

Key Idea
( a − b ) 2 = a 2 − 2 a b + b 2 Read backwards, a 2 ± 2 a b + b 2 factorises as ( a ± b ) 2 .

To factorise a trinomial, first take out any common factor.

Then check whether two terms are perfect squares and the middle term is twice the product of their roots.

Example 6
Expand (3p − 4q)2.
Solution. Take a = 3p and b = 4q.
a2 = 9p2.
2ab = 2(3p)(4q)
= 24pq.
b2 = 16q2.
(3p − 4q)2 = 9p2 − 24pq + 16q2.
Example 7
Find 972.
Solution. 97 = 100 − 3.
972 = 1002 − 2(100)(3) + 32.
= 10000 − 600 + 9.
= 9409.
Example 8
Prove that for any three consecutive squares, (smallest + largest) − 2(middle) = 2.
Solution. Let the three integers be n − 1, n, n + 1.
(n − 1)2 = n2 − 2n + 1.
(n + 1)2 = n2 + 2n + 1.
Sum of smallest and largest = 2n2 + 2.
Twice the middle = 2n2.
Difference = (2n2 + 2) − 2n2 = 2.
This holds for every n, so the result is always 2.
Example 9
Factorise completely 50p2 + 60pq + 18q2.
Solution. Common factor 2: 50p2 + 60pq + 18q2 = 2(25p2 + 30pq + 9q2).
25p2 = (5p)2 and 9q2 = (3q)2.
30pq = 2(5p)(3q).
So 25p2 + 30pq + 9q2 = (5p + 3q)2.
Hence 50p2 + 60pq + 18q2 = 2(5p + 3q)2.
Example 10
Factorise 4x2 − 12x + 9.
Solution. 4x2 = (2x)2 and 9 = 32.
12x = 2(2x)(3).
So 4x2 − 12x + 9 = (2x − 3)2.

4.4

Three Terms and the Difference of Squares

Key Idea
( a + b + c ) 2 = a 2 + b 2 + c 2 + 2 a b + 2 b c + 2 c a ( a + b )( a − b ) = a 2 − b 2

For the first identity put d = b + c, expand (a + d)2, then expand d2.

Śhrīdharāchārya’s method (750 CE): from a2 − b2 = (a + b)(a − b) we get N2 = (N + b)(N − b) + b2. Choose b so that N + b or N − b is a round number.

Keep the sign with each term when a term is negative: (3x − 2y + 4z)2 has b = −2y.

Example 11
Expand (3x − 2y + 4z)2.
Solution. Take a = 3x, b = −2y, c = 4z.
a2 + b2 + c2 = 9x2 + 4y2 + 16z2.
2ab = 2(3x)(−2y)
= −12xy.
2bc = 2(−2y)(4z)
= −16yz.
2ca = 2(4z)(3x)
= 24zx.
Sum: 9x2 + 4y2 + 16z2 − 12xy − 16yz + 24zx.
Example 12
Calculate 552 by Śhrīdharāchārya’s method.
Solution. Choose b = 5.
552 = (55 + 5)(55 − 5) + 52.
= 60 × 50 + 25.
= 3000 + 25.
= 3025.
Example 13
Calculate 982 by the same method.
Solution. Choose b = 2.
982 = (98 + 2)(98 − 2) + 22.
= 100 × 96 + 4.
= 9604.
Example 14
Find 103 × 97.
Solution. 103 = 100 + 3 and 97 = 100 − 3.
103 × 97 = (100 + 3)(100 − 3).
= 1002 − 32.
= 10000 − 9.
= 9991.
Example 15
If a + b + c = 9 and ab + bc + ca = 26, find a2 + b2 + c2.
Solution. (a + b + c)2 = a2 + b2 + c2 + 2(ab + bc + ca).
81 = a2 + b2 + c2 + 52.
a2 + b2 + c2 = 81 − 52.
= 29.

4.5

Products of Binomials and Splitting the Middle Term

Key Idea
( x + a )( x + b ) = x 2 + ( a + b ) x + a b ( a x + b )( c x + d ) = a c x 2 + ( a d + b c ) x + b d

To factorise x2 + Bx + C, find two numbers a and b with sum B and product C.

Then split the middle term and group in pairs.

For px2 + qx + r, find two numbers whose product is pr and whose sum is q.

Signs: if C > 0 both numbers have the sign of B; if C < 0 they have opposite signs.

Example 16
Expand (x + 7)(x − 3).
Solution. Here a = 7 and b = −3.
a + b = 4.
ab = −21.
(x + 7)(x − 3) = x2 + 4x − 21.
Example 17
Factorise x2 + 7x + 12.
Solution. Need sum 7 and product 12.
The numbers are 3 and 4.
x2 + 7x + 12 = x2 + 3x + 4x + 12.
= x(x + 3) + 4(x + 3).
= (x + 3)(x + 4).
Example 18
Factorise x2 − 5x + 6.
Solution. Need sum −5 and product 6.
Both numbers are negative: −2 and −3.
x2 − 5x + 6 = x2 − 2x − 3x + 6.
= x(x − 2) − 3(x − 2).
= (x − 2)(x − 3).
Example 19
Factorise x2 + 2x − 15.
Solution. Need sum 2 and product −15.
The numbers are 5 and −3.
x2 + 2x − 15 = x2 + 5x − 3x − 15.
= x(x + 5) − 3(x + 5).
= (x + 5)(x − 3).
Example 20
Factorise 6x2 + 11x + 3.
Solution. pr = 6 × 3
= 18 and the sum must be 11.
The numbers are 9 and 2.
6x2 + 11x + 3 = 6x2 + 9x + 2x + 3.
= 3x(2x + 3) + 1(2x + 3).
= (2x + 3)(3x + 1).

Chapter 4: Algebraic Identities 4.7 Cubic Identities Ganita Manjari · Class 9
4.7

Cubic Identities

Key Idea
( a + b ) 3 = a 3 + 3 a 2 b + 3 a b 2 + b 3 = a 3 + b 3 + 3 a b ( a + b ) ( a − b ) 3 = a 3 − 3 a 2 b + 3 a b 2 − b 3 = a 3 − b 3 − 3 a b ( a − b ) x 3 + y 3 = ( x + y )( x 2 − x y + y 2 ) x 3 − y 3 = ( x − y )( x 2 + x y + y 2 ) x 3 + y 3 + z 3 − 3 x y z = ( x + y + z )( x 2 + y 2 + z 2 − x y − y z − z x )

A cube of edge a + b splits into cubes a3 and b3 and six cuboids: three of a2b and three of ab2.

In x2 − xy + y2 and x2 + xy + y2 the middle sign is opposite to the sign in the bracket on the left for the sum of cubes, and the same for the difference of cubes.

If x + y + z = 0, then x3 + y3 + z3 = 3xyz.

Example 21
Expand (2x + 3)3.
Solution. Take a = 2x and b = 3.
a3 = 8x3.
3a2b = 3(4x2)(3)
= 36x2.
3ab2 = 3(2x)(9)
= 54x.
b3 = 27.
(2x + 3)3 = 8x3 + 36x2 + 54x + 27.
Example 22
Expand (3y − 2)3.
Solution. Take a = 3y and b = 2.
a3 = 27y3.
3a2b = 3(9y2)(2)
= 54y2.
3ab2 = 3(3y)(4)
= 36y.
b3 = 8.
(3y − 2)3 = 27y3 − 54y2 + 36y − 8.
Example 23
Find 1013.
Solution. 101 = 100 + 1.
1013 = 1003 + 3(100)2(1) + 3(100)(1)2 + 13.
= 1000000 + 30000 + 300 + 1.
= 1030301.
Example 24
Factorise 27x3 + 8.
Solution. 27x3 = (3x)3 and 8 = 23.
Use a3 + b3 = (a + b)(a2 − ab + b2) with a = 3x, b = 2.
= (3x + 2)((3x)2 − (3x)(2) + 22).
= (3x + 2)(9x2 − 6x + 4).
Example 25
Factorise x3 − 64.
Solution. 64 = 43.
Use a3 − b3 = (a − b)(a2 + ab + b2) with a = x, b = 4.
= (x − 4)(x2 + 4x + 16).
Example 26
If x + y = 7 and xy = 10, find x3 + y3.
Solution. x3 + y3 = (x + y)3 − 3xy(x + y).
= 73 − 3(10)(7).
= 343 − 210.
= 133.

Chapter 4: Algebraic Identities 4.8 Simplifying Expressions and Word Problems Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 27
Given x + y + z = 10, xyz = 25 and x2 + y2 + z2 = 38, find x3 + y3 + z3.
Solution. (x + y + z)2 = x2 + y2 + z2 + 2(xy + yz + zx).
100 = 38 + 2(xy + yz + zx).
xy + yz + zx = 31.
Master identity: x3 + y3 + z3 − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x2 + y2 + z2 − xy − yz − zx).
x3 + y3 + z3 − 75 = 10(38 − 31).
x3 + y3 + z3 − 75 = 70.
x3 + y3 + z3 = 145.
4.8

Simplifying Expressions and Word Problems

Key Idea
To simplify a rational expression, factorise numerator and denominator, then cancel non-zero common factors. State the values excluded because they make the denominator 0. In word problems form an equation, factorise to solve it, and reject answers that do not make sense (for example a negative length).
Example 28
Simplify (x2 − 9)/(x2 + x − 6).
Solution. Numerator: x2 − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3).
Denominator: x2 + x − 6 = (x + 3)(x − 2).
(x2 − 9)/(x2 + x − 6) = (x − 3)(x + 3)/((x + 3)(x − 2)).
Cancel the common factor x + 3.
= (x − 3)/(x − 2), for x ≠ −3 and x ≠ 2.
Example 29
A rectangular pool has breadth 4 m less than its length and area 96 m². Find its dimensions.
Solution. Let length = x m.
Then breadth = (x − 4) m.
Area: x(x − 4) = 96.
x2 − 4x − 96 = 0.
Need sum −4 and product −96: the numbers are −12 and 8.
x2 − 12x + 8x − 96 = 0.
x(x − 12) + 8(x − 12) = 0.
(x − 12)(x + 8) = 0.
So x = 12 or x = −8.
Length cannot be negative, so x = 12.
Length = 12 m and breadth = 8 m.
Example 30
The sum of the squares of two consecutive positive integers is 61. Find them.
Solution. Let the integers be n and n + 1.
n2 + (n + 1)2 = 61.
2n2 + 2n + 1 = 61.
n2 + n − 30 = 0.
Need sum 1 and product −30: the numbers are 6 and −5.
n2 + 6n − 5n − 30 = 0.
n(n + 6) − 5(n + 6) = 0.
(n + 6)(n − 5) = 0.
Since n > 0, n = 5.
The integers are 5 and 6.

Chapter 5: Circles Overview & Key Ideas Ganita Manjari · Class 9
CHAPTER 5
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

Circles

The chapter at a glance

Idea Statement
Circle, locus All points at a fixed distance r from the centre. A locus is the set of points satisfying a condition.
Chord, diameter Chord joins two points of the circle. Diameter = 2 r is the longest chord.
Symmetry Rotation by any angle about the centre; reflection in every diameter.
Equidistant from A , B The perpendicular bisector of A B .
Circles through points 1 or 2 points: infinitely many. 3 collinear: none. 3 non-collinear: exactly one (circumcircle).
Circumcentre Meets the perpendicular bisectors. Acute: inside. Right: midpoint of hypotenuse. Obtuse: outside.
Equal chords Equal chords ⇔ equal angles at the centre ⇔ equal distances from the centre.
Perpendicular to a chord The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. L = 2√( r 2 − d 2 ) .
Longer chord Longer chord is closer to the centre. Diameter: d = 0 .
Inscribed angle Angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference on the same arc.
Same segment, semicircle Angles in the same segment are equal. Angle in a semicircle = 90° .
Cyclic quadrilateral Opposite angles sum to 180° (and the converse). Exterior angle = interior opposite angle.
Brahmagupta’s formula Area of a cyclic quadrilateral = √(( s − a )( s − b )( s − c )( s − d )) , s = semi-perimeter.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 60 of 215
Chapter 5: Circles 5.1 The Circle and Locus Ganita Manjari · Class 9
5.1

The Circle and Locus

Key Idea
A circle is the set of all points in a plane at the same distance from a fixed point, the centre . That constant distance is the radius r . A set of points satisfying a condition is a locus . So a circle is the locus of points at distance r from the centre.

A chord joins two points of the circle. A chord through the centre is a diameter: d = 2r, the longest chord.

An arc is a connected part of the circle. A diameter cuts the circle into two semicircles.

All radii of a circle are equal. This is used in almost every proof.

Example 1
A circle has radius 7.5 cm. Find its diameter and the length of its longest chord.
Solution. Diameter = 2r.
= 2 × 7.5.
= 15 cm.
The longest chord is a diameter.
So the longest chord is 15 cm.
Example 2
A point moves so that it is always 4 cm from a fixed point O. What is its locus? What if it must be at most 4 cm from O?
Solution. Points at a fixed distance 4 cm from O form a circle with centre O and radius 4 cm.
Points at most 4 cm from O fill that circle and its inside.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 61 of 215
Chapter 5: Circles 5.2 Symmetries of a Circle Ganita Manjari · Class 9
5.2

Symmetries of a Circle

Key Idea
A circle looks the same after rotation about its centre by any angle , and after reflection in any diameter . The locus of points equidistant from two points A and B is the perpendicular bisector of A B .

So a circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry: every diameter.

A circle is determined by its centre and radius.

Example 3
How many lines of symmetry does a circle have?
Solution. Fold the circle along any diameter.
The two halves coincide.
There are infinitely many diameters.
So a circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry.
Example 4
Points A and B are 6 cm apart. Describe the locus of points equidistant from them.
Solution. The locus is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
It passes through the midpoint M of AB.
AM = MB
= 3 cm.
Every point of the locus is at equal distances from A and B.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 62 of 215
Chapter 5: Circles 5.3 Circles Through Given Points Ganita Manjari · Class 9
5.3

Circles Through Given Points

Key Idea
Theorem 1. Exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points A , B , C . It is the circumcircle of triangle A B C . Its centre is the circumcentre , where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet.

Through 1 point: infinitely many circles. Through 2 points A, B: infinitely many; their centres lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.

The smallest circle through A and B has AB as diameter: radius = AB/2.

Through 3 collinear points: no circle, since the perpendicular bisectors are parallel and never meet.

Right triangle: circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so circumradius = hypotenuse / 2.

Example 5
Two points are 14 cm apart. Find the least possible radius of a circle through both.
Solution. The smallest such circle has the segment as diameter.
rmin = 14/2.
= 7 cm.
Example 6
A right triangle has sides 9 cm, 12 cm and 15 cm. Find its circumradius.
Solution. 92 + 122 = 81 + 144
= 225
= 152, so it is a right triangle.
The hypotenuse is 15 cm.
The circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.
Circumradius = 15/2.
= 7.5 cm.
Example 7
Can a circle pass through A(0, 0), B(2, 0) and C(4, 0)?
Solution. All three points lie on the x-axis, so they are collinear.
Three collinear points lie on no circle.
So no such circle exists.
Example 8
A triangle has angles 40°, 100° and 40°. Where does its circumcentre lie?
Solution. One angle is 100°, which is obtuse.
The triangle is obtuse-angled.
So the circumcentre lies outside the triangle.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 63 of 215
Chapter 5: Circles 5.4 Chords and the Angles They Subtend Ganita Manjari · Class 9
5.4

Chords and the Angles They Subtend

Key Idea
Theorem 2. Equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre. Theorem 3. Chords that subtend equal angles at the centre are equal.

Proof of Theorem 2 uses SSS congruence; proof of Theorem 3 uses SAS congruence.

A longer chord subtends a larger angle at the centre.

Example 9
Prove Theorem 2: equal chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O subtend equal angles at O.
Solution. Join OA, OB, OC, OD.
In Δ OAB and Δ OCD: OA = OC (radii).
OB = OD (radii).
AB = CD (given).
So Δ OAB ≅ Δ OCD (SSS).
Hence ∠AOB = ∠COD (corresponding parts).
Example 10
Prove Theorem 3: if ∠AOB = ∠COD then AB = CD.
Solution. In Δ OAB and Δ OCD: OA = OC (radii).
∠AOB = ∠COD (given).
OB = OD (radii).
So Δ OAB ≅ Δ OCD (SAS).
Hence AB = CD.
Example 11
Chords AB and CD of a circle are equal and ∠AOB = 64°. Find ∠COD.
Solution. Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre.
∠COD = ∠AOB.
= 64°.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 64 of 215
Chapter 5: Circles 5.5 Perpendiculars from the Centre and Distances of Chords Ganita Manjari · Class 9
5.5

Perpendiculars from the Centre and Distances of Chords

Key Idea
Theorem 5. The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord. (Converse: the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it.) For a chord of length L at distance d from the centre: r 2 = d 2 + ( L /2) 2 , so L = 2√( r 2 − d 2 ) .
Key Idea
Theorems 6 and 7. Equal chords are equally far from the centre, and chords equally far from the centre are equal. Theorem 8. A longer chord is closer to the centre. The diameter is longest, with d = 0 .
Example 12
Prove Theorem 5: if OM ⊥ AB then AM = MB.
Solution. Join OA and OB.
In right triangles OMA and OMB: OA = OB (radii), the hypotenuses.
OM = OM (common).
∠OMA = ∠OMB
= 90°.
So Δ OMA ≅ Δ OMB (RHS).
Hence AM = MB.
Example 13
A chord is 6 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 10 cm. Find its length.
Solution. L = 2√(r2 − d2).
= 2√(102 − 62).
= 2√(100 − 36).
= 2√64.
= 2 × 8.
= 16 cm.
Example 14
A circle of radius 5 cm has parallel chords of lengths 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the distance between them if they are on opposite sides of the centre, and if they are on the same side.
Solution. Chord of 6 cm: half-length 3, so d1 = √(52 − 32) = √16 = 4 cm.
Chord of 8 cm: half-length 4, so d2 = √(52 − 42) = √9 = 3 cm.
Opposite sides: distance = d1 + d2 = 4 + 3 = 7 cm.
Same side: distance = d1 − d2 = 4 − 3 = 1 cm.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 65 of 215
Chapter 5: Circles 5.7 Angles Subtended by an Arc Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 15
In a circle of radius 10 cm, which is closer to the centre: a chord of 12 cm or a chord of 16 cm?
Solution. For 12 cm: d = √(102 − 62) = √64 = 8 cm.
For 16 cm: d = √(102 − 82) = √36 = 6 cm.
6 < 8, so the 16 cm chord is closer.
The longer chord is closer to the centre.
5.7

Angles Subtended by an Arc

Key Idea
Theorem 9 (inscribed angle). The angle at the centre is twice the angle at any point of the remaining circumference: ∠ A O B = 2∠ A P B . Corollaries. Angles in the same segment are equal. The angle in a semicircle is 90° .

Angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal, wherever the point is on the major arc.

A diameter subtends 90° at every other point of the circle, because the central angle is 180°.

The angle on the minor arc side of the chord is 180° minus the angle on the major arc side.

Example 16
An arc subtends 110° at the centre. Find the angle it subtends at a point on the remaining circumference.
Solution. Angle at the circumference = ½ × angle at the centre.
= ½ × 110°.
= 55°.
Example 17
∠APB = 40° for a point P on a circle. Find ∠AQB for another point Q on the same arc side of AB.
Solution. P and Q lie in the same segment.
Angles in the same segment are equal.
∠AQB = ∠APB
= 40°.
Example 18
AB is a diameter and C is a point on the circle with ∠CAB = 35°. Find ∠ACB and ∠ABC.
Solution. Angle in a semicircle: ∠ACB = 90°.
In Δ ABC: ∠ABC = 180° − 90° − 35°.
= 55°.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 66 of 215
Chapter 5: Circles 5.8 Cyclic Quadrilaterals Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 19
An arc subtends 140° at the centre. Find the angle it subtends at a point on the major arc and at a point on the minor arc.
Solution. Point on the major arc: ½ × 140° = 70°.
The point on the minor arc and the point on the major arc are opposite vertices of a cyclic quadrilateral.
Angle at the minor arc = 180° − 70°.
= 110°.
5.8

Cyclic Quadrilaterals

Key Idea
Points on one circle are concyclic . A quadrilateral with all four vertices on a circle is cyclic . Theorem 11. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180° . Converse: if opposite angles sum to 180° , the quadrilateral is cyclic. Exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral = interior opposite angle.

Exterior angle at D is ∠CDE: it equals the interior opposite angle ∠ABC.

The only parallelogram that can be cyclic is a rectangle.

Brahmagupta’s formula: for a cyclic quadrilateral with sides a, b, c, d and semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c + d)/2, area = √((s − a)(s − b)(s − c)(s − d)).

Example 20
PQRS is cyclic with ∠P = (3x + 5)° and ∠R = (5x − 25)°. Find x, ∠P and ∠R.
Solution. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.
(3x + 5) + (5x − 25) = 180.
8x − 20 = 180.
8x = 200.
x = 25.
∠P = 3(25) + 5
= 80°.
∠R = 5(25) − 25
= 100°.
Check: 80° + 100° = 180°.
Example 21
ABCD is cyclic with ∠BAD = 85°. Side BC is extended to E. Find ∠DCE.
Solution. ∠DCE is the exterior angle at C.
Exterior angle = interior opposite angle.
∠DCE = ∠BAD.
= 85°.
Example 22
A quadrilateral ABCD has ∠A = 100°, ∠B = 110°, ∠C = 80°, ∠D = 70°. Is it cyclic?
Solution. ∠A + ∠C = 100° + 80°
= 180°.
∠B + ∠D = 110° + 70°
= 180°.
Both pairs of opposite angles are supplementary.
By the converse theorem, ABCD is cyclic.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 67 of 215
Chapter 5: Circles Chapter Theory Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 23
Find the area of a cyclic quadrilateral with sides 3, 3, 4, 4.
Solution. s = (3 + 3 + 4 + 4)/2
= 7.
s − 3 = 4 and s − 4 = 3.
Area = √((7 − 3)(7 − 3)(7 − 4)(7 − 4)).
= √(4 × 4 × 3 × 3).
= 4 × 3.
= 12 square units.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 68 of 215

Chapter 5 Solutions · Question 7 – Question 12
Question 5.7
Half the chord = 8 cm.
r2 = 62 + 82.
= 36 + 64.

r = 10 cm.
Question 5.8
Let AB be a chord, M its midpoint, and O the centre.
Join OA and OB.
In Δ OMA and Δ OMB: OA = OB (radii).
AM = BM (M is the midpoint).
OM = OM (common).
So Δ OMA ≅ Δ OMB (SSS).
∠OMA = ∠OMB.
They form a linear pair, so ∠OMA + ∠OMB = 180°.
Each angle is 90°, so OM ⊥ AB.
OM is perpendicular to AB at its midpoint, so it lies along the perpendicular bisector.
Hence the perpendicular bisector passes through O.
Question 5.9

x = 38.

Question 5.10
s = (5 + 5 + 12 + 12)/2
= 17.

= √(12 × 12 × 5 × 5).

Question 5.11
Let O be the centre.
Draw OM ⊥ AB and ON ⊥ CD.
Equal chords are equally far from the centre, so OM = ON.
In right triangles OMP and ONP: OP = OP (common).
OM = ON.
So Δ OMP ≅ Δ ONP (RHS) and MP = NP.
AM = CN (half of equal chords).
AP = AM + MP
= CN + NP
= CP.
BM = DN (half of equal chords).
BP = BM − MP
= DN − NP
= DP.
Question 5.12
Let ABCD be a parallelogram inscribed in a circle.
It is cyclic, so ∠A + ∠C = 180°.
Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so ∠A = ∠C.
2∠A = 180°.
∠A = 90°.
A parallelogram with one right angle is a rectangle.

∠ABC = 90°.
The chord AC subtends 90° at B on the circle.
A chord that subtends 90° at the circumference is a diameter.
So AC is a diameter.
In the same way BD is a diameter.
Diameters pass through the centre.
So the intersection point of AC and BD is the centre.

So Δ OAB ≅ Δ OAC (SSS).

r2 = x2 + 122.

Equal chords are at equal distances from the centre.

The vertices M, N, O, P lie in this order round the circle.

Let AB be a chord and O the centre.
Join OA and OB.

= 2r.

Let CD be any chord through A and OM ⊥ CD.

Chord length = 2√(r2 − OM2).

Join OA.
OA = OB
= OC (radii).
In Δ OAB: ∠OAB = ∠OBA = a (equal sides).
In Δ OAC: ∠OAC = ∠OCA = b.
∠BAC = a + b.

a + b + (a + b) = 180°.
2(a + b) = 180°.
∠BAC = a + b

Question 5.23
A diameter perpendicular to a chord bisects it.
So AB is the perpendicular bisector of CC′ and of DD′.
C′ is the reflection of C in AB, and D′ is the reflection of D in AB.
Reflection keeps midpoints.
So M′ is the reflection of M in AB.
The line joining a point to its reflection is perpendicular to the mirror line.
Hence MM′ ⊥ AB.
Question 5.24
OA = OB
= OC
= OD (radii), so four isosceles triangles are formed.
Let the base angles be: ∠OAB = ∠OBA = q, ∠OBC = ∠OCB = u, ∠OCD = ∠ODC = v, ∠ODA = ∠OAD = p.
∠A = p + q and ∠C = u + v.
∠B = q + u and ∠D = v + p.
Sum of angles of ABCD is 360°.
(p + q) + (q + u) + (u + v) + (v + p) = 360°.
2(p + q + u + v) = 360°.
p + q + u + v = 180°.
∠A + ∠C = (p + q) + (u + v)
= 180°.

CHAPTER 6
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

Measuring Space: Perimeter and Area

The formulas at a glance

Idea Formula
Perimeter Square 4 a . Rectangle 2( a + b ) . Equilateral triangle 3 a .
Circumference C = π d = 2π r . Use π ≈ 22/7 or 3.14 . π is irrational.
Arc length 2π r × θ/360° .
Lane stagger 2π w for lane width w over one full lap.

Brahmagupta’s formula Cyclic quadrilateral: √(( s − a )( s − b )( s − c )( s − d )) , s = semi-perimeter.
Circle, sector Circle π r 2 . Sector π r 2 × θ/360° .
Scaling Lengths × k gives areas × k 2 .
Baudhāyana a b = (( a + b )/2) 2 − (( a − b )/2) 2 .

Chapter 6: Measuring Space 6.1 Perimeter and the 400 m Track Ganita Manjari · Class 9
6.1

Perimeter and the 400 m Track

Key Idea
Perimeter is the total length of the boundary of a plane figure. Square of side a : 4 a . Rectangle a × b : 2( a + b ) . Equilateral triangle of side a : 3 a .

In a relay race the outer lanes start ahead of the inner lanes because the outer bends are longer. The gap between starting points is the stagger.

A 400 m track is two equal straight stretches and two semicircular bends that together make one full circle.

Example 1
A rectangular garden is 18 m long and 12 m broad. How much fencing is needed to go round it?
Solution. Fencing = perimeter.
= 2(18 + 12).
= 2 × 30.
= 60 m.
Example 2
The perimeter of a rectangle is 36 cm and its length is 2 cm more than its breadth. Find its sides.
Solution. Let the breadth be b cm.
Then the length is (b + 2) cm.
2(b + b + 2) = 36.
2b + 2 = 18.
b = 8.
Length = 8 + 2 = 10.
The sides are 10 cm and 8 cm.
Example 3
The two straight stretches of a 400 m track are 84.39 m each. Find the length of the two bends together and the radius of each bend (take π = 3.1416).
Solution. Length of the bends = 400 − 2 × 84.39.
= 400 − 168.78.
= 231.22 m.
The two semicircular bends make one circle, so 2πr = 231.22.
r = 231.22/(2 × 3.1416).
≈ 36.8 m.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 77 of 215
Chapter 6: Measuring Space 6.2 Circumference and the Story of π Ganita Manjari · Class 9
6.2

Circumference and the Story of π

Key Idea
For every circle, circumference ÷ diameter is the same number π . C = π d = 2π r
Who and when What they found
Mesopotamia, c. 1900 BCE Circle is longer than the inscribed hexagon; π ≈ 3 1/8 = 3.125 .
Archimedes, 250 BCE Trapped π between 96-sided polygons: 3 10/71 < π < 3 1/7 (3.1408 to 3.1428).
Liu Hui (263 CE), Zu Chongzhi (480 CE) Used polygons of 24,576 sides; π ≈ 355/113 = 3.1415929 , the best ratio known for about 800 years.
Āryabhaṭa, 499 CE π ≈ 62832/20000 = 3.1416 , called āsanna (approximate).
Brahmagupta, 628 CE π ≈ √10 ≈ 3.1623 .
Mādhava, c. 1400 CE First exact infinite series for π , giving π correct to 11 decimal places.
Lambert, 1761 Proved that π is irrational.

22/7 is only a good approximation (3.142857…); π itself never terminates or repeats.

Use π = 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7, and 3.14 otherwise, unless the question says what to use.

Example 4
Find the circumference of a circle of radius 21 cm (use π = 22/7).
Solution. C = 2πr.
= 2 × 22/7 × 21.
= 2 × 22 × 3.
= 132 cm.
Example 5
A wheel has diameter 70 cm. How many complete turns does it make in a distance of 1.1 km?
Solution. Circumference = πd.
= 22/7 × 70.
= 220 cm.
Distance = 1.1 km = 110000 cm.
Number of turns = 110000/220.
= 500.

Chapter 6: Measuring Space 6.4 Arc Length and Lane Staggers Ganita Manjari · Class 9
6.4

Arc Length and Lane Staggers

Key Idea
An arc subtending θ° at the centre is the fraction θ/360 of the circle, by rotational symmetry. Arc length = 2π r × θ/360

Lane stagger. On a track with lane width w, the outer runner’s bends have radius r + w. Over one lap the extra distance is 2π(r + w) − 2πr = 2πw.

The stagger depends only on the lane width, not on the size of the track.

Example 6
Find the length of an arc of 60° in a circle of radius 21 cm (use π = 22/7).
Solution. Arc length = 2πr × θ/360.
= 2 × 22/7 × 21 × 60/360.
= 132 × 1/6.
= 22 cm.
Example 7
On a 400 m track the lane width is 1.22 m. Find the stagger between Lane 1 and Lane 2, and between Lane 1 and Lane 4 (take π = 3.1416).
Solution. Both runners have the same straight stretches.
Lane 1 to Lane 2: stagger = 2πw.
= 2 × 3.1416 × 1.22.
≈ 7.66 m.
Lane 1 to Lane 4 is 3 lane widths: stagger = 2π(3w).
= 3 × 7.66.
≈ 22.99 m.
Example 8
An arc of length 11 cm lies on a circle of radius 7 cm. Find the angle it subtends at the centre (use π = 22/7).
Solution. Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 cm.
The arc is 11/44 = 1/4 of the circle.
θ = 1/4 × 360°.
= 90°.

Chapter 6: Measuring Space 6.5 The Semicircle Path Paradox Ganita Manjari · Class 9
6.5

The Semicircle Path Paradox

Key Idea
If P Q is divided into parts and a semicircle is drawn on each part as diameter, the total length of the small semicircles equals the length of the large semicircle on P Q .
Example 9
Prove that the arc a on PQ has the same length as the arcs b, c, d together.
Solution. Let the radii of a, b, c, d be ra, rb, rc, rd.
Length of arc a = πra.
Total length of the small arcs = πrb + πrc + πrd.
= π(rb + rc + rd).
The diameters add up to PQ: 2ra = 2rb + 2rc + 2rd.
So ra = rb + rc + rd.
Hence πra = π(rb + rc + rd).
The two paths have equal length.
Example 10
PQ = 14 cm is cut into 6 cm and 8 cm. Check the result with numbers (use π = 22/7).
Solution. Large semicircle: radius 7, length = 22/7 × 7 = 22 cm.
Small semicircle on 6 cm: radius 3, length = 22/7 × 3.
Small semicircle on 8 cm: radius 4, length = 22/7 × 4.
Sum = 22/7 × (3 + 4).
= 22 cm.
Both paths are 22 cm long.

Chapter 6: Measuring Space 6.6 Area of a Parallelogram, Triangle and Other Figures Ganita Manjari · Class 9
6.6

Area of a Parallelogram, Triangle and Other Figures

Key Idea
Parallelogram = b h . Triangle = ½ b h . Median theorem. A median of a triangle divides it into two triangles of equal area. Trapezium = ½( a + b ) h . Kite or rhombus = ½ d 1 d 2 .

A trapezium is half of a parallelogram of base a + b and height h made from two copies of itself.

Diagonals of a kite or rhombus are perpendicular; the area is half the product of the diagonals.

If every length is multiplied by k, the area is multiplied by k2.

Example 11
Find the area of a parallelogram with base 12 cm and height 7 cm, and of a triangle with base 15 cm and height 8 cm.
Solution. Parallelogram: bh = 12 × 7.
= 84 cm².
Triangle: ½bh = ½ × 15 × 8.
= 60 cm².
Example 12
A triangle has area 90 cm² and base 15 cm. Find its height.
Solution. ½ × 15 × h = 90.
15h = 180.
h = 12 cm.
Example 13
The area of triangle ABC is 48 cm² and D is the midpoint of BC. Find the area of triangle ABD.
Solution. AD is a median.
A median divides the triangle into two triangles of equal area.
Area of ABD = 48/2.
= 24 cm².

Chapter 6: Measuring Space 6.8.1 Heron’s and Brahmagupta’s Formulas Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 14
Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 9 cm and 15 cm and height 6 cm.
Solution. Area = ½(a + b)h.
= ½ × (9 + 15) × 6.
= ½ × 24 × 6.
= 72 cm².
Example 15
A rhombus has diagonals 12 cm and 16 cm. Find its area and its perimeter.
Solution. Area = ½d1d2.
= ½ × 12 × 16.
= 96 cm².
The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so half-diagonals are 6 and 8.
Side = √(62 + 82).
= √100.
= 10 cm.
Perimeter = 4 × 10 = 40 cm.
6.8.1

Heron’s and Brahmagupta’s Formulas

Key Idea
Heron’s formula. Triangle with sides a , b , c and s = ( a + b + c )/2 : area = √( s ( s − a )( s − b )( s − c )) . Brahmagupta’s formula (628 CE). Cyclic quadrilateral with sides a , b , c , d and s = ( a + b + c + d )/2 : area = √(( s − a )( s − b )( s − c )( s − d )) .

Use Heron’s formula when the height is not given.

If the fourth side shrinks to d = 0, Brahmagupta’s formula becomes Heron’s formula, so Heron’s formula is a special case.

To find a height, equate Heron’s area with ½ × base × height.

Example 16
Find the area of a triangle with sides 9 cm, 10 cm and 17 cm.
Solution. s = (9 + 10 + 17)/2.
= 18 cm.
s − a = 9
s − b = 8
s − c = 1.
Area = √(18 × 9 × 8 × 1).
= √1296.
= 36 cm².
Example 17
Find the area of an equilateral triangle of side 8 cm.
Solution. s = 24/2
= 12.
s − a = s − b
= s − c
= 4.
Area = √(12 × 4 × 4 × 4).
= √768.
= 16√3.
≈ 27.71 cm².
Example 18
A triangle has sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. Find its area and the height on the side of 14 cm.
Solution. s = 42/2
= 21.
Area = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6).
= √7056.
= 84 cm².
½ × 14 × h = 84.
7h = 84.
h = 12 cm.

Chapter 6: Measuring Space 6.9 Baudhāyana’s Squaring of a Rectangle Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 19
Find the area of a cyclic quadrilateral with sides 6, 6, 8, 8 cm.
Solution. s = (6 + 6 + 8 + 8)/2
= 14.
s − 6 = 8 and s − 8 = 6.
Area = √(8 × 8 × 6 × 6).
= 8 × 6.
= 48 cm².
6.9

Baudhāyana’s Squaring of a Rectangle

Key Idea
Baudhāyana (c. 800 BCE) built a square equal in area to a given a × b rectangle. a b = (( a + b )/2) 2 − (( a − b )/2) 2

Take a right triangle with hypotenuse (a + b)/2 and one leg (a − b)/2.

By the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem its other leg is √(ab), the side of the required square.

Example 20
Find the side of the square equal in area to a rectangle 9 m by 4 m, using Baudhāyana’s method.
Solution. (a + b)/2 = (9 + 4)/2
= 6.5.
(a − b)/2 = (9 − 4)/2
= 2.5.
Other leg2 = 6.52 − 2.52.
= 42.25 − 6.25.
= 36.
Other leg = 6 m.
Check: area of rectangle = 9 × 4 = 36 = 62.

Chapter 6: Measuring Space 6.10 Area of a Circle and of a Sector Ganita Manjari · Class 9
6.10

Area of a Circle and of a Sector

Key Idea
Area of a circle = π r 2 . Area of a sector with angle θ° = π r 2 × θ/360 . Nīlakaṇṭha’s picture (1500 CE): cut the circle into thin sectors and interlock them into a parallelogram of base π r (half the circumference) and height r .
Example 21
A clock’s minute hand is 7 cm long. Find the area swept by it in 10 minutes (use π = 22/7).
Solution. In 60 minutes the hand turns 360°.
In 10 minutes it turns 10/60 × 360° = 60°.
Area = πr2 × 60/360.
= 22/7 × 49 × 1/6.
= 154/6.
≈ 25.67 cm².
Example 22
Find the area of a sector of angle 90° in a circle of radius 14 cm (use π = 22/7).
Solution. Area = πr2 × 90/360.
= 22/7 × 196 × 1/4.
= 616/4.
= 154 cm².
Example 23
A circular ring has outer radius 9 cm and inner radius 5 cm. Find its area (use π = 22/7).
Solution. Area = π(R2 − r2).
= 22/7 × (81 − 25).
= 22/7 × 56.
= 176 cm².

Let the sides be x, y and u, v.
Same perimeter: x + y = u + v.
Same area: xy = uv.
(x − y)2 = (x + y)2 − 4xy.
(u − v)2 = (u + v)2 − 4uv.
So (x − y)2 = (u − v)2 and x − y = ±(u − v).
With x + y = u + v this gives x = u, y = v or x = v, y = u.

Diagonal AC splits it into Δ ABC and Δ ACD.

= ½(a + b)h.

= ½ × BD × AO + ½ × BD × OC.
= ½ × BD × (AO + OC).
= ½ × BD × AC.
= ½d1d2.

Chapter 6: Measuring Space Stepwise Solutions (Q 6.13 – Q 6.18) Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Chapter 6 Solutions · Question 13 – Question 18
Question 6.13
Doubling both sides of a rectangle: area = 2a × 2b = 4ab.
This is 4 times ab: 4 copies fit.
Doubling the sides of a triangle multiplies its area by 22 = 4 (Heron’s formula).
Joining midpoints of the larger triangle gives 4 copies of the smaller.
Tripling the sides multiplies the area by 32 = 9.
So 9 copies of the smaller triangle fit in the larger.
Areas scale by k2 when lengths scale by k.
Question 6.14
Let the square have side D.
One circle: diameter D, area = π(D/2)2 = πD2/4.
Fraction = (πD2/4)/D2 = π/4.
Four circles: each has diameter D/2 and radius D/4.
Area of four = 4 × π(D/4)2 = πD2/4.
Fraction = π/4.
Both arrangements cover π/4 ≈ 78.5%.
Question 6.15
Let the radii be R (outer) and r (inner).
OA ⊥ BC because BC touches the inner circle at A.
A is the midpoint of BC, so AC = l/2.
In right Δ OAC: R2 = r2 + (l/2)2.
R2 − r2 = l2/4.
Area between the circles = πR2 − πr2.
= π(R2 − r2).
= πl2/4.
Question 6.16
Let the legs be a, b and the hypotenuse c, so a2 + b2 = c2.
Area(A) = ½π(a/2)2 = πa2/8.
Area(B) = ½π(b/2)2 = πb2/8.
Area(C) = ½π(c/2)2 = πc2/8.
Multiply a2 + b2 = c2 by π/8.
πa2/8 + πb2/8 = πc2/8.
Area(A) + Area(B) = Area(C).
Question 6.17
Take a square of side a.
Its area is a2.
Cut out a small square of side b from one corner: area b2.
The remaining L-shape has area a2 − b2.
Cut the L-shape along a line and rearrange the two pieces.
They form a rectangle of length a + b and width a − b.
Area of the rectangle = (a + b)(a − b).
So (a + b)(a − b) = a2 − b2.
Question 6.18
Draw a square of side a + b + c.
Its area is (a + b + c)2.
Divide each side into parts a, b, c and draw lines across.
This gives 9 pieces.
Three squares: a2, b2, c2.
Six rectangles: two each of ab, bc, ca.
Adding all pieces: a2 + b2 + c2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca.
So (a + b + c)2 = a2 + b2 + c2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca.

Chapter 6: Measuring Space Stepwise Solutions (Q 6.19 – Q 6.22) Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Chapter 6 Solutions · Question 19 – Question 22
Question 6.19
Each circle has diameter D/n.
Radius of each = D/(2n).
Area of one circle = π(D/2n)2 = πD2/(4n2).
Total area of n2 circles = n2 × πD2/(4n2).
= πD2/4.
Fraction covered = (πD2/4)/D2 = π/4.
n cancels, so the fraction is π/4 for every n.
Question 6.20
Each petal lies between two adjacent semicircles of radius 1.
Each petal is bounded by two quarter-circle arcs of radius 1.
Length of one quarter arc = ¼ × 2π × 1 = π/2.
Perimeter of one petal = 2 × π/2 = π.
Four petals: perimeter = 4π ≈ 12.57 units.
One petal = 2 × (quarter circle − right triangle).
= 2 × (π/4 − ½).
= π/2 − 1.
Area of four petals = 4 × (π/2 − 1).
= 2π − 4 ≈ 2.28 square units.
Question 6.21
The centres are r apart, so each common point makes an equilateral triangle with the centres.
Each circle’s arc inside the other subtends 120° at its centre.
Segment area = sector − triangle.
= πr2/3 − (√3/4)r2.
Common region (lens) = 2 × segment = 2πr2/3 − (√3/2)r2.
Union = 2πr2 − lens.
= 2πr2 − 2πr2/3 + (√3/2)r2.
= r2(4π/3 + √3/2).
Question 6.22
BP = PQ
= QC
= BC/3.
All three triangles have vertex A and bases on BC.
So all have the same height h, the distance from A to BC.
Area of ABP = ½ × (BC/3) × h.
Area of APQ = ½ × (BC/3) × h.
Area of AQC = ½ × (BC/3) × h.
The three areas are equal.

Chapter 7: Mathematics of Maybe Overview & Key Ideas Ganita Manjari · Class 9
CHAPTER 7
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability

The chapter at a glance

Idea Statement
Random experiment Can be repeated under identical conditions; all outcomes are known; the result of one trial cannot be predicted.
Probability scale 0 ≤ P ( E ) ≤ 1 . 0 impossible, 0.5 even chance, 1 certain.
Experimental probability Times E occurred ÷ total trials (relative frequency).
Theoretical probability n ( E )/ n ( S ) when all outcomes are equally likely.
Complement P ( n o t E ) = 1 − P ( E ) .
Sample space, event S is the set of all outcomes; an event E is a subset of S .
Counting rule m ways followed by n ways give m × n combinations.
Tree diagram Multiply along a branch. Add the branches that make the event.
With, without replacement With replacement the second stage is unchanged. Without replacement the counts, and so the probabilities, change.
Large numbers More trials bring experimental probability close to theoretical probability.
Gambler’s fallacy Past tosses do not change the next one: a fair coin has no memory.
Area probability P = favourable area ÷ total area.

Chapter 7: Mathematics of Maybe 7.1 Probability and Randomness Ganita Manjari · Class 9
7.1

Probability and Randomness

Key Idea
Probability measures the chance of an event, just as length measures distance. It measures uncertainty . A random experiment is repeated under identical conditions, all its possible outcomes are known, but the outcome of any single trial cannot be predicted.

Examples: tossing a coin, rolling a die, drawing a slip in a lucky draw.

Weather is random because thousands of small factors (humidity, wind, pressure, temperature) affect it, yet past records still let us assign useful probabilities.

Example 1
Which of these is a random experiment? (a) Tossing a coin (b) Heating water to 100 °C at sea level and noting whether it boils.
Solution. (a) Both outcomes, head and tail, are known.
The result of one toss cannot be predicted.
So (a) is a random experiment.
(b) Water always boils there, so the result can be predicted.
So (b) is not a random experiment.
7.1.2

The Probability Scale

Key Idea
For every event E : 0 ≤ P ( E ) ≤ 1 (or 0% to 100%). P = 0 impossible. P = 0.5 even chance. P = 1 certain.
Example 2
Rank on the 0 to 1 scale: (i) the next day after Sunday is Monday, (ii) snow in Mumbai in July, (iii) heads on a fair coin.
Solution. (i) This always happens: certain, P = 1.
(ii) This cannot happen in Mumbai’s July: impossible, P = 0.
(iii) Two equally likely outcomes: even chance, P = 0.5.
Example 3
A fair die is rolled once. What is P(getting 7) and P(getting a number from 1 to 6)?
Solution. A die shows only 1 to 6, so getting 7 cannot happen.
P(7) = 0.
Every roll gives a number from 1 to 6.
P(1 to 6) = 1.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 93 of 215
Chapter 7: Mathematics of Maybe 7.2.1 Experimental Probability Ganita Manjari · Class 9
7.2.1

Experimental Probability

Key Idea
Experimental probability is the relative frequency: it comes from data collected by repeated trials.

It can change when the experiment is repeated.

A sample can be used to estimate for a larger population: expected number = P × total.

Example 4
A die is rolled 50 times and shows 4 exactly 8 times. Find the experimental probability of a 4.
Solution. P(4) = times 4 occurred ÷ total rolls.
= 8/50.
= 0.16.
Example 5
A sample of 40 students is asked about favourite clubs: 11 chose Arts and 9 chose Sports. Find the probability that a sampled student prefers Arts. Estimate how many of the 800 students in the school prefer Sports.
Solution. P(Arts) = 11/40
= 0.275.
P(Sports) = 9/40.
Estimate = 9/40 × 800.
= 9 × 20.
= 180 students.
Example 6
A sample of 30 sweets has 10 red, 8 green, 7 yellow and 5 blue. Estimate the yellow sweets in a bag of 600.
Solution. P(yellow) = 7/30.
Estimate = 7/30 × 600.
= 7 × 20.
= 140 sweets.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 94 of 215
Chapter 7: Mathematics of Maybe 7.2.2 Theoretical Probability Ganita Manjari · Class 9
7.2.2

Theoretical Probability

Key Idea
This formula is valid only when all outcomes are equally likely (a fair coin, a fair die, a well-shuffled deck). Complement: P ( n o t E ) = 1 − P ( E ) .

Outcomes are not equally likely when the chances differ: a bag with 3 red and 7 blue marbles gives P(red) = 3/10 and P(blue) = 7/10.

Snakes and Ladders began in ancient India as the teaching game Jñān Chaupaḍ: ladders stood for virtues and snakes for vices, with dice deciding the moves.

Example 7
A fair die is rolled once. Find the theoretical probability of rolling a 4 and of rolling an even number.
Solution. S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, so n(S) = 6.
Rolling a 4: n(E) = 1.
P(4) = 1/6.
Even numbers: 2, 4, 6, so n(E) = 3.
P(even) = 3/6.
= 1/2.
Example 8
A bag has 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. One ball is picked at random. Find the probability that it is not red.
Solution. Total balls = 5 + 3 + 2 = 10.
P(red) = 5/10
= 1/2.
P(not red) = 1 − 1/2.
= 1/2.
Example 9
A fair die is rolled. Find the probability of getting a number greater than 4, and use it to find the probability of getting 4 or less.
Solution. Numbers greater than 4: 5 and 6, so n(E) = 2.
P(>4) = 2/6
= 1/3.
P(4 or less) = 1 − 1/3.
= 2/3.

Chapter 7: Mathematics of Maybe 7.2.3 Sampling, the Law of Large Numbers and the Gambler’s Fallacy Ganita Manjari · Class 9
7.2.3

Sampling, the Law of Large Numbers and the Gambler’s Fallacy

Key Idea
Law of large numbers. As the number of trials grows, experimental probability gets closer and closer to theoretical probability. Gambler’s fallacy. Believing that after 6 heads in a row tails is “due”. Tosses are independent, so the next toss is still P ( t a i l s ) = 1/2 .

In 10 tosses the experimental probability may be far from 0.5; in 10,000 tosses it is very close.

Surveying a whole population is impractical, so a representative sample is used to estimate.

Example 10
In a sample of 50 students, 20 prefer mangoes. The school has 1500 students. Estimate how many mangoes to order, if each prefers one.
Solution. P(mango) = 20/50
= 0.4.
Estimate = 0.4 × 1500.
= 600.
About 600 mangoes should be ordered.
Example 11
A fair coin shows heads 6 times in a row. What is the probability of tails on the 7th toss?
Solution. Each toss is independent of earlier tosses.
The coin has no memory.
So P(tails) = 1/2 on the 7th toss.

Chapter 7: Mathematics of Maybe 7.3 Sample Spaces and Events Ganita Manjari · Class 9
7.3

Sample Spaces and Events

Key Idea
The sample space S is the set of all possible outcomes; n ( S ) is its size. An event E is any set of outcomes: a subset of S . Counting rule: if one choice can be made in m ways and another in n ways, together there are m × n combinations.
Experiment Sample space S n ( S )
One coin {H, T} 2
One die {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} 6
Two coins {HH, HT, TH, TT} 4
Three coins {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT} 8
Two dice 36 ordered pairs 36
Example 12
Two coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting exactly one head.
Solution. S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}.
n(S) = 4.
E = {HT, TH}.
n(E) = 2.
P(E) = 2/4.
= 1/2.
Example 13
Three coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting exactly one head.
Solution. n(S) = 8.
E = {HTT, THT, TTH}.
n(E) = 3.
P(E) = 3/8.
Example 14
List the sample space when a die is rolled and a coin is tossed together.
Solution. Write each outcome as (die, coin).
Die 1: (1, H), (1, T).
Die 2: (2, H), (2, T).
Die 3: (3, H), (3, T).
Die 4: (4, H), (4, T).
Die 5: (5, H), (5, T).
Die 6: (6, H), (6, T).
n(S) = 6 × 2
= 12.
Example 15
A village fair sells 3 snacks (samosa, pakora, bhaji) and 2 drinks (chai, lassi). How many snack-and-drink combinations are there? Find P(samosa).
Solution. Number of combinations = 3 × 2 = 6.
Combinations with samosa: (samosa, chai) and (samosa, lassi).
n(E) = 2.
P(samosa) = 2/6.
= 1/3.
