Chapter 7: Mathematics of Maybe 7.4 Tree Diagrams Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 16
Two fair dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum is 8.
Solution. n(S) = 6 × 6
= 36.
Sum 8: (2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 3), (6, 2).
n(E) = 5.
P(sum 8) = 5/36.
7.4

Tree Diagrams

Key Idea
A tree diagram lists the outcomes of a multi-step experiment as branches. Multiply the probabilities along a branch. Add the branches that belong to the event. All branches together add to 1.

With replacement: the second stage has the same probabilities as the first.

Without replacement: the item drawn first is not returned, so the totals and counts change for the second stage.

Example 17
Basket A has 1 apple and 2 oranges; basket B has 1 banana and 1 mango. One fruit is picked from each. Find P(apple and banana).
Solution. Label the oranges O1, O2 so that all 3 fruits in A are equally likely.
S = {(A, B), (A, M), (O1, B), (O1, M), (O2, B), (O2, M)}.
n(S) = 6.
Favourable: only (A, B), so n(E) = 1.
P = 1/6.
Check with the tree: P = 1/3 × 1/2 = 1/6.
Example 18
A box has 3 red, 4 black and 2 green pens. A pen is picked, put back, and a friend picks one. Find the probability that both pens have the same colour.
Solution. 9 pens in all.
Probabilities: P(R) = 3/9, P(B) = 4/9, P(G) = 2/9.
Picks are with replacement, so the second stage is the same.
P(RR) = 3/9 × 3/9
= 9/81.
P(BB) = 4/9 × 4/9
= 16/81.
P(GG) = 2/9 × 2/9
= 4/81.
Add the three branches: 9/81 + 16/81 + 4/81.
= 29/81.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 98 of 215
Chapter 7: Mathematics of Maybe 7.5 Probability from Area Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 19
A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other without replacement. Find P(both red).
Solution. First draw: P(R) = 3/5.
One red is gone: 2 red remain among 4 balls.
Second draw: P(R) = 2/4.
P(RR) = 3/5 × 2/4.
= 6/20.
= 3/10.
7.5

Probability from Area

Key Idea
When a point lands at random on a region, geometric probability = (area of the wanted part) ÷ (area of the whole region).
Example 20
A dye is dropped at random on a rectangle 4 m by 3 m. What is the probability that it lands inside a circle of radius 1 m drawn in the rectangle?
Solution. Area of the rectangle = 4 × 3 = 12 m².
Area of the circle = π × 12 = π m².
P = π/12.
≈ 0.26.

Primes greater than 5 (sum at most 12): 7 and 11.
Sum 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1): 6 outcomes.
Sum 11: (5,6), (6,5): 2 outcomes.
P = 8/36
= 2/9.
(ii)Ordered pairs: 9 × 8 = 72.
Red-Green: 4 × 3 + 3 × 4 = 24.
Red-Blue: 4 × 2 + 2 × 4 = 16.
Green-Blue: 3 × 2 + 2 × 3 = 12.
Different colours: 24 + 16 + 12 = 52.
P = 52/72
= 13/18.
(iii)n(S) = 8.
First head and exactly two heads: HHT, HTH.
P = 2/8
= 1/4.
(iv)Total arrangements = 4! = 24.
Even if the last digit is 2 or 4.
Last digit 2: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.
Last digit 4: 6.
Even numbers = 12.
P = 12/24
= 1/2.
(v)P(correct) = 1/4 and P(wrong) = 3/4.
Exactly 2 correct can happen in 3 ways: CCW, CWC, WCC.
Each has probability 1/4 × 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/64.
P = 3 × 3/64
= 9/64.

Area of the rectangle = 3 × 2 = 6 m².
Radius of the circle = 1/2 m.

P = (π/4)/6.
= π/24.
≈ 0.13.

CHAPTER 8
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

Exploring Sequences and Progressions

The chapter at a glance

Idea Statement
Sequence An ordered list of numbers t 1 , t 2 , t 3 , … . t n is the term at position n .
Explicit rule Gives t n directly from n , for example t n = 2 n − 1 .
Recursive rule Gives t n from earlier terms, for example t 1 = 1 , t n = t n−1 + 3 .
Triangular, square numbers t n = n ( n + 1)/2 and s n = n 2 = 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2 n − 1) .
Virahānka–Fibonacci V 1 = 1 , V 2 = 2 , V n = V n−1 + V n−2 : 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …
AP Constant difference d . t n = a + ( n − 1) d . Graph points lie on a straight line.
Sum of an AP S n = n /2 [2 a + ( n − 1) d ] = n /2 ( a + l ) .
Sum of 1 to n S n = n ( n + 1)/2 (Āryabhaṭa, 499 CE).
GP Constant ratio r . t n = a r n−1 . Graph points lie on a curve.

Chapter 8: Sequences & Progressions 8.1 What Is a Sequence? Ganita Manjari · Class 9
8.1

What Is a Sequence?

Key Idea
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. Each number is a term ; t n is the term at position n . Order matters: 1, 2, 3 and 3, 2, 1 are different sequences.

Triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, … have tn = n(n + 1)/2.

Square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, … have sn = n2.

Each square is the sum of consecutive odd numbers: 1 = 1, 4 = 1 + 3, 9 = 1 + 3 + 5, 16 = 1 + 3 + 5 + 7, so n2 = 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1).

Adding the next row of dots to tn−1 gives tn = tn−1 + n.

Example 1
Find the 10th triangular number and decide whether 28 is triangular.
Solution. t10 = 10 × 11/2.
= 55.
Let n(n + 1)/2 = 28.
n(n + 1) = 56.
7 × 8 = 56, so n = 7.
So 28 is the 7th triangular number.
Example 2
Write 25 as a sum of consecutive odd numbers.
Solution. 25 = 52.
The sum of the first 5 odd numbers is 52.
25 = 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9.
Example 3
Find 1 + 3 + 5 + … + 99.
Solution. The terms are the first n odd numbers, where 2n − 1 = 99.
2n = 100, so n = 50.
The sum is n2.
= 502.
= 2500.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 107 of 215
Chapter 8: Sequences & Progressions 8.2 Explicit and Recursive Rules, and the Virahānka–Fibonacci Sequence Ganita Manjari · Class 9
8.2

Explicit and Recursive Rules, and the Virahānka–Fibonacci Sequence

Key Idea
Explicit rule: t n is calculated from the position n alone, for example u n = 2 n − 1 gives the odd numbers. Recursive rule: t n is calculated from earlier terms; the first term(s) must be given, for example t 1 = 1 , t n = t n−1 + 3 .

Virahānka (7th century CE) counted the poetic metres that fill n beats using short (1 beat) and long (2 beats) syllables. The counts 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … follow Vn = Vn−1 + Vn−2.

Gopāla (c. 1135) and Hemachandra (c. 1150) developed it before Fibonacci wrote of it in Europe (c. 1200).

A sequence can often be described by either kind of rule; the explicit rule is quicker for far-off terms.

Example 4
A sequence has explicit rule sn = 5n − 2. Find the 62nd term and decide whether 471 is a term.
Solution. s62 = 5(62) − 2.
= 310 − 2.
= 308.
Put 5n − 2 = 471.
5n = 473.
n = 94.6.
A position must be a natural number, so 471 is not a term.
Example 5
A sequence has tn = 3n + 4. Is 100 a term?
Solution. Put 3n + 4 = 100.
3n = 96.
n = 32.
So 100 is the 32nd term.
Example 6
Write the first five terms of t1 = 1, tn = tn−1 + 3, and find an explicit rule.
Solution. t1 = 1.
t2 = 1 + 3
= 4.
t3 = 4 + 3
= 7.
t4 = 7 + 3
= 10.
t5 = 10 + 3
= 13.
Each term adds 3, starting from 1.
tn = 1 + 3(n − 1).
= 3n − 2.
Example 7
Write the first ten Virahānka–Fibonacci numbers, and say in how many ways a length of 5 beats can be filled.
Solution. V1 = 1 and V2 = 2.
V3 = 2 + 1
= 3.
V4 = 3 + 2
= 5.
V5 = 5 + 3
= 8.
V6 = 8 + 5
= 13.
V7 = 13 + 8
= 21.
V8 = 21 + 13
= 34.
V9 = 34 + 21
= 55.
V10 = 55 + 34
= 89.
A length of 5 beats can be filled in V5 = 8 ways.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 108 of 215
Chapter 8: Sequences & Progressions 8.4 Arithmetic Progressions Ganita Manjari · Class 9
8.4

Arithmetic Progressions

Key Idea
An arithmetic progression (AP) has a constant common difference d : a , a + d , a + 2 d , … t n = a + ( n − 1) d . Recursive form: t 1 = a , t n = t n−1 + d .

Test for an AP: all consecutive differences are equal.

To find the number of terms: n = (l − a)/d + 1, where l is the last term.

An AP is a linear pattern: tn = dn + (a − d), so it connects with Chapter 2.

Example 8
Find the 7th term of the AP 5, 9, 13, …
Solution. a = 5 and d = 9 − 5 = 4.
t7 = a + 6d.
= 5 + 6(4).
= 29.
Example 9
Which term of the AP 3, 8, 13, … is 98?
Solution. a = 3 and d = 5.
3 + (n − 1)5 = 98.
(n − 1)5 = 95.
n − 1 = 19.
n = 20.
98 is the 20th term.
Example 10
How many terms are there in the AP 7, 13, 19, …, 205?
Solution. a = 7
d = 6
l = 205.
205 = 7 + (n − 1)6.
198 = (n − 1)6.
n − 1 = 33.
n = 34.
Example 11
In an AP, t3 = 10 and t8 = 25. Find a and d.
Solution. a + 2d = 10.
a + 7d = 25.
Subtract: 5d = 15.
d = 3.
a = 10 − 2(3).
= 4.
Example 12
A taxi charges a booking fee of ₹200 plus ₹40 per km. Write the fare sequence for 1, 2, 3 km and find the fare for 10 km.
Solution. 1 km: 200 + 40 = 240.
2 km: 200 + 80 = 280.
3 km: 200 + 120 = 320.
This is an AP with a = 240 and d = 40.
tn = 240 + (n − 1)40.
= 200 + 40n.
t10 = 200 + 400.
= ₹600.

Chapter 8: Sequences & Progressions 8.5 Sum of the First n Natural Numbers and of an AP Ganita Manjari · Class 9
8.5

Sum of the First n Natural Numbers and of an AP

Key Idea
Write the sum forwards and backwards and add pair by pair: each pair gives n + 1 , and there are n pairs, so 2 S n = n ( n + 1) . Āryabhaṭa (499 CE): the sum is the average of the first and last terms multiplied by the number of terms.

For an AP with first term a, last term l and n terms: Sn = n/2 (a + l).

A range sum is a difference: 25 + 26 + … + 58 = S58 − S24.

Example 13
Find 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 100.
Solution. S100 = 100 × 101/2.
= 50 × 101.
= 5050.
Example 14
Find 25 + 26 + 27 + … + 58.
Solution. The sum is S58 − S24.
S58 = 58 × 59/2.
= 29 × 59.
= 1711.
S24 = 24 × 25/2.
= 12 × 25.
= 300.
Sum = 1711 − 300.
= 1411.
Example 15
Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the AP 3, 7, 11, …
Solution. a = 3
d = 4
n = 20.
S20 = 20/2 × [2(3) + 19(4)].
= 10 × [6 + 76].
= 10 × 82.
= 820.
Example 16
Find the sum of all multiples of 5 from 10 to 100.
Solution. The terms form an AP: 10, 15, …, 100.
a = 10
d = 5
l = 100.
100 = 10 + (n − 1)5, so n = 19.
S = n/2 (a + l).
= 19/2 × 110.
= 19 × 55.
= 1045.
Example 17
Find the sum of the even numbers from 2 to 50.
Solution. 2 + 4 + … + 50 = 2(1 + 2 + … + 25).
1 + 2 + … + 25 = 25 × 26/2
= 325.
Sum = 2 × 325.
= 650.

Chapter 8: Sequences & Progressions 8.6 Geometric Progressions Ganita Manjari · Class 9
8.6

Geometric Progressions

Key Idea
A geometric progression (GP) has a constant common ratio r : a , a r , a r 2 , … t n = a · r n−1 . Recursive form: t 1 = a , t n = r · t n−1 .
AP GP
Rule add the same d multiply by the same r
n -th term a + ( n − 1) d a r n−1
Growth linear (straight line) exponential (curve)
Test equal differences equal ratios

If r > 1 the terms grow; if 0 < r < 1 they shrink towards 0; if r < 0 the signs alternate.

Any three consecutive terms x, y, z of a GP satisfy y2 = xz.

Example 18
Find the 8th term of the GP 3, 6, 12, …
Solution. a = 3 and r = 6/3 = 2.
t8 = ar7.
= 3 × 27.
= 3 × 128.
= 384.
Example 19
Which term of the GP 1, 3, 9, … is 729?
Solution. a = 1 and r = 3.
3n−1 = 729.
729 = 36.
n − 1 = 6.
n = 7.
Example 20
In a GP, t3 = 12 and t6 = 96. Find a and r.
Solution. ar2 = 12.
ar5 = 96.
Divide: r3 = 96/12 = 8.
r = 2.
a = 12/r2
= 12/4.
= 3.
Example 21
A tank holds 64 litres and loses half its water every day. How much is left after 5 days?
Solution. This is a GP with a = 64 and r = 1/2.
Amount after 5 days = 64 × (1/2)5.
= 64/32.
= 2 litres.

Chapter 8: Sequences & Progressions 8.6.1 Fractals: the Sierpiński Triangle and Bouncing Balls Ganita Manjari · Class 9
8.6.1

Fractals: the Sierpiński Triangle and Bouncing Balls

Key Idea
A fractal is a self-similar shape that repeats at smaller and smaller scales. Sierpiński triangle. At stage n there are t n = 3 n triangles (a GP with r = 3 ), and the shaded area is s n = (3/4) n of the original (a GP with r = 3/4 ).

At each stage the middle triangle of every black triangle is removed: 3 triangles remain from each 1, and each has 1/4 of the area, so the total shaded area is multiplied by 3/4.

A bouncing ball rebounding to a fixed fraction r of its previous height has heights forming a GP with ratio r.

Example 22
Find the number of black triangles and the shaded fraction of the area at stage 5 of the Sierpiński triangle.
Solution. Number of triangles = 35.
= 243.
Shaded fraction = (3/4)5.
= 243/1024.
≈ 0.237.
Example 23
A ball is dropped from 24 ft and rebounds to 75% of its previous height each time. Find the heights after 3 bounces and after which bounce the height first falls below 4 ft.
Solution. Bounce 1: 24 × 0.75 = 18 ft.
Bounce 2: 18 × 0.75 = 13.5 ft.
Bounce 3: 13.5 × 0.75 = 10.125 ft.
Bounce 4: 7.594 ft.
Bounce 5: 5.695 ft.
Bounce 6: 4.271 ft.
Bounce 7: 3.203 ft.
The height first falls below 4 ft after the 7th bounce.
Example 24
A ball dropped from 16 m rebounds to half its previous height each time. How high does it go after the 4th bounce?
Solution. a = 16 and r = 1/2.
Height after 4 bounces = 16 × (1/2)4.
= 16/16.
= 1 m.

Question 8.13
Let k numbers start from a: a + (a + 1) + … + (a + k − 1) = 100.

a ≥ 1.

Question 8.14
Let the terms be a/r, a, ar.
Product: a3 = −1, so a = −1.

1/r + 1 + r = −13/12.
12(r2 + r + 1) = −13r.
12r2 + 25r + 12 = 0.
12r2 + 16r + 9r + 12 = 0.
4r(3r + 4) + 3(3r + 4) = 0.
(4r + 3)(3r + 4) = 0.
r = −3/4 or r = −4/3.
For r = −3/4 the terms are 4/3, −1, 3/4.
For r = −4/3 the terms are 3/4, −1, 4/3.
Question 8.15
Let the terms be a, ar, ar2.
a(1 + r + r2) = 26.
a2(1 + r2 + r4) = 364.
Divide the second by the square of the first.
(1 + r2 + r4)/(1 + r + r2)2 = 364/676
= 7/13.
1 + r2 + r4 = (1 + r + r2)(1 − r + r2).
(1 − r + r2)/(1 + r + r2) = 7/13.
13(1 − r + r2) = 7(1 + r + r2).
6r2 − 20r + 6 = 0.
3r2 − 10r + 3 = 0.
(3r − 1)(r − 3) = 0.
r = 3 or r = 1/3.
For r = 3: 13a = 26, so a = 2.
The terms are 2, 6, 18 (or 18, 6, 2 for r = 1/3).

Chapter 9: Propositions & Converses Overview & Key Ideas Ganita Manjari · Class 9
CHAPTER 9
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

Propositions and their Converses

The chapter at a glance

Idea Statement
Proposition A statement that is definitely true or definitely false. Usually “If P , then Q ”: P is the hypothesis, Q the conclusion.
Converse “If Q , then P ”: hypothesis and conclusion swapped.
Four cases Proposition and converse can be both true, only one true, or both false.
Both true Written “ P if and only if Q ”.
Justifying a true statement Give a general argument valid for every case (use letters, not particular numbers).
Counterexample One example satisfying the hypothesis but not the conclusion. One counterexample disproves a statement.
Examples do not prove Checking a few cases never proves a general statement.
Divisibility Divisible by a and by b is the same as divisible by lcm ( a , b ) ; equal to a b only when gcd is 1.
Perfect squares Product of perfect squares is a perfect square; the converse is false.
Number of factors p 2 has 3 factors; p q ( p ≠ q primes) has 4; the converses need care.
Contrapositive “If P , then Q ” is equivalent to “If not Q , then not P ”.
Necessary, sufficient P ⇒ Q : P is sufficient for Q ; Q is necessary for P . Both ways: iff.
Squares and factors A positive integer is a perfect square if and only if it has an odd number of factors.
Geometry pairs Isosceles triangle theorem and its converse; corresponding angles and parallel lines; Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem and its converse.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 118 of 215
Chapter 9: Propositions & Converses 9.1 Propositions Ganita Manjari · Class 9
9.1

Propositions

Key Idea
A proposition is a mathematical statement that is either true or false, never both. Most are written “ If P , then Q ”. P is the hypothesis (what we assume) and Q is the conclusion (what we claim).

“Is 7 prime?” is a question, not a proposition. “Close the door” is an instruction.

“If a number is a multiple of 6, then it is a multiple of 3” is a proposition, and it is true.

A statement with an unspecified variable, such as x + 2 = 5, is not yet a proposition; it becomes one for a given x.

Statements can often be rewritten in “if-then” form: “Equal angles in a triangle have equal opposite sides” is “If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite them are equal”.

Example 1
Write the hypothesis and the conclusion of: “If two angles are vertically opposite, then they are equal.”
Solution. Hypothesis: the two angles are vertically opposite.
Conclusion: the two angles are equal.
Example 2
Decide whether each is a proposition: (a) 17 is a prime number. (b) What is the square of 5? (c) If a number ends in 0, then it is divisible by 10.
Solution. (a) It is definitely true, so it is a proposition.
(b) It is a question and has no truth value, so it is not.
(c) It is definitely true, so it is a proposition.

Chapter 9: Propositions & Converses 9.2 The Converse of a Proposition Ganita Manjari · Class 9
9.2

The Converse of a Proposition

Key Idea
The converse of “If P , then Q ” is “If Q , then P ”. A true proposition may have a false converse. The proposition and its converse must each be checked separately .
Proposition Converse Example
true true If x = y then x + a = y + a ; and the converse (cancel a ).
true false If a number is a multiple of 6, it is a multiple of 3; but 9 is a multiple of 3 and not of 6.
false true If two triangles have equal area, then they are congruent (false); the converse “congruent ⇒ equal area” is true.
false false If a number is divisible by 4, then it is odd (false); the converse “odd ⇒ divisible by 4” is also false.

Wording: “when”, “whenever” and “implies” can hide the direction. “A number has an odd number of factors when it is a perfect square” means “If a number is a perfect square, then it has an odd number of factors”; “when” does not turn it into the converse.

Real life: “If it rains on an uncovered road, the road gets wet” is true. “If the road is wet, then it has rained” is false: a water tanker may have spilled.

When both a proposition and its converse are true we write “P if and only if Q”.

Example 3
Write the converse of “If a triangle is equilateral, then all its angles are 60°” and decide whether it is true.
Solution. Converse: If all angles of a triangle are 60°, then it is equilateral.
Angles equal means opposite sides are equal.
So all three sides are equal.
The converse is true.
Example 4
Write the converse of “If a number ends in 0, then it is divisible by 5” and test it.
Solution. Proposition: a number ending in 0 is 10k.
10k = 5 × 2k, so it is divisible by 5: true.
Converse: If a number is divisible by 5, then it ends in 0.
Try 15: divisible by 5 but ends in 5.
So the converse is false.
Example 5
Show that both “If a positive integer is a multiple of 4, then it ends in 4” and its converse are false.
Solution. Proposition: take 8, a multiple of 4 that ends in 8.
So the proposition is false.
Converse: if a positive integer ends in 4, then it is a multiple of 4.
Take 14, which ends in 4.
14 ÷ 4 is not a whole number.
So the converse is false too.

Chapter 9: Propositions & Converses 9.3 Justification and Counterexamples Ganita Manjari · Class 9
9.3

Justification and Counterexamples

Key Idea
To show a statement is true , give a general argument that works for every case, using letters such as n = 24 k . To show a statement is false , give one counterexample : an example where the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails.

Checking many examples never proves a general statement.

Contrapositive: “If P, then Q” is equivalent to “If not Q, then not P”. Proving the contrapositive is sometimes easier, as in divisibility questions.

Even a famous-looking rule can fail: n2 + n + 11 is prime for n = 0, 1, …, 9, but n = 10 gives 121 = 11 × 11.

Counterexamples for “if-then” statements must satisfy the if part.

Example 6
Prove that the product of two even numbers is divisible by 4.
Solution. Let the numbers be 2a and 2b.
Their product is 2a × 2b.
= 4ab.
4ab is divisible by 4.
This works for every pair of even numbers.
Example 7
Prove that the sum of two consecutive integers is odd.
Solution. Let the integers be n and n + 1.
Sum = n + (n + 1).
= 2n + 1.
2n + 1 is always odd.
Example 8
Fermat conjectured that 22^n + 1 is prime for every n = 0, 1, 2, … Check small cases and disprove the claim.
Solution. n = 0: 21 + 1 = 3, prime.
n = 1: 22 + 1 = 5, prime.
n = 2: 24 + 1 = 17, prime.
n = 3: 28 + 1 = 257, prime.
n = 4: 216 + 1 = 65537, prime.
n = 5: 232 + 1 = 4294967297.
= 641 × 6700417.
This is composite (Euler, 1732), so Fermat’s claim is false.
Example 9
Find a counterexample to “All numbers of the form n2 + n + 41 are prime”.
Solution. Try n = 41.
412 + 41 + 41 = 41(41 + 1 + 1).
= 41 × 43.
= 1763.
1763 is not prime, so the claim is false.
Example 10
Find a counterexample to “If n > 1, then n2 > 2n”.
Solution. Take n = 2.
n2 = 4 and 2n = 4.
4 > 4 is false.
The statement is false, with counterexample n = 2.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 121 of 215
Chapter 9: Propositions & Converses 9.4 Propositions from Number Theory Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 11
Find a counterexample to “If x2 = 9, then x = 3”.
Solution. Take x = −3.
(−3)2 = 9, so the hypothesis holds.
x = −3 ≠ 3, so the conclusion fails.
9.4

Propositions from Number Theory

Key Idea
If n is divisible by a and by b , it is divisible by lcm ( a , b ) . If gcd ( a , b ) = 1 , lcm = a b and the converse “divisible by a and b ⇒ divisible by a b ” is true . If gcd ( a , b ) > 1 the converse can fail: 12 is divisible by 4 and 6, but not by 24.

Digit-sum rule for 3 (and 9): a number is divisible by 3 if and only if its digit sum is a multiple of 3 (same for 9).

Factors: p2 (p prime) has exactly 3 factors: 1, p, p2. pq (p ≠ q primes) has exactly 4: 1, p, q, pq. The number 8 also has 4 factors, so “4 factors ⇒ product of two primes” is false.

Factors come in pairs; the number of factors is odd exactly when the number is a perfect square.

Perfect squares: if a = m2 and b = n2, then ab = (mn)2. The converse is false: 2 × 8 = 16.

Example 12
Prove: If n is divisible by 15, then it is divisible by both 3 and 5. Is the converse true?
Solution. Let n = 15k.
n = 3 × 5k, so 3 divides n.
n = 5 × 3k, so 5 divides n.
Converse: if n is divisible by 3 and 5, then it is divisible by 15.
gcd(3, 5) = 1, so lcm = 15.
A number divisible by both is divisible by their lcm.
The converse is true.
Example 13
Test the statement “If the digit sum of a number is a multiple of 9, then the number is divisible by 9” on 738.
Solution. Digit sum = 7 + 3 + 8 = 18.
18 is a multiple of 9.
738 = 9 × 82.
So 738 is divisible by 9, as claimed.
Example 14
Prove: a positive integer is a perfect square if and only if it has an odd number of factors.
Solution. Pair each factor f of n with its partner n/f.
If f ≠ n/f, the pair has two different factors.
A factor is its own partner when f × f = n.
That happens exactly when n is a perfect square, with f = √n.
A perfect square has exactly one such factor, since a positive number has one positive square root.
Count of factors = (an even number) + 1, which is odd.
A non-square has no self-partnered factor, so all its factors pair up.
So it has an even number of factors.
Hence n is a perfect square if and only if it has an odd number of factors.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 122 of 215
Chapter 9: Propositions & Converses 9.5 Propositions from Geometry Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 15
Why does 49 have exactly three factors while 36 has an odd number of factors?
Solution. 49 = 72 with 7 prime.
Its factors are 1, 7 and 49: exactly 3.
Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36.
They pair up: (1, 36), (2, 18), (3, 12), (4, 9).
The factor 6 pairs with itself because 6 × 6 = 36.
So the count is 4 × 2 + 1 = 9, which is odd.
Example 16
Disprove: “If a and b are perfect squares, then a + b is a perfect square.”
Solution. Take a = 1 and b = 4.
Both are perfect squares.
a + b = 5.
5 is not a perfect square.
So the statement is false.
9.5

Propositions from Geometry

Key Idea
Isosceles triangle theorem and converse. If A B = A C , then ∠ B = ∠ C ; and if ∠ B = ∠ C , then A B = A C . Both are true. Parallel lines. If l ∥ m , corresponding angles are equal; and if corresponding angles are equal, l ∥ m . Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem and converse. In a right triangle a 2 + b 2 = c 2 ; and if a 2 + b 2 = c 2 in a triangle, it is right-angled.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 123 of 215
Chapter 9: Propositions & Converses Chapter Theory Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 17
Prove the converse of the isosceles triangle theorem: if ∠B = ∠C in Δ ABC, then AB = AC.
Solution. Draw AD ⊥ BC with D on BC.
In Δ ABD and Δ ACD: ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°.
∠BAD = 180° − 90° − ∠B.
∠CAD = 180° − 90° − ∠C.
Since ∠B = ∠C, ∠BAD = ∠CAD.
AD = AD (common).
So Δ ABD ≅ Δ ACD (ASA).
Hence AB = AC (corresponding sides).
Example 18
Prove the converse of the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem: if a2 + b2 = c2 in a triangle with sides a, b, c, then it is right-angled.
Solution. Build a right triangle with legs a and b.
Its hypotenuse x satisfies x2 = a2 + b2.
Given a2 + b2 = c2, we get x2 = c2.
So x = c.
Both triangles have sides a, b, c.
They are congruent (SSS).
The original triangle has a right angle, opposite the side c.
Example 19
Is a triangle with sides 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm right-angled?
Solution. 52 + 122 = 25 + 144.
= 169.
= 132.
By the converse of the theorem, it is right-angled, with the right angle opposite the 13 cm side.
Example 20
Show that “If two triangles have the same area, then they are congruent” is false, but its converse is true.
Solution. Triangle 1: base 4 cm, height 3 cm, area = ½ × 4 × 3 = 6 cm².
Triangle 2: base 6 cm, height 2 cm, area = ½ × 6 × 2 = 6 cm².
The areas are equal, but the shapes differ, so the triangles are not congruent.
The proposition is false.
Converse: congruent triangles have the same area.
Congruent triangles coincide when placed on each other.
So their areas are equal.
The converse is true.
Example 21
The proposition “If a quadrilateral is a rectangle, then its diagonals are equal” is true. Is the converse true?
Solution. Converse: If the diagonals of a quadrilateral are equal, then it is a rectangle.
Take an isosceles trapezium.
Its diagonals are equal.
But its angles are not all right angles.
So it is not a rectangle.
The converse is false.

Chapter 9: Propositions & Converses 9.6 Necessary, Sufficient and “If and Only If” Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 22
Lines l ∥ m are cut by a transversal and one corresponding angle is 65°. Find the other, and say what the converse tells us.
Solution. Corresponding angles are equal for parallel lines.
The other corresponding angle is 65°.
Converse: if a transversal makes equal corresponding angles with two lines, the lines are parallel.
So the equality of corresponding angles tests whether lines are parallel.
9.6

Necessary, Sufficient and “If and Only If”

Key Idea
If P implies Q , then P is a sufficient condition for Q and Q is a necessary condition for P . If both P implies Q and Q implies P are true, we write P if and only if Q (iff).

Sufficient means enough: P guarantees Q. Necessary means unavoidable: without Q, P cannot hold.

In “If a number is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by 3”, divisibility by 6 is sufficient for divisibility by 3, and divisibility by 3 is necessary for divisibility by 6, but not sufficient (9).

Example 23
In “If n is divisible by 24, then it is divisible by 4”, name a sufficient and a necessary condition.
Solution. Sufficient condition for divisibility by 4: n is divisible by 24.
Necessary condition for divisibility by 24: n is divisible by 4.
It is not sufficient: 12 is divisible by 4 but not by 24.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 125 of 215
Chapter 9: Propositions & Converses 9.7 Writing Good Mathematical Answers Ganita Manjari · Class 9
9.7

Writing Good Mathematical Answers

Key Idea
A final answer “true” or “false” is only part of the work. You must also explain why .

Step 1. Write the proposition in “if-then” form.

Step 2. Decide true or false. If true, give a general argument; if false, give a counterexample that satisfies the “if” part.

Step 3. Write the converse by swapping hypothesis and conclusion.

Step 4. Repeat Steps 2 for the converse. Never assume the converse is true (or false) because the proposition is.

Step 5. If both are true, state the result as “P if and only if Q”.

Example 24
Treat the statement: “If n is divisible by 10, then it is divisible by 5.”
Solution. It is already in if-then form.
Let n = 10k.
n = 5 × 2k, so it is divisible by 5: true.
Converse: If n is divisible by 5, then it is divisible by 10.
Counterexample: n = 15.
15 is divisible by 5, not by 10.
The converse is false.
Example 25
Express “a number is divisible by 3” and “its digit sum is a multiple of 3” using if-then sentences.
Solution. Statement 1: If a number is divisible by 3, then its digit sum is a multiple of 3.
Statement 2: If the digit sum of a number is a multiple of 3, then it is divisible by 3.
Each is the converse of the other, and both are true.
So a number is divisible by 3 if and only if its digit sum is a multiple of 3.

VERIFIED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTIONS

Chapter 9: Solutions to Chapter-End Questions

Question 9.1
Proposition: true.
This is the corresponding-angles property of parallel lines.
Converse: If the corresponding angles formed by a transversal with two lines are equal, then the two lines are parallel.
The converse is true.
Equal corresponding angles are exactly the test for parallel lines.
So l ∥ m implies α = β, and α = β implies l ∥ m.
Question 9.2
Proposition: true.
Every angle of a square is 90°.
Converse: If all the angles of a quadrilateral are equal, then it is a square.
The converse is false.
Counterexample: a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm has four equal angles of 90°.
Its sides are not all equal, so it is not a square.
Question 9.3
Proposition: true.
Adding the same number to equal numbers gives equal results.
Converse: If a + x = a + y, then x = y.
The converse is true.
Subtract a from both sides.
a + x − a = a + y − a.
x = y.
Question 9.4
Proposition: true.
Equal numbers have equal squares.
Converse: If x2 = y2, then x = y.
The converse is false.
Counterexample: x = 2 and y = −2.
x2 = 4
= y2 but 2 ≠ −2.
Question 9.5
Proposition: true.
Equal numbers have equal cubes.
Converse: If x3 = y3, then x = y.
The converse is true.
Take the real cube root of both sides.
Each real number has only one real cube root.
So x = y.
Question 9.6
Proposition: true.
Let a = m2 and b = n2 with m, n integers.
ab = m2 n2
= (mn)2.
mn is an integer, so ab is a perfect square.
Converse: If ab is a perfect square, then a and b are perfect squares.
The converse is false.
Counterexample: a = 2 and b = 8.
ab = 16
= 42, but neither 2 nor 8 is a perfect square.

Chapter 9: Propositions & Converses Stepwise Solutions (Q 9.7 – Q 9.12) Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Chapter 9 Solutions · Question 7 – Question 12
Question 9.7
Proposition: true.
Let n = 24k.
n = 4 × 6k and n = 6 × 4k.
So n is divisible by 4 and by 6.
Converse: If n is divisible by both 4 and 6, then it is divisible by 24.
The converse is false.
Counterexample: n = 12.
12 is divisible by 4 and 6, but not by 24.
Question 9.8
Proposition: true.
Let n = 60k.
n = 5 × 12k and n = 12 × 5k.
So n is divisible by 5 and by 12.
Converse: If n is divisible by both 5 and 12, then it is divisible by 60.
The converse is true.
lcm(5, 12) = 60 because gcd(5, 12) = 1.
A number divisible by both is divisible by their lcm, 60.
Question 9.9
Proposition: true.
Let n = p2 with p prime.
The only factors are 1, p and p2.
So there are exactly 3 factors.
Converse: If n has exactly 3 factors, then it is the square of a prime.
The converse is true.
Let the factors be 1, p and n, with 1 < p < n.
Since p divides n, so does n ÷ p.
n ÷ p lies between 1 and n, so it is p.
Then n = p2.
If p were composite, a factor of p between 1 and p would be a fourth factor of n.
So p is prime and n = p2.
Question 9.10
Proposition: true.
Let n = pq with p ≠ q primes.
The divisors are 1, p, q, pq.
These are four different numbers and there are no others.
Converse: If n has exactly 4 divisors, then it is a product of two unequal primes.
The converse is false.
Counterexample: n = 8.
Its divisors are 1, 2, 4, 8: exactly four.
But 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 is not a product of two unequal primes.
Question 9.11
Proposition: true.
If n were a multiple of 3, then n + 3 would be too.
Then 3 would be a common factor, contradicting the hypothesis.
So n is not a multiple of 3.
Converse: If n is not a multiple of 3, then n and n + 3 have no common factor other than 1.
The converse is true.
Any common factor of n and n + 3 divides (n + 3) − n = 3.
So it is 1 or 3.
It cannot be 3, since 3 does not divide n.
So the only common factor is 1.
Question 9.12
Proposition: true.
AB = AC gives ∠ABC = ∠BCA.
BI and CI bisect equal angles, so ∠IBC = ∠ICB.
So BI = CI in Δ BIC.
In Δ CIE and Δ BIF: ∠ICE = ∠IBF (halves of equal angles).
∠CIE = ∠BIF (vertically opposite).
CI = BI.
So Δ CIE ≅ Δ BIF (ASA).
Hence IE = IF.
Converse: if IE = IF, then AB = AC.
It is false.
Counterexample: ∠A = 60°, ∠B = 90°, ∠C = 30°.
AI bisects ∠A, so ∠EAI = ∠IAF = 30°.
∠ABE = 45° and ∠ACF = 15°.
∠AEB = 180° − 60° − 45°
= 75°.
∠AFC = 180° − 60° − 15°
= 105°.
Mark G on ray AB with AG = AE and join IG.
Δ AEI ≅ Δ AGI (SAS), so IE = IG and ∠AGI = 75°.
G cannot lie between A and F (then Δ IFG would have two angles of 105°).
G ≠ F because ∠AGI = 75° ≠ 105° = ∠AFI.
So F lies between A and G, and ∠IGF = 75°.
∠IFG = 180° − 105°
= 75°.
Δ IFG has equal base angles, so IF = IG.
Hence IE = IG = IF.
But ∠B ≠ ∠C, so AB ≠ AC.
So the converse is false.

Question 9.17
(i)(a) Yes.
Every quadrilateral of type Q has equal diagonals.
So the sticks must be equal.
(i)(b) It may matter.

If Q means rectangles, the equal sticks must be put together at their midpoints.
Equal lengths are necessary but not sufficient.
(ii)(a) Equal sticks guarantee a quadrilateral of type Q.
The statement does not rule out type Q from unequal sticks.
(ii)(b) Any way of joining equal sticks (into a proper quadrilateral) gives type Q.
The diagonals are then equal, so the statement applies.

Chapter 10: Understanding Data Overview & Key Ideas Ganita Manjari · Class 9
CHAPTER 10
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

How Quantities Combine: Understanding Data

The chapter at a glance

Idea Statement
Combined mean Two groups with means a , b and sizes n , m : ( a × n + b × m )/( n + m ) .
Average of averages The simple mean of group means is right only when the group sizes are equal .
Weighted mean Σ w i x i / Σ w i . The weights can be sizes, volumes, marks ratios or frequencies.
Properties Equal weights give the ordinary mean. Multiplying all weights by k > 0 changes nothing. The mean lies between the smallest and largest value.
Mixtures Concentration = amount of active ingredient ÷ total quantity. Use volume as the weight.
Updating a mean New mean = (old total ± change) ÷ new count.
Dilution The solute stays the same; the total volume grows.
Rating schemes Convert marks to percentages first, then apply the weights.
Stacked bar chart Shows totals and parts (absolute values).
100% stacked bar chart Shows shares only. It cannot compare absolute amounts across bars.
Conversions Stacked to 100% stacked is always possible; the reverse is not.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 132 of 215
Chapter 10: Understanding Data 10.1 Combined Mean: Average of Averages Ganita Manjari · Class 9
10.1

Combined Mean: Average of Averages

Key Idea
Mean = total of all values ÷ number of values. To combine two groups, add their totals and divide by the total count .

Averaging the two group means treats both groups as equally large, which is wrong if their sizes differ.

Equal sizes: if all groups have the same size p, then (a + b + c)p/3p = (a + b + c)/3, so the simple mean of the means works.

Recover a group’s total from its mean: total = mean × count.

Example 1
A badminton academy has 8 seniors with average height 165.5 cm and 3 juniors with average height 149.33 cm. Find the average height of all 11 trainees.
Solution. Total height of seniors = 8 × 165.5 = 1324 cm.
Total height of juniors = 3 × 149.33 ≈ 448 cm.
Combined total = 1324 + 448 = 1772 cm.
Number of trainees = 8 + 3 = 11.
Combined mean = 1772/11.
≈ 161.09 cm.
The simple average of the two means gives 157.4 cm, which is wrong because seniors outnumber juniors.
Example 2
Jaspreet cycles on 5 weekdays in each of 3 weeks, with weekly averages 12.8, 15.8 and 18.0 minutes. Find her average over all 15 days.
Solution. All three weeks have the same number of days (5), so the weights are equal.
Combined mean = (12.8 + 15.8 + 18.0)/3.
= 46.6/3.
≈ 15.53 minutes.
Check with totals: (64 + 79 + 90)/15 = 233/15 ≈ 15.53.
Example 3
Class A has 40 students with mean 60; Class B has 20 students with mean 70. Find the combined mean.
Solution. Total marks of A = 40 × 60 = 2400.
Total marks of B = 20 × 70 = 1400.
Combined total = 3800.
Number of students = 60.
Combined mean = 3800/60.
≈ 63.33.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 133 of 215
Chapter 10: Understanding Data 10.2 The Weighted Average Ganita Manjari · Class 9
10.2

The Weighted Average

Key Idea
In a weighted average each value is multiplied by its weight : how large, frequent or important it is. “Weight” need not be physical weight.

Equal weights give the ordinary mean.

Multiplying all weights by the same k > 0 leaves the weighted average unchanged.

Bounding: the weighted mean lies between the smallest and largest value.

Brahmagupta (628 CE) used it for the mean depth of an uneven pit; Śrīdharācārya (750 CE) used it for the purity (varṇa) of mixed gold.

Example 4
A pit has length 3 hastas at depth 8, 5 hastas at depth 6, and 2 hastas at depth 4. Find its mean depth.
Solution. Weights are the lengths: 3, 5, 2.
Total length = 10 hastas.
Σwx = 3 × 8 + 5 × 6 + 2 × 4.
= 24 + 30 + 8.
= 62.
Mean depth = 62/10.
= 6.2 hastas.
Example 5
Values 10, 20, 30 have weights 1, 1, 1 and then weights 2, 2, 2. Compare the weighted means.
Solution. Weights 1, 1, 1: (10 + 20 + 30)/3 = 20.
Weights 2, 2, 2: (20 + 40 + 60)/6.
= 120/6.
= 20.
Doubling all weights leaves the weighted mean unchanged.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 134 of 215
Chapter 10: Understanding Data 10.3 Mixtures, Concentration and Purity Ganita Manjari · Class 9
10.3

Mixtures, Concentration and Purity

Key Idea
Concentration of a mixture = amount of active ingredient ÷ total quantity . Equal quantities: the concentration is the midpoint. Unequal quantities: it is pulled towards the larger quantity.

The concentration of a mixture of two sources always lies between the two source concentrations (endpoints included).

Never subtract percentages directly; add the amounts of solute.

Example 6
Equal quantities of lemonade with 10% and 20% jaggery are mixed. Find the jaggery concentration.
Solution. Let each glass hold y units.
Jaggery in glass 1 = 0.1y.
Jaggery in glass 2 = 0.2y.
Total jaggery = 0.3y.
Total volume = 2y.
Concentration = 0.3y/2y.
= 0.15 = 15%.
Example 7
A bowl of 500 mL lemonade has 10% jaggery and a glass of 200 mL has 20%. Find the mixture’s concentration.
Solution. Estimate: the bowl is larger, so the answer is below 15%.
Jaggery in the bowl = 0.10 × 500 = 50 mL.
Jaggery in the glass = 0.20 × 200 = 40 mL.
Total jaggery = 90 mL.
Total volume = 700 mL.
Concentration = 90/700.
≈ 12.86%.
Example 8
Batch A is 200 kg at 70% copper, Batch B is 120 kg at 50% copper, and Batch C is 45% copper. The three together are 55% copper. Find the weight of Batch C.
Solution. Let Batch C weigh y kg.
Copper in A = 0.70 × 200 = 140 kg.
Copper in B = 0.50 × 120 = 60 kg.
Copper in C = 0.45y kg.
Total weight = 320 + y kg.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 135 of 215
Chapter 10: Understanding Data 0.55 = (200 + 0.45y)/(320 + y). Ganita Manjari · Class 9
0.55

= (200 + 0.45y)/(320 + y).

0.55(320 + y) = 200 + 0.45y.

176 + 0.55y = 200 + 0.45y.

0.10y = 24.

y = 240 kg.

10.4

Marks, Profit and Custom Weights

Key Idea
When marks are out of different totals, convert each to a percentage first , then apply the weights. A ratio such as 3 : 2 : 5 means the weights are 3, 2 and 5 (total 10).

Hotel and restaurant ratings, exam scores and profit margins all use weights.

Weighting recent reviews more heavily is a deliberate choice of weights.

Example 9
Rehmat scored 60% in internals, 64% in the project and 73% in the final exam. They are combined in the ratio 3 : 2 : 5. Find the annual score.
Solution. Weights are 3, 2 and 5
total weight = 10.
Σwx = 60 × 3 + 64 × 2 + 73 × 5.
= 180 + 128 + 365.
= 673.
Annual score = 673/10.
= 67.3%.
Equal weights would give 197/3 ≈ 65.67%, which is different.
Example 10
A customer rates Food 5, Service 3 and Ambience 4. The weights are Food : Service : Ambience = 4 : 3 : 2. Find the combined rating.
Solution. Σwx = 5 × 4 + 3 × 3 + 4 × 2.
= 20 + 9 + 8.
= 37.
Total weight = 4 + 3 + 2 = 9.
Combined rating = 37/9.
≈ 4.11 out of 5.
Example 11
A student scores 42 out of 50, 48 out of 60 and 90 out of 100 in three parts with weights 2 : 3 : 5. Find the weighted percentage.
Solution. Convert to percentages: 42/50 = 84%.
48/60 = 80%.
90/100 = 90%.
Σwx = 84 × 2 + 80 × 3 + 90 × 5.
= 168 + 240 + 450.
= 858.
Weighted percentage = 858/10.
= 85.8%.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 136 of 215
Chapter 10: Understanding Data 10.5 How an Average Changes Ganita Manjari · Class 9
10.5

How an Average Changes

Key Idea
Keep the old total visible: old total = old mean × old count. New mean = (old total ± the value added or removed) ÷ (new count).

A new value above the old mean raises the mean; below lowers it; equal to the mean leaves it unchanged.

When values leave, subtract their total and their count.

Example 12
The mean of 10 scores is 40. An 11th score of 62 is added. Find the new mean.
Solution. Old total = 10 × 40 = 400.
New total = 400 + 62 = 462.
New count = 11.
New mean = 462/11.
= 42.
It rose because 62 is above 40.
Example 13
The mean of 6 numbers is 50. One of them, 70, is removed. Find the mean of the remaining numbers.
Solution. Total = 6 × 50 = 300.
New total = 300 − 70 = 230.
New count = 5.
New mean = 230/5.
= 46.
Example 14
A class of 30 has mean 55. A new student scores 86. Find the new mean.
Solution. Old total = 30 × 55 = 1650.
New total = 1650 + 86 = 1736.
New count = 31.
New mean = 1736/31.
= 56.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 137 of 215
Chapter 10: Understanding Data 10.6 Dilution and Possible Target Values Ganita Manjari · Class 9
10.6

Dilution and Possible Target Values

Key Idea
When pure water is added to a solution, the amount of solute stays the same and the total volume increases. New concentration = amount of solute ÷ new total volume.

A mixture of two concentrations cannot be stronger than both or weaker than both.

Write an equation for the amount of solute before and after mixing.

Example 15
5 litres of juice with 12% sugar is diluted with 3 litres of water. Find the new concentration.
Solution. Sugar = 0.12 × 5 = 0.6 L.
New volume = 5 + 3 = 8 L.
New concentration = 0.6/8.
= 0.075.
= 7.5%.
Example 16
20 litres of a 10% solution is to be diluted to 8%. How much water must be added?
Solution. Solute = 0.10 × 20 = 2 L.
Let w litres of water be added.
2/(20 + w) = 0.08.
20 + w = 25.
w = 5 litres.
Example 17
Can mixing a 4% and a 9% solution give a 12% solution?
Solution. A mixture lies between the two source concentrations.
The range is 4% to 9%.
12% is above both.
So it is not possible.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 138 of 215
Chapter 10: Understanding Data 10.7 Unknown Counts and Frequency Tables Ganita Manjari · Class 9
10.7

Unknown Counts and Frequency Tables

Key Idea
Use a letter for each unknown group size, and let the total count give a second equation. Overall mean = (sum of value × frequency) ÷ (sum of the frequencies).

If a group’s mean is above the overall mean, that group pulls the combined mean up. The overall mean lies nearer the group with more members.

For ratings, multiply each rating by the number of customers who gave it before adding.

Example 18
The mean mark of 40 students is 62. The boys’ mean is 70 and the girls’ mean is 50. How many are boys and girls?
Solution. Let there be x boys and y girls.
x + y = 40.
70x + 50y = 62 × 40
= 2480.
70x + 50(40 − x) = 2480.
20x + 2000 = 2480.
20x = 480.
x = 24.
y = 16.
24 boys and 16 girls.
Example 19
A shop collects ratings: 5 stars from 4 people, 4 stars from 3, 3 stars from 2 and 2 stars from 1. Find the mean rating.
Solution. Total people = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10.
Σ(rating × count) = 20 + 12 + 6 + 2.
= 40.
Mean rating = 40/10.
= 4.0.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 139 of 215
Chapter 10: Understanding Data 10.8 Tables, Stacked Bars and 100% Stacked Bars Ganita Manjari · Class 9
10.8

Tables, Stacked Bars and 100% Stacked Bars

Key Idea
Cluster columns compare categories side by side but hide totals. Stacked bars show the total and the parts. 100% stacked bars give every bar the same length and show shares only , like a pie chart.

To read a middle segment of a stacked bar, subtract its lower end from its upper end.

To make a 100% stacked bar, divide each part by that bar’s total.

Stacked to 100% stacked: always possible. The reverse: not possible without the totals.

If every bar has the same total (such as 24 hours in a day), the chart is both stacked and 100% stacked.

Example 20
Family A spends ₹8,425 in a week, of which ₹1,700 is on food. What share of its budget goes to food?
Solution. Share = 1700/8425.
≈ 0.2018.
≈ 20.2%.
Example 21
A house used 360 kWh for lighting out of 1000 kWh in 2005 and 220 kWh out of 2000 kWh in 2025. Compare the shares.
Solution. 2005: 360/1000 × 100 = 36%.
2025: 220/2000 × 100 = 11%.
The amount fell from 360 to 220 kWh.
The share fell much more, from 36% to 11%, because total use doubled.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 140 of 215
Chapter 10: Understanding Data 10.9 What Can We Infer from Percentages? Ganita Manjari · Class 9
10.9

What Can We Infer from Percentages?

Key Idea
Within one bar a 100% chart compares parts correctly. Across bars a 100% chart cannot compare absolute amounts, because the totals are not shown.
Example 22
A 100% chart shows Fatima’s blooms: summer 50%, monsoon 30%, winter 20%; Naveen’s: summer 40%, monsoon 35%, winter 25%. Can we say Fatima had more summer blooms than Naveen?
Solution. Within Fatima’s garden, 50% is more than 30%, so summer beats monsoon.
Across gardens we need the totals, which the chart does not give.
Case 1: Fatima 210 blooms (105 in summer), Naveen 120 blooms (48 in summer).
Fatima has more.
Case 2: Fatima 180 blooms (90 in summer), Naveen 240 blooms (96 in summer).
Fatima has fewer.
Both cases give the same 100% chart.
So the statement cannot be inferred.
Example 23
A day has 24 hours. Is a chart of how people spend a day a stacked chart or a 100% stacked chart?
Solution. Every bar has the same total: 24 hours.
So the segment lengths show both hours and percentages.
It is both.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 141 of 215

Chapter 10: Understanding Data Stepwise Solutions (Q 10.19 – Q 10.23) Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Chapter 10 Solutions · Question 19 – Question 23
Question 10.19
Original mean = Σwixi/Σwi.
New weights are 2wi.
New mean = Σ(2wi xi)/Σ(2wi).
= 2Σwixi/2Σwi.
= Σwixi/Σwi.
The mean is unchanged: the factor 2 cancels.
Question 10.20
Let the ordinary mean be mord and the weighted mean mw.
New numerator = Σ(wi + 1)xi = Σwixi + Σxi.
New denominator = Σwi + n.
New mean = (Σwi xi + Σxi)/(Σwi + n).
This is the combined mean of the weighted mean (weight Σwi) and the ordinary mean (weight n).
So the new mean lies between the old weighted mean and the ordinary mean.
It stays the same only if they are equal, for example when all weights were already equal.

(v)Possible: chickens fall sharply, cows and sheep fall slightly.
Possible: (iii), (iv), (v).

Averaging the family averages ignores family size.
For student i: members ni, average age ai.
Total age of that family = ni × ai.
Total age of everyone = Σ(ni × ai).
Total number of people = Σni.
Average age = Σ(ni ai)/Σni.
This is a weighted mean with family sizes as weights.

Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms Overview & Key Ideas Ganita Manjari · Class 9
CHAPTER 11
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

The World of Algorithms

The chapter at a glance

Idea Statement
Algorithm A precise, finite, correct step-by-step procedure. Its efficiency is judged by how the work grows with the size of the input.
Column addition Align the digits from the right, add column by column with a carry. Effort grows with the number of digits , not the value.
Carry In base 10 the carry is never more than 1, since 9 + 9 + 1 = 19 < 20 .
Divisors by scanning Test every j from 1 to n : exactly n checks.
Divisor pairs If d | n then n / d | n . Testing j ≤ ⌊√ n ⌋ finds all divisors.
GCD, first algorithm Common divisors of m and n ; report the largest.
Refinements Scan once; stop at m i n ( m , n ) ; keep only the latest common divisor; scan backwards and stop at the first common divisor.
Euclid (c. 300 BCE) g c d ( m , n ) = g c d ( n , m − n ) for m ≥ n .
Āryabhaṭa (499 CE) g c d ( m , n ) = g c d ( n , m m o d n ) . Steps grow with the number of digits.
LCM l c m ( m , n ) = ( m × n )/ g c d ( m , n ) .
Prime factorisation Prime exponents: gcd takes the minimum, lcm the maximum.
Word “algorithm” From al-Khwārizmī (c. 820 CE), who wrote on Indian place-value arithmetic.

Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms 11.1 What Is an Algorithm? Ganita Manjari · Class 9
11.1

What Is an Algorithm?

Key Idea
An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step procedure that arrives at an answer. A good algorithm is precise (anyone can follow it the same way), finite (it always stops), correct (it can be justified) and efficient .

To add 5 and 7 by counting dots we draw 5 dots, 7 more, and count 12. For 473 + 695 this would be hopeless.

The Indian base-ten place-value system lets us add column by column from the right with a carry.

If counting a dot takes 1 second and adding one column with carry takes 15 seconds, then adding 3,347 + 2,729 takes about 6,076 seconds by counting but only 4 × 15 = 60 seconds by columns: about 100 times faster.

Going from a 3-digit to a 4-digit number multiplies the dots by 10 but adds only one column: the effort grows with the number of digits.

Example 1
Compare the time to add 334 + 272 by counting dots (1 second per dot) and by the column algorithm (15 seconds per column).
Solution. Sum = 334 + 272 = 606.
Counting dots: 606 seconds, about 10 minutes.
Column algorithm: 3 columns.
3 × 15 = 45 seconds.
Ratio = 606/45.
≈ 13.
The column algorithm is about 13 times faster.
Example 2
Add 473 and 695 stage by stage.
Solution. Units: 3 + 5 = 8, so write 8, carry 0.
Tens: 7 + 9 = 16, so write 6, carry 1.
Hundreds: 4 + 6 + 1 = 11, so write 11.
The sum is 1168.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 150 of 215
Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms 11.2 The Column Addition Algorithm and Why It Works Ganita Manjari · Class 9
11.2

The Column Addition Algorithm and Why It Works

Key Idea
Algorithm to add two numbers. Step 1. Write the numbers one below the other, digits aligned from the right. Step 2. Add the rightmost digits. If the sum is less than 10 write it and set carry = 0; otherwise write the units digit and set carry = 1. Step 3. Move one column left. Add the two digits and the carry; handle the result as in Step 2. Step 4. Repeat Step 3 until no digits remain. Step 5. If carry = 1, write 1 to the left of the bottom row.

Why it works (place value). A = ak10k + … + a110 + a0. When a0 + b0 ≥ 10 we write a0 + b0 = 10c1 + s0 and move the ten to the next place, so each group of ten at 10i becomes a one at 10i+1.

The carry is at most 1. Each digit is at most 9 and the incoming carry at most 1, so the column sum is at most 9 + 9 + 1 = 19 < 20.

Missing digits count as 0, so numbers of different lengths can be added.

Decimals: align the numbers by the decimal point and pad with zeros.

Example 3
Add 8764 and 2359 using the algorithm.
Solution. Units: 4 + 9 = 13.
Write 3, carry 1.
Tens: 6 + 5 + 1 = 12.
Write 2, carry 1.
Hundreds: 7 + 3 + 1 = 11.
Write 1, carry 1.
Thousands: 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.
Write 1, carry 1.
No digits remain and carry = 1, so write 1 on the left (Step 5).
The sum is 11123.
Example 4
Show that Step 5 is needed to add 999 and 1.
Solution. Units: 9 + 1 = 10.
Write 0, carry 1.
Tens: 9 + 0 + 1 = 10.
Write 0, carry 1.
Hundreds: 9 + 0 + 1 = 10.
Write 0, carry 1.
Without Step 5 the answer would be 000.
With Step 5 we write the carry 1: 1000.
This is correct.
Example 5
Add 12.35 and 4.8.
Solution. Align the decimal points.
Pad 4.8 as 4.80.
Hundredths: 5 + 0 = 5.
Tenths: 3 + 8 = 11.
Write 1, carry 1.
Units: 2 + 4 + 1 = 7.
Tens: 1 + 0 = 1.
The sum is 17.15.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 151 of 215
Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms 11.3 Computing the Divisors of a Number; Data Structures Ganita Manjari · Class 9
11.3

Computing the Divisors of a Number; Data Structures

Key Idea
Algorithm divisors( n ). Step 1. Start with an empty list list-of-divisors. Step 2. For each j = 1, 2, 3, …, n : if j divides n , add j to the list. Step 3. Output the list.

Running through the steps one by one is called executing the algorithm.

The algorithm needs exactly n checks: if n becomes 10 times larger, the work becomes 10 times larger.

Naming intermediate quantities (like list-of-divisors and j) and keeping ordered collections is the start of data structures.

Example 6
Execute divisors(12).
Solution. Start with list = [].
j = 1 divides 12: list = [1].
j = 2 divides 12: list = [1, 2].
j = 3 divides 12: list = [1, 2, 3].
j = 4 divides 12: list = [1, 2, 3, 4].
j = 5 does not divide 12: list unchanged.
j = 6 divides 12: list = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6].
j = 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 do not divide 12.
j = 12 divides 12: list = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12].
Output: [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12] after 12 checks.
Example 7
Write divisors(30) and say how many checks the algorithm makes.
Solution. Test j = 1 to 30.
Divisors of 30: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30.
So divisors(30) = [1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30].
Number of checks = 30.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 152 of 215
Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms 11.4 Greatest Common Divisor: the First Algorithm Ganita Manjari · Class 9
11.4

Greatest Common Divisor: the First Algorithm

Key Idea
The greatest common divisor gcd ( m , n ) is the largest number that divides both m and n . First algorithm. (1) List divisors of m . (2) List divisors of n . (3) Start with an empty list common-divisors. (4) For each x in divisors of m : if x is in divisors of n , add x . (5) Report the rightmost element of common-divisors.

For 54,000 and 81,000 this means 54000 + 81000 = 135000 divisibility checks and thousands of comparisons, though each has 80 divisors: we need much smarter algorithms.

The answer is the rightmost element only because the list is in increasing order.

Example 8
Use the first algorithm to find gcd(18, 24).
Solution. divisors(18) = [1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18].
divisors(24) = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24].
Common divisors = [1, 2, 3, 6].
The rightmost element is 6.
So gcd(18, 24) = 6.
Example 9
Use the first algorithm to find gcd(7, 15).
Solution. divisors(7) = [1, 7].
divisors(15) = [1, 3, 5, 15].
Common divisors = [1].
gcd(7, 15) = 1.
Numbers with gcd 1 are called coprime.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 153 of 215
Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms 11.5 Three Refinements of the GCD Algorithm Ganita Manjari · Class 9
11.5

Three Refinements of the GCD Algorithm

Key Idea
Refinement 1. Scan j = 1 to max ( m , n ) once, collecting divisors of both: max ( m , n ) checks instead of m + n . Refinement 2. A common divisor cannot exceed min ( m , n ) : scan only k = 1 to min ( m , n ) . Refinement 3. Keep a single variable most-recent-common-divisor (start at 1) and update it whenever k divides both. No lists are needed.

Even Refinement 3 scans up to min(m, n), so the work grows with the value of the smaller number.

Backward scan: start k at min(m, n) and go down; the first k that divides both is the gcd, so we can stop at once.

Example 10
Trace Refinement 3 for gcd(8, 12).
Solution. min(8, 12) = 8.
Set most-recent = 1.
k = 2 divides 8 and 12: most-recent = 2.
k = 3 does not divide 8: unchanged.
k = 4 divides 8 and 12: most-recent = 4.
k = 5, 6, 7 do not divide 8: unchanged.
k = 8 does not divide 12: unchanged.
The scan ends.
gcd(8, 12) = 4.
Example 11
Use the backward scan to find gcd(50, 100).
Solution. Start at k = min(50, 100) = 50.
Does 50 divide 50? Yes.
Does 50 divide 100? Yes.
The first common divisor from the top is the gcd.
Stop: gcd(50, 100) = 50 in 1 step.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 154 of 215
Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms 11.6 Euclid’s Subtraction Algorithm Ganita Manjari · Class 9
11.6

Euclid’s Subtraction Algorithm

Key Idea
Euclid’s principle (c. 300 BCE). For m ≥ n : gcd ( m , n ) = gcd ( n , m − n ) . Algorithm. (1) If m < n , reverse them. (2) If n = 0 , report m . (3) Otherwise compute gcd ( n , m − n ) .

Each step replaces the pair by smaller numbers, so the process stops.

Flaw: gcd(99, 2) takes 49 subtractions; in general gcd(2k + 1, 2) takes k. The number of steps grows with the value, not the number of digits.

Example 12
Prove Euclid’s principle: common divisors of m and n are the common divisors of n and m − n.
Solution. Let d divide both m and n.
Then m = ad and n = bd.
m − n = ad − bd
= (a − b)d.
So d divides m − n.
Conversely let d divide n and m − n.
Then n = xd and m − n = yd.
m = n + (m − n)
= (x + y)d.
So d divides m.
The two pairs have the same common divisors, so the same gcd.
Example 13
Run Euclid’s subtraction algorithm on gcd(48, 18).
Solution. gcd(48, 18) = gcd(18, 30) since 48 − 18 = 30.
18 < 30: reverse to gcd(30, 18).
gcd(30, 18) = gcd(18, 12) since 30 − 18 = 12.
gcd(18, 12) = gcd(12, 6) since 18 − 12 = 6.
gcd(12, 6) = gcd(6, 6) since 12 − 6 = 6.
gcd(6, 6) = gcd(6, 0) since 6 − 6 = 0.
n = 0, so the answer is 6.
Example 14
How many subtractions does Euclid’s algorithm need for gcd(101, 2)?
Solution. 101 = 2 × 50 + 1, so k = 50.
Subtract 2 repeatedly: 101, 99, 97, …, 3, 1.
From 101 to 1 there are 50 subtractions.
Then gcd(2, 1), gcd(1, 1), gcd(1, 0) = 1.
The work is about 50 steps for a two-digit number.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 155 of 215
Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms 11.7 Āryabhaṭa’s Division Algorithm Ganita Manjari · Class 9
11.7

Āryabhaṭa’s Division Algorithm

Key Idea
Repeated subtraction of n from m stops with the remainder m m o d n , so we can replace many subtractions by one division. gcd ( m , n ) = gcd ( n , m m o d n ) . Algorithm. (1) If m < n , reverse. (2) If n = 0 , report m . (3) Otherwise compute gcd ( n , m m o d n ) .

gcd(99, 2): 99 mod 2 = 1, then gcd(2, 1), then 2 mod 1 = 0: gcd(1, 0) = 1, only 2 reductions instead of 49.

The number of reductions grows with the number of digits, so very large numbers are handled quickly.

Described in the Āryabhaṭīya (499 CE) using Indian place-value numerals.

Example 15
Find gcd(48, 18) by Āryabhaṭa’s division algorithm.
Solution. 48 mod 18 = 12.
gcd(48, 18) = gcd(18, 12).
18 mod 12 = 6.
gcd(18, 12) = gcd(12, 6).
12 mod 6 = 0.
gcd(12, 6) = gcd(6, 0).
n = 0, so gcd = 6 after 3 reductions.
Example 16
Find gcd(252, 105).
Solution. 252 = 105 × 2 + 42.
gcd(252, 105) = gcd(105, 42).
105 = 42 × 2 + 21.
gcd(105, 42) = gcd(42, 21).
42 = 21 × 2 + 0.
gcd(42, 21) = gcd(21, 0).
gcd = 21.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 156 of 215
Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms 11.8 A Pinch of History: Where “Algorithm” Comes From Ganita Manjari · Class 9
11.8

A Pinch of History: Where “Algorithm” Comes From

Muhammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī (780–850 CE) worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad and admired Indian mathematics.

Around 820 CE he wrote a treatise on the Indian place-value system and the four operations. The Arabic original is lost; its 12th-century Latin translation, Liber Algorismi de numero Indorum, spread Indian arithmetic across Europe.

The Latin form of his name, Algoritmi, gave the word algorismus for Indian methods of calculation, which became algorism and then algorithm.

Today “algorithm” means any well-defined, step-by-step procedure for a class of problems.

11.9

Divisor Pairs, Primes and Prime Factorisation

Key Idea
Divisors come in pairs : if d | n then n / d | n and d × ( n / d ) = n . In every pair one divisor is ≤ √ n . So testing j = 1 to ⌊√ n ⌋ finds all divisors. A prime has exactly two divisors. For gcd and lcm use the prime exponents: minimum for gcd, maximum for lcm.

Proof. If d and d′ with dd′ = n were both greater than √n, then dd′ > √n × √n = n, a contradiction.

The list of divisors found in pairs is not in increasing order, so sort it (or keep a running maximum) when computing a gcd from it.

Prime test: n > 1 is prime exactly when it has no divisor from 2 to ⌊√n⌋.

lcm and gcd: lcm(m, n) × gcd(m, n) = m × n.

Example 17
Find all divisors of 36 by testing numbers only up to ⌊√36⌋.
Solution. ⌊√36⌋ = 6.
1 | 36: pair (1, 36).
2 | 36: pair (2, 18).
3 | 36: pair (3, 12).
4 | 36: pair (4, 9).
5 does not divide 36.
6 | 36: pair (6, 6), a single divisor.
Divisors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36.
There are 9 divisors, found in 6 checks.
Example 18
Is 97 prime?
Solution. √97 is about 9.8, so ⌊√97⌋ = 9.
Test j = 2 to 9.
97 is odd, so 2 does not divide it.
9 + 7 = 16, not a multiple of 3, so 3 does not divide it.
97 does not end in 0 or 5.
7 × 13 = 91 and 7 × 14 = 98, so 7 does not divide it.
Numbers 4, 6, 8, 9 cannot divide 97 because 2 and 3 do not.
No number from 2 to 9 divides 97.
So 97 is prime.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 157 of 215
Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms Chapter Theory Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 19
Use prime factorisations to find gcd and lcm of 360 and 84.
Solution. 360 = 23 × 32 × 5.
84 = 22 × 3 × 7.
Write both with all primes 2, 3, 5, 7.
360 = 23 × 32 × 51 × 70.
84 = 22 × 31 × 50 × 71.
gcd takes the minimum exponents: 22 × 31 × 50 × 70.
= 12.
lcm takes the maximum exponents: 23 × 32 × 51 × 71.
= 8 × 9 × 5 × 7.
= 2520.
Check: 12 × 2520 = 30240 = 360 × 84.
Example 20
Find lcm(18, 24) using the gcd.
Solution. gcd(18, 24) = 6.
lcm = (18/6) × 24.
= 3 × 24.
= 72.
Dividing first keeps the numbers small.

Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms Stepwise Solutions (Q 11.1 – Q 11.6) Ganita Manjari · Class 9
VERIFIED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTIONS

Chapter 11: Solutions to Chapter-End Questions

Question 11.1
Step 1: write 6583 above 3947, aligned from the right.
Step 2 (units): 3 + 7 = 10.
Write 0, carry 1.
Step 3 (tens): 8 + 4 + 1 = 13.
Write 3, carry 1.
Step 3 (hundreds): 5 + 9 + 1 = 15.
Write 5, carry 1.
Step 3 (thousands): 6 + 3 + 1 = 10.
Write 0, carry 1.
Step 4: no more digits.
Step 5: carry is 1, so write 1 on the left.
The result is 10530.
Check: 6583 + 3947 = 10530.
The algorithm works.
Question 11.2
Align from the right.
Units: 8 + 3 = 11.
Write 1, carry 1.
Tens: 1 + 6 + 1 = 8.
Write 8, carry 0.
Hundreds: 7 + 5 = 12.
Write 2, carry 1.
Thousands: 2 + 0 + 1 = 3 (the 3-digit number has no digit here, which counts as 0).
Ten-thousands: 4 + 0 = 4.
The sum is 43281.
Yes, provided a missing leading digit is taken as 0.
Question 11.3
The position of a digit decides its value: units, tens, hundreds, …
Aligning from the right puts equal place values in the same column.
If 523 and 41 were aligned from the left, the 4 (which means 40) would be added to the 5 (which means 500).
That treats 40 as 400 and gives a wrong sum.
So only quantities of the same place value may be added.
Question 11.4
Each digit is at most 9.
In the units column the sum is at most 9 + 9 = 18, so the carry is at most 1.
In any later column the incoming carry is at most 1.
The column sum is at most 9 + 9 + 1 = 19.
19 = 1 × 10 + 9, so the new carry is at most 1.
Since 19 < 20, the carry can never be 2 or more.
Question 11.5
Step 5 matters only when the leftmost column produces a carry.
Works without Step 5: 1234 + 2345.
Leftmost column: 1 + 2 = 3, carry 0.
The answer 3579 is correct.
Fails without Step 5: 473 + 695.
Leftmost column: 4 + 6 + 1 = 11, write 1, carry 1.
Without Step 5 the leading 1 is lost: 168 instead of 1168.
Also 9999 + 1 would give 0000 instead of 10000.
Question 11.6
Step 2 becomes: for each j = n, n − 1, …, 1.
Each j that divides n is added to the list.
The output comes in decreasing order, for example [18, 9, 6, 3, 2, 1].
The number of checks is still n.
So the work is unchanged.

Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms Stepwise Solutions (Q 11.7 – Q 11.12) Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Chapter 11 Solutions · Question 7 – Question 12
Question 11.7
Start with k = min(m, n) and decrease k by 1 each time.
The first k that divides both m and n is the largest common divisor.
So we stop at once and report k.
Example: gcd(50, 100) stops at the first check, k = 50.
The forward scan would have done 50 checks.
This early exit can be much faster.
Question 11.8
Use two pointers i (List 1) and j (List 2), both starting at 1, and an empty list result.
Step 1: while both lists have elements left, compare List 1[i] and List 2[j].
Step 2: if List 1[i] < List 2[j], add List 1[i] to result and increase i.
Step 3: if they are equal, increase both i and j.
Step 4: if List 1[i] > List 2[j], increase j.
Step 5: when List 2 ends, add the remaining elements of List 1 to result.
For List 2 minus List 1, swap the roles of the lists.
Each element is looked at once: at most N1 + N2 steps.
Question 11.9
Use the relation lcm(m, n) × gcd(m, n) = m × n.
Step 1: compute g = gcd(m, n) by Āryabhaṭa’s algorithm.
Step 2: compute q = m/g.
Step 3: output q × n.
Example: gcd(6, 8) = 2, q = 3, lcm = 3 × 8 = 24.
Another method: start with max(m, n) and keep adding it until the number is divisible by min(m, n).
Question 11.10
(i)If d | n then n/d | n.
In every pair one member is at most √n.
So we only examine j = 1 to ⌊√n⌋: that is ⌊√n⌋ numbers.
For n = 10000 that is 100 checks instead of 10000.
(ii)The gcd algorithm reports the rightmost common divisor.
Pairs are produced as [1, n, 2, n/2, …], which is not increasing.
So the list must be sorted first, or a running maximum kept.
Then the algorithm works.
Question 11.11
(i)825 = 375 × 2 + 75.
375 = 75 × 5 + 0.
gcd = 75.
(ii)81000 = 51000 × 1 + 30000.
51000 = 30000 × 1 + 21000.
30000 = 21000 × 1 + 9000.
21000 = 9000 × 2 + 3000.
9000 = 3000 × 3 + 0.
gcd = 3000.
(iii)1789287 = 237656 × 7 + 125695.
237656 = 125695 × 1 + 111961.
125695 = 111961 × 1 + 13734.
111961 = 13734 × 8 + 2089.
13734 = 2089 × 6 + 1200.
2089 = 1200 × 1 + 889.
1200 = 889 × 1 + 311.
889 = 311 × 2 + 267.
311 = 267 × 1 + 44.
267 = 44 × 6 + 3.
44 = 3 × 14 + 2.
3 = 2 × 1 + 1.
2 = 1 × 2 + 0.
gcd = 1 (the numbers are coprime).
(iv)2587392 = 157656 × 16 + 64896.
157656 = 64896 × 2 + 27864.
64896 = 27864 × 2 + 9168.
27864 = 9168 × 3 + 360.
9168 = 360 × 25 + 168.
360 = 168 × 2 + 24.
168 = 24 × 7 + 0.
gcd = 24.
Question 11.12
Divide: m = qn + r with r = m mod n, so r = m − qn.
(⇒) Let d divide m and n.
m = ad and n = bd.
r = ad − q(bd)
= (a − qb)d.
So d divides r as well as n.
(⇐) Let d divide n and r.
n = bd and r = cd.
m = qn + r
= (qb + c)d.
So d divides m as well as n.
The pairs {m, n} and {n, r} therefore have the same common divisors.
Hence gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, m mod n).

Chapter 11: The World of Algorithms Stepwise Solutions (Q 11.13 – Q 11.15) Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Chapter 11 Solutions · Question 13 – Question 15
Question 11.13
Method 1, using divisors.
Step 1: if n ≤ 1, report False.
Step 2: compute L = divisors(n).
Step 3: if L has exactly 2 elements (1 and n), report True.
Step 4: otherwise report False.
Method 2, faster (trial division).
Step 1: if n ≤ 1 report False
if n = 2 report True.
Step 2: if n mod 2 = 0 report False.
Step 3: for each odd j from 3 to ⌊√n⌋: if j divides n, report False.
Step 4: report True.
Question 11.14
Step 1: start with an empty list prime-divisors.
Step 2: compute all-divisors = divisors(n).
Step 3: for each d in all-divisors: if prime(d) is True, add d to prime-divisors.
Step 4: output prime-divisors.
Example: divisors(180) = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 30, 36, 45, 60, 90, 180].
The primes among them are 2, 3, 5.
primedivisors(180) = [2, 3, 5].
Question 11.15
Algorithm.
Step 1: set temp = n, d = 2, and an empty dictionary factors.
Step 2: while d × d ≤ temp: count = 0.
Step 3: while d divides temp, divide temp by d and add 1 to count.
Step 4: if count > 0, record factors[d] = count.
Increase d by 1.
Step 5: if temp > 1, record factors[temp] = 1.
Step 6: output factors.
(i)Representations of 180: the dictionary {2: 2, 3: 2, 5: 1}, the list of pairs [(2, 2), (3, 2), (5, 1)], or the list [2, 2, 3, 3, 5].
(ii)List all primes that occur in either number, using exponent 0 where a prime is missing.
gcd takes the minimum exponent of each prime.
lcm takes the maximum exponent of each prime.
Example: 180 = 22 32 5 and 75 = 3 · 52.
gcd = 20 × 31 × 51 = 15.
lcm = 22 × 32 × 52 = 900.

Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals Overview & Key Ideas Ganita Manjari · Class 9
CHAPTER 12
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

Quadrilaterals

The chapter at a glance

Idea Statement
Types Convex, non-convex (a reflex angle), self-intersecting (opposite sides cross), non-planar. Angle sum of a plane simple quadrilateral is 360°.
Parallelogram Opposite sides parallel. Then opposite sides and angles are equal, adjacent angles are supplementary and the diagonals bisect each other.
Tests for a parallelogram Both pairs of opposite sides equal; or one pair equal and parallel; or diagonals bisect each other.
Special parallelograms Rectangle: one right angle (equal diagonals). Rhombus: four equal sides (perpendicular diagonals). Square: both.
Midpoint theorem P , Q midpoints of A B , A C : P Q ∥ B C and P Q = ½ B C . Converse: a line through the midpoint of one side parallel to a second side bisects the third.
Centroid Medians meet at G , dividing each in the ratio 2 : 1 from the vertex.
Varignon parallelogram The midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral form a parallelogram with sides half the diagonals.
Trapezium midline E F ∥ A B ∥ D C and E F = ½( A B + D C ) .
Tiling Copies meet around a point only if the angles add to 360°. Triangles, parallelograms and every quadrilateral tile; regular pentagons do not.
Polygons Angle sum ( n − 2) × 180° . Diagonals n ( n − 3)/2 . Four lengths form a quadrilateral iff the largest is less than the sum of the other three.
Coordinates Midpoint (( x 1 + x 2 )/2, ( y 1 + y 2 )/2) . For a parallelogram A B C D : D = A + C − B .
