Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals 12.1 Quadrilaterals and Their Types Ganita Manjari · Class 9
12.1

Quadrilaterals and Their Types

Key Idea
A quadrilateral (4-gon) is formed by four distinct points A , B , C , D joined in order by A B , B C , C D , D A , with no three consecutive points on a line. A C and B D are its diagonals . The internal angle at a vertex is the angle between the two sides at that vertex that contains the opposite vertex . This works for non-convex quadrilaterals too.

Convex: every internal angle is less than 180° and both diagonals lie inside.

Non-convex: one internal angle is greater than 180° (a reflex angle); one diagonal lies outside.

Self-intersecting: two opposite sides cross, so the figure is not a simple polygon.

Non-planar: the four points do not lie in one plane; it is a spatial figure, not a flat polygon.

Opposite sides have no common endpoint; opposite angles have no common side.

Example 1
In a quadrilateral ABCD, ∠A = 95°, ∠B = 80°, ∠C = 110°. Find ∠D.
Solution. The angle sum of a plane simple quadrilateral is 360°.
∠D = 360° − (95° + 80° + 110°).
= 360° − 285°.
= 75°.
Example 2
Can a convex quadrilateral have angles 100°, 100°, 100°, 100°?
Solution. The sum is 4 × 100° = 400°.
A plane simple quadrilateral has angle sum 360°.
400° ≠ 360°.
So no such quadrilateral exists.
Example 3
A quadrilateral has an internal angle of 210°. Name its type.
Solution. An internal angle greater than 180° is a reflex angle.
So the quadrilateral is non-convex.
The other three angles add up to 360° − 210° = 150°.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 165 of 215
Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals 12.2 Parallelograms, Rectangles, Rhombuses and Squares Ganita Manjari · Class 9
12.2

Parallelograms, Rectangles, Rhombuses and Squares

Key Idea
A parallelogram has both pairs of opposite sides parallel. Then: opposite sides are equal; opposite angles are equal; adjacent angles are supplementary; the diagonals bisect each other . Rectangle: a parallelogram with one right angle (all angles 90°, equal diagonals). Rhombus: a parallelogram with four equal sides (perpendicular diagonals that bisect the angles). Square: both.
Figure Sides Angles Diagonals
Parallelogram opposite equal opposite equal bisect each other
Rectangle opposite equal all 90° equal, bisect
Rhombus all four equal opposite equal perpendicular, bisect angles
Square all four equal all 90° equal, perpendicular
Key Idea
Three tests for a parallelogram (each alone is enough): Test 1: both pairs of opposite sides are equal. Test 2: one pair of opposite sides is both equal and parallel. Test 3: the diagonals bisect each other.

Use each test exactly as stated: one equal pair, or one parallel pair, alone is not enough.

Converses: a parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle; a parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals is a rhombus.

Example 4
Prove Test 1: if AB = CD and BC = DA in quadrilateral ABCD, then it is a parallelogram.
Solution. Draw diagonal AC.
In Δ ABC and Δ CDA: AB = CD (given).
BC = DA (given).
AC = CA (common).
So Δ ABC ≅ Δ CDA (SSS).
∠BAC = ∠DCA, so AB ∥ CD (alternate angles).
∠BCA = ∠DAC, so BC ∥ AD.
Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel: ABCD is a parallelogram.
Example 5
Prove Test 2: if AB = CD and AB ∥ CD, then ABCD is a parallelogram.
Solution. Draw diagonal AC.
∠BAC = ∠DCA (alternate angles, AB ∥ CD).
AB = CD (given).
AC = CA (common).
So Δ BAC ≅ Δ DCA (SAS).
Hence ∠BCA = ∠DAC.
These are alternate angles, so BC ∥ AD.
Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel: ABCD is a parallelogram.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 166 of 215
Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals Chapter Theory Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 6
Prove Test 3: if the diagonals AC and BD meet at O with AO = OC and BO = OD, then ABCD is a parallelogram.
Solution. ∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite).
In Δ AOB and Δ COD: AO = OC and BO = OD (given).
So Δ AOB ≅ Δ COD (SAS).
Hence ∠ABO = ∠CDO, so AB ∥ CD (alternate angles).
In the same way Δ AOD ≅ Δ COB gives AD ∥ BC.
Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel: ABCD is a parallelogram.
Example 7
The diagonals of a quadrilateral meet at O with AO = OC = 4 cm and BO = OD = 3 cm. Classify it.
Solution. The diagonals bisect each other.
By Test 3, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
No right angle or equal sides are given.
So we cannot say it is a rectangle or a rhombus.
Example 8
Two adjacent angles of a parallelogram are 3x and 2x. Find all four angles.
Solution. Adjacent angles are supplementary.
3x + 2x = 180°.
x = 36°.
The angles are 108° and 72°.
Opposite angles are equal: 108°, 72°, 108°, 72°.
Example 9
A rhombus has side 13 cm and one diagonal 10 cm. Find the other diagonal and the area.
Solution. The diagonals bisect each other at right angles.
Half of the given diagonal = 5 cm.
Half of the other diagonal = √(132 − 52).
= √(169 − 25).
= √144.
= 12 cm.
The other diagonal = 24 cm.
Area = ½ × 10 × 24 = 120 cm².
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 167 of 215
Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals 12.3 Proofs Using Parallel Lines and Congruent Triangles Ganita Manjari · Class 9
12.3

Proofs Using Parallel Lines and Congruent Triangles

Key Idea
Draw a diagonal , find two congruent triangles by SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS, and transfer the equality or parallelism. Write: Given , Construction , Reason (name the theorem) and Conclusion (what was to be shown).

Useful angle facts: alternate angles, corresponding angles and vertically opposite angles between parallel lines.

Never use a converse unless its extra condition has been established.

Example 10
Prove that the opposite sides and angles of a parallelogram are equal, and that its diagonals bisect each other.
Solution. Let ABCD be a parallelogram.
Draw diagonal AC.
∠BAC = ∠DCA (alternate angles, AB ∥ CD).
∠BCA = ∠DAC (alternate angles, AD ∥ BC).
AC = CA (common).
So Δ ABC ≅ Δ CDA (ASA).
AB = CD
BC = AD and ∠B = ∠D.
Adding ∠BAC + ∠CAD: ∠A = ∠C.
Let the diagonals meet at O.
In Δ AOB and Δ COD: ∠OAB = ∠OCD, ∠AOB = ∠COD and AB = CD.
So Δ AOB ≅ Δ COD (AAS).
AO = OC and BO = OD: the diagonals bisect each other.
Example 11
Prove that the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular.
Solution. Let ABCD be a rhombus with diagonals meeting at O.
AB = BC
= CD
= DA.
The diagonals bisect each other: AO = OC and BO = OD.
In Δ AOB and Δ COB: AB = CB, AO = CO, BO = BO.
So Δ AOB ≅ Δ COB (SSS).
∠AOB = ∠COB.
They form a straight angle: ∠AOB + ∠COB = 180°.
So each is 90°.
The diagonals are perpendicular.
Example 12
Prove that a parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle.
Solution. Let ABCD be a parallelogram with AC = BD.
In Δ ABC and Δ DCB: AB = DC (opposite sides).
BC = CB (common).
AC = DB (given).
So Δ ABC ≅ Δ DCB (SSS).
∠ABC = ∠DCB.
Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary: ∠ABC + ∠DCB = 180°.
So ∠ABC = 90°.
A parallelogram with one right angle is a rectangle.
Example 13
Prove that a parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals is a rhombus.
Solution. Let the diagonals of parallelogram ABCD meet at O with AC ⊥ BD.
AO = OC (diagonals bisect each other).
In Δ AOB and Δ COB: AO = CO.
∠AOB = ∠COB
= 90°.
BO = BO (common).
So Δ AOB ≅ Δ COB (SAS).
AB = CB.
Adjacent sides are equal, so all four sides are equal.
ABCD is a rhombus.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 168 of 215
Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals 12.4 The Midpoint Theorem and the Centroid Ganita Manjari · Class 9
12.4

The Midpoint Theorem and the Centroid

Key Idea
Midpoint theorem. If P and Q are the midpoints of A B and A C in Δ A B C , then P Q ∥ B C and P Q = ½ B C . Converse. A line through the midpoint of one side parallel to a second side bisects the third side. Basic proportionality. If P Q ∥ B C , then A P / P B = A Q / Q C . Centroid. The three medians meet at G , and A G : G D = 2 : 1 along each median.
Example 14
Prove the Midpoint Theorem.
Solution. Let P, Q be the midpoints of AB, AC.
Through P draw a line parallel to BC meeting AC at Q′.
Δ APQ′ and Δ ABC have equal corresponding angles, so they are similar.
AP/AB = 1/2, so AQ′/AC = 1/2.
So Q′ is the midpoint of AC, which is Q.
Hence PQ ∥ BC.
Also PQ/BC = AP/AB = 1/2.
So PQ = ½BC.
Example 15
In Δ ABC the sides are 8 cm, 10 cm and 12 cm. A triangle is formed by joining the midpoints of the sides. Find its perimeter.
Solution. Each side of the new triangle is half of the corresponding side.
Sides: 4, 5, 6 cm.
Perimeter = 4 + 5 + 6.
= 15 cm.
This is half the perimeter of Δ ABC.
Example 16
In Δ ABC, P is the midpoint of AB and PQ ∥ BC meets AC at Q. Given AC = 14 cm, find AQ and QC.
Solution. By the converse, Q is the midpoint of AC.
AQ = ½ × 14.
= 7 cm.
QC = 7 cm.
Example 17
In Δ ABC, PQ ∥ BC with P on AB and Q on AC. AP = 3, PB = 6, AQ = 4. Find QC.
Solution. By the basic proportionality theorem, AP/PB = AQ/QC.
3/6 = 4/QC.
QC = 4 × 6/3.
= 8.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 169 of 215
Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals 12.5 The Varignon Parallelogram Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 18
The median AD of a triangle is 12 cm. Find AG and GD where G is the centroid.
Solution. G divides AD in the ratio 2 : 1 from A.
AG = 2/3 × 12
= 8 cm.
GD = 1/3 × 12
= 4 cm.
Example 19
A(0, 0), B(6, 0), C(0, 9) are the vertices of a triangle. Find the centroid using the 2 : 1 ratio.
Solution. The midpoint of BC is D = ((6 + 0)/2, (0 + 9)/2) = (3, 4.5).
G = A + 2/3 (D − A).
= (0 + 2/3 × 3, 0 + 2/3 × 4.5).
= (2, 3).
12.5

The Varignon Parallelogram

Key Idea
Join the midpoints P , Q , R , S of the sides of any quadrilateral A B C D in order: P Q R S is a parallelogram . Its sides are parallel to the diagonals of A B C D and half their lengths .

It holds for convex, non-convex and self-intersecting quadrilaterals, and also in space.

If AC = BD then PQRS is a rhombus; if AC ⊥ BD then it is a rectangle; if both, a square.

PQRS shrinks to a segment when the diagonals of ABCD are parallel.

Example 20
Prove that PQRS is a parallelogram.
Solution. In Δ ABC: P, Q are midpoints of AB, BC.
So PQ ∥ AC and PQ = ½AC.
In Δ ADC: S, R are midpoints of AD, DC.
So SR ∥ AC and SR = ½AC.
Hence PQ ∥ SR and PQ = SR.
One pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel.
By Test 2, PQRS is a parallelogram.
Example 21
The diagonals of a quadrilateral are 10 cm and 14 cm. Find the perimeter of its Varignon parallelogram.
Solution. Sides of PQRS are half the diagonals.
Sides: 5 cm and 7 cm.
Perimeter = 2(5 + 7).
= 24 cm.
Example 22
What is the Varignon parallelogram of a rectangle?
Solution. The diagonals of a rectangle are equal.
So PQ = QR (each is half a diagonal).
A parallelogram with equal adjacent sides is a rhombus.
So it is a rhombus.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 170 of 215
Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals 12.6 The Trapezium Midline Ganita Manjari · Class 9
12.6

The Trapezium Midline

Key Idea
A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides. If E , F are the midpoints of the non-parallel sides, then E F ∥ A B ∥ D C and E F = ½( A B + D C ) .
Example 23
Prove the trapezium midline theorem.
Solution. Let AB ∥ DC, with E, F the midpoints of AD, BC.
Draw diagonal AC.
In Δ ADC the line through E parallel to DC meets AC at its midpoint G.
So EG = ½DC.
In Δ ABC the line through G parallel to AB meets BC at its midpoint.
That midpoint is F, so GF = ½AB.
E
G
F lie on one line parallel to AB and DC.
EF = EG + GF.
= ½DC + ½AB.
= ½(AB + DC).
Example 24
The parallel sides of a trapezium are 12 cm and 8 cm. Find the length of its midline.
Solution. EF = ½(AB + DC).
= ½ × (12 + 8).
= 10 cm.
Example 25
The midline of a trapezium is 15 cm and one parallel side is 22 cm. Find the other.
Solution. 15 = ½(22 + x).
30 = 22 + x.
x = 8 cm.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 171 of 215
Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals 12.7 Tiling the Plane Ganita Manjari · Class 9
12.7

Tiling the Plane

Key Idea
Copies tile the plane if they cover it with no gaps or overlaps. Around a point the angles must add to 360° . Every triangle and every quadrilateral (even non-convex) tiles the plane. A regular pentagon does not.

Triangle: attach a half-turn copy along a side to get a parallelogram; translate it in two directions.

Quadrilateral: the four angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°, so four copies fit round a point.

Regular polygons alone: triangle (6 × 60°), square (4 × 90°) and hexagon (3 × 120°) tile. Pentagon (108°) and octagon (135°) do not, since 360° is not a whole-number multiple.

Example 26
Show that a regular pentagon cannot tile the plane.
Solution. Interior angle = (5 − 2) × 180°/5.
= 540°/5.
= 108°.
Copies meeting at a point need k × 108° = 360°.
360/108 = 10/3, not a whole number.
So gaps or overlaps always occur.
Example 27
Which of these regular polygons tile the plane alone: triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, octagon?
Solution. Interior angles: 60°, 90°, 108°, 120°, 135°.
360/60 = 6, whole: triangle tiles.
360/90 = 4, whole: square tiles.
360/108 = 10/3, not whole: pentagon does not.
360/120 = 3, whole: hexagon tiles.
360/135 = 8/3, not whole: octagon does not.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 172 of 215
Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals 12.8 Polygons, Areas and Existence of Quadrilaterals Ganita Manjari · Class 9
12.8

Polygons, Areas and Existence of Quadrilaterals

Key Idea
Angle sum of a plane simple n -gon = ( n − 2) × 180° (draw diagonals from one vertex: n − 2 triangles). Number of diagonals = n ( n − 3)/2 . A quadrilateral with sides a , b , c , d exists iff the largest is less than the sum of the other three . Trapezium area = ½( s u m o f p a r a l l e l s i d e s ) × h e i g h t .
Example 28
Find the angle sum and the number of diagonals of an octagon.
Solution. n = 8.
Angle sum = (8 − 2) × 180°.
= 1080°.
Diagonals = 8 × 5/2.
= 20.
Example 29
Find each interior angle of a regular decagon.
Solution. n = 10.
Angle sum = 8 × 180° = 1440°.
Each angle = 1440°/10.
= 144°.
Example 30
Can a quadrilateral have sides 3, 4, 5, 13? What about 3, 4, 5, 10?
Solution. Largest side must be less than the sum of the others.
For 3, 4, 5, 13: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12.
13 < 12 is false, so no.
For 3, 4, 5, 10: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12.
10 < 12 is true, so yes.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 173 of 215
Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals 12.9 Coordinates and Symmetry Ganita Manjari · Class 9
12.9

Coordinates and Symmetry

Key Idea
Midpoint of ( x 1 , y 1 ) and ( x 2 , y 2 ) : (( x 1 + x 2 )/2, ( y 1 + y 2 )/2) . In a parallelogram A B C D the diagonals share a midpoint, so D = A + C − B . Central symmetry: a half-turn about the intersection O of the diagonals maps A ↔ C and B ↔ D .
Figure Reflection axes Rotational symmetry
General parallelogram none half-turn only
Rectangle 2 (through midpoints of opposite sides) half-turn
Rhombus 2 (the diagonals) half-turn
Square 4 90°, 180°, 270°
General quadrilateral usually none usually none
Example 31
Find the midpoint of A(−2, 4) and C(6, 0).
Solution. x = (−2 + 6)/2
= 2.
y = (4 + 0)/2
= 2.
M = (2, 2).
Example 32
A(1, 1), B(5, 1), C(6, 4) are consecutive vertices of a parallelogram. Find D and check.
Solution. D = A + C − B.
xD = 1 + 6 − 5
= 2.
yD = 1 + 4 − 1
= 4.
D = (2, 4).
Midpoint of AC = (3.5, 2.5).
Midpoint of BD = ((5 + 2)/2, (1 + 4)/2) = (3.5, 2.5).
The midpoints agree, so the diagonals bisect each other.
Example 33
A(−2, −1), B(2, −1), C(4, 2) are consecutive vertices of a parallelogram. Find D.
Solution. xD = −2 + 4 − 2
= 0.
yD = −1 + 2 − (−1)
= 2.
D = (0, 2).
Example 34
Show that a half-turn about O maps a parallelogram onto itself.
Solution. The diagonals bisect each other at O.
A half-turn about O sends A to C, since O is the midpoint of AC.
It sends B to D, since O is the midpoint of BD.
So the vertices exchange in pairs.
Sides and angles match in pairs.
Hence the parallelogram maps onto itself and O is its centre of symmetry.

Chapter 12: Solutions to Chapter-End Questions

Question 12.1
(i)Sides sharing an endpoint with AB: AD and BC.
The side with no common endpoint with AB: CD.
(ii)Angles sharing a side with ∠A: ∠B and ∠D.
The angle sharing no side with ∠A: ∠C.
(iii)Opposite sides are two sides with no common endpoint.
Opposite angles are two angles that have no side in common.
Question 12.2

Two lines that meet at a point lie in one plane.
So A, B, C, D all lie in the plane of AB and CD.
Hence the quadrilateral is planar.
No: a self-intersecting quadrilateral cannot be non-planar.
Question 12.3
(i)True.
Adjacent angles are supplementary, so a right angle forces all four to be 90°.
(ii)False.
The diagonals of every rhombus are perpendicular.
A rhombus that is not a square (angles 60° and 120°) is a counterexample.
(iii)True: proved in Section 12.3 using SSS on triangles ABC and DCB.
Question 12.4
Each interior angle of a regular pentagon is 540°/5 = 108°.
Around a point we would need k × 108° = 360°.
360/108 = 10/3, not a whole number.
So the regular pentagon cannot tile the plane.
Question 12.5
EF = ½(3 + 5)
= 4 cm.

If x ≤ 11: the largest side is 11, so 11 < 2 + 5 + x, giving x > 4.
If x > 11: x < 2 + 5 + 11 = 18.
So 4 < x < 18.
x = 100: impossible.
x = 10: possible.
x = 1: impossible.

Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals Stepwise Solutions (Q 12.7 – Q 12.12) Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Chapter 12 Solutions · Question 7 – Question 12
Question 12.7
From each vertex there are n − 3 diagonals (not to itself or its two neighbours).
Each diagonal is counted twice.
Number of diagonals = n(n − 3)/2.
For n = 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8: 0, 2, 5, 9, 14, 20.
Adding a side adds (n + 1)(n − 2)/2 − n(n − 3)/2.
= (n2 − n − 2 − n2 + 3n)/2.
= (2n − 2)/2 = n − 1 diagonals.
Question 12.8
Draw diagonals from one vertex to the n − 3 non-adjacent vertices.
They divide the polygon into n − 2 triangles.
Each triangle has angle sum 180°.
Sum = (n − 2) × 180°.
n = 3, 4, 5, 6, 7: 180°, 360°, 540°, 720°, 900°.
Question 12.9
At the vertex draw the two rays that contain the two sides.
These rays form two angles, one smaller and one larger than 180° (or both 180°).
Choose the one whose interior contains the opposite vertex.
That is the internal angle at the vertex.
In a non-convex quadrilateral the chosen angle can exceed 180°.
Question 12.10
∠BAC = ∠CAD (given).
∠BAC = ∠ACD (alternate angles, AB ∥ CD).
∠CAD = ∠ACB (alternate angles, AD ∥ BC).
So ∠ACD = ∠ACB: AC bisects ∠C.
In Δ ABC: ∠BAC = ∠ACB.
So AB = BC (sides opposite equal angles).
Adjacent sides of the parallelogram are equal, so all four sides are equal.
ABCD is a rhombus.
Question 12.11
(i)Yes.
A diagonal bisecting the angles at both its ends makes congruent triangles (ASA), giving four equal sides.
(ii)Yes.
Diagonals bisecting each other make a parallelogram
perpendicular diagonals make it a rhombus.
(iii)No.
An isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals but is not a rectangle.
Add the condition “it is a parallelogram”
then it is a rectangle.
Question 12.12
By the midpoint theorem PQ = ½BC, PR = ½AC, QR = ½AB.
Δ APQ has sides AP = ½AB
AQ = ½AC
PQ = ½BC.
Δ PQR has sides QR = ½AB
PR = ½AC
PQ = ½BC.
Corresponding sides are equal, so Δ PQR ≅ Δ QPA (SSS).
The same argument works for the triangles at B and C.
To rebuild: through P draw a line parallel to QR, through Q one parallel to PR, through R one parallel to PQ.
The three lines form Δ ABC.
Yes, ABC can be reconstructed.

Chapter 12: Quadrilaterals Stepwise Solutions (Q 12.13 – Q 12.18) Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Chapter 12 Solutions · Question 13 – Question 18
Question 12.13
Let MN meet AD at E.
MN ∥ BC (midpoint theorem).
So ME ∥ BD.
In Δ ABD, M is the midpoint of AB and ME ∥ BD.
By the converse of the midpoint theorem, E is the midpoint of AD.
So MN bisects AD.
Question 12.14
Let E be the midpoint of AD.
In Δ ADC: E, G are midpoints of AD, AC, so EG ∥ DC.
In Δ ADB: E, H are midpoints of AD, DB, so EH ∥ AB.
AB ∥ DC, so EG and EH are both parallel to AB through E.
Hence E, G, H are on one line parallel to AB.
So GH ∥ AB.
AB ≠ CD makes ABCD a genuine trapezium (not a parallelogram)
the result also holds for a parallelogram.
Question 12.15
(i)PQRS is a parallelogram (Varignon).
PR and QS are its diagonals.
Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
(ii)PQ = ½AC and QR = ½BD.
If AC = BD, then PQ = QR.
A parallelogram with equal adjacent sides is a rhombus.
The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular, so PR ⊥ QS.
Converse: if PR ⊥ QS, then PQRS is a parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals, hence a rhombus.
Then PQ = QR, so ½AC = ½BD and AC = BD.
The converse is true.
Question 12.16
DP = BQ, so DQ = DP + PQ = BQ + PQ = BP.
In Δ ABP and Δ CDQ: AB = CD (opposite sides).
∠ABP = ∠CDQ (alternate angles, AB ∥ CD).
BP = DQ (shown).
So Δ ABP ≅ Δ CDQ (SAS).
AP = CQ and ∠APB = ∠CQD.
∠APQ = 180° − ∠APB and ∠CQP = 180° − ∠CQD, so ∠APQ = ∠CQP.
These are alternate angles for AP and CQ, so AP ∥ CQ.
One pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel.
APCQ is a parallelogram (vertices in the order A
P
C
Q).
Question 12.17
In Δ AOP and Δ COQ: ∠OAP = ∠OCQ (alternate angles, AB ∥ CD).
AO = OC (diagonals bisect each other).
∠AOP = ∠COQ (vertically opposite).
So Δ AOP ≅ Δ COQ (ASA).
OP = OQ.
O is the midpoint of PQ.
Question 12.18
Δ APQ ~ Δ ABC, so AP/AB = AQ/AC.
(i)AB = 3, ratio = 1/3, so AC = 3√5.
QC = AC − AQ
= 3√5 − √5
= 2√5.
(ii)AB = 4/3, ratio = 3/4, so AC = 4√5/3.
QC = 4√5/3 − √5
= √5/3.
(iii)AB = 5/3, ratio = 3/5, so AC = 5√5/3.
QC = 5√5/3 − √5
= 2√5/3.
(iv)AB/AP = AC/AQ.
(AP + PB)/AP = (AQ + QC)/AQ.
1 + PB/AP = 1 + QC/AQ.
PB/AP = QC/AQ.
So AP/PB = AQ/QC.

Chapter 12 Solutions · Question 19 – Question 24
Question 12.19
(i)Extend PQ to S with QS = PQ.
AQ = QC and ∠AQP = ∠CQS (vertically opposite).
Δ AQP ≅ Δ CQS (SAS).
CS = AP
= PB and CS ∥ AP.
So PBCS has PB equal and parallel to CS: a parallelogram.
PS ∥ BC and PS = BC.
PQ = ½PS
= ½BC and PQ ∥ BC.
(ii)Let P be the midpoint of AB and PQ ∥ BC.
Through C draw CS ∥ BA meeting PQ extended at S.
PBCS is a parallelogram, so CS = PB = AP.
Δ APQ ≅ Δ CSQ (ASA).
So AQ = QC: Q is the midpoint of AC.
Question 12.20
(i)Let EF meet AC at G.
In Δ ADC: E is the midpoint of AD and EG ∥ DC.
So G is the midpoint of AC and EG = ½DC.
In Δ CAB: G is the midpoint of AC and GF ∥ AB.
So F is the midpoint of BC and GF = ½AB.
EF = EG + GF
= ½(AB + CD).
(ii)Draw EF′ ∥ AB meeting BC at F′.
By (i), F′ is the midpoint of BC, so F′ = F.
Hence EF ∥ AB.
Question 12.21
Adjacent angles are supplementary: ∠A + ∠B = 180°.
The bisectors at A and B meet at an angle of 180° − (∠A/2 + ∠B/2) = 90°.
So bisectors at adjacent vertices are perpendicular.
The bisectors at A and C make equal angles (∠A/2 = ∠C/2) with the parallel lines AB, CD.
Corresponding angles are equal, so they are parallel.
The four bisectors give two pairs of parallel lines with adjacent lines perpendicular.
Their intersection points form a rectangle.
If AB = BC the parallelogram is a rhombus: the bisectors at A, C coincide (along AC) and those at B, D coincide (along BD).
Then there are only two lines and no rectangle.
Question 12.22
(i)Choose any point A.
Since P is the midpoint of AB, B = 2P − A.
Since Q is the midpoint of BC, C = 2Q − B.
Since R is the midpoint of CD, D = 2R − C.
S = P + R − Q (parallelogram), so S is automatically the midpoint of DA.
(ii)A was chosen freely, so every choice of A gives a different quadrilateral with the same PQRS.
(iii)PQ = ½AC and QR = ½BD with PQ ∥ AC, QR ∥ BD.
If PQRS is a square: PQ = QR gives AC = BD
PQ ⊥ QR gives AC ⊥ BD.
Conversely, if AC = BD and AC ⊥ BD: PQ = QR and PQ ⊥ QR.
A parallelogram with equal adjacent sides and a right angle is a square.
Question 12.23
E lies on AB and on CD.
In Δ EAD: ∠EAD = ∠A and ∠EDA = ∠D.
So ∠A + ∠D = 180° − ∠AED.
In Δ EBC: ∠EBC = ∠B and ∠ECB = ∠C.
So ∠B + ∠C = 180° − ∠BEC.
∠AED = ∠BEC (vertically opposite).
Sum = 360° − 2∠AED.
∠AED > 0, so the sum is less than 360°.
For a sum of 2° take ∠AED = 179°.
360° − 2 × 179° = 2°.
So yes, such a figure can be drawn.
Question 12.24
(i)DN ∥ MB and DN = MB (halves of equal parallel sides).
So DMBN is a parallelogram and DM ∥ NB.
Let DM meet AC at P and NB meet AC at Q.
In Δ ABQ: M is the midpoint of AB and MP ∥ BQ, so P is the midpoint of AQ: AP = PQ.
In Δ CDP: N is the midpoint of CD and NQ ∥ DP, so Q is the midpoint of CP: PQ = QC.
So AP = PQ = QC: AC is trisected.
(ii)Method 1: draw a parallelogram having PQ as a diagonal and repeat the construction.
Method 2 (Exercise 11): draw a ray from P, mark three equal steps, join the last mark to Q and draw parallels through the other marks.
By the basic proportionality theorem the parallels cut PQ into three equal parts.
Method 3 (centroid): make PQ the median AD of a triangle ABC (P = A, Q = D with D the midpoint of BC).
Draw a second median
the centroid G divides AD in the ratio 2 : 1, so G is one trisection point.
The midpoint of AG gives the other.

Question 12.25
No.
Take a square A(0, 0), B(3, 0), C(3, 3), D(0, 3).
Choose the points one-third of the way along each side: P(1, 0), Q(3, 1), R(2, 3), S(0, 2).

Question 12.26
Let ABCD be non-planar and draw diagonal AC.
At each end of AC three edges meet in space.
In any such corner, one face angle is less than the sum of the other two.
So ∠BAD < ∠BAC + ∠CAD.
Likewise ∠BCD < ∠BCA + ∠ACD.
∠A + ∠B + ∠C + ∠D < (∠BAC + ∠B + ∠BCA) + (∠CAD + ∠D + ∠ACD).
Each bracket is the angle sum of a triangle, 180°.
So the sum is less than 360°.
For 2°: make a long thin kite and fold the hinge until B and D nearly meet.
All four angles can be made as small as we like, so a sum of 2° is possible.
Question 12.27
Take A(0, 0), B(1, 0), C(1, 1), D(0, 1), so the area is 1.
Line from A to (1, 0.5): y = 0.5x.
Line from D to (0.5, 0): y = 1 − 2x.
Intersection: 0.5x = 1 − 2x, so x = 0.4 and y = 0.2.
By the 90° symmetry the other vertices are (0.8, 0.4), (0.6, 0.8), (0.2, 0.6).
Side of the shaded square = √((0.8 − 0.4)2 + (0.4 − 0.2)2).
= √(0.16 + 0.04).
= √0.2.
Area = (√0.2)2 = 0.2 = 1/5.
Exactly 1/5 of the square is shaded.

Chapter 13: Two Variables, One Line Overview & Key Ideas Ganita Manjari · Class 9
CHAPTER 13
CLASS 9 MATHEMATICS · GANITA MANJARI

Two Variables, One Line

The chapter at a glance

Idea Statement
Standard form a x + b y + c = 0 , with a and b not both zero. Single-variable equations are special cases ( x + 0 y − 8 = 0 ).
Solution An ordered pair ( u , v ) that satisfies the equation. There are infinitely many.
Graph A straight line; every point on it is a solution and every solution is a point on it.
Intercepts y -intercept (0, − c / b ) ; x -intercept (− c / a , 0) . The line passes through the origin iff c = 0 .
Slope m = rise ÷ run = ( y 2 − y 1 )/( x 2 − x 1 ) . For y = m x + d : slope m , y -intercept d . From a x + b y + c = 0 : m = − a / b .
Types of slope Positive rises, negative falls, zero is horizontal, vertical lines have undefined slope.
Pair of equations Two conditions on two unknowns: a 1 x + b 1 y + c 1 = 0 and a 2 x + b 2 y + c 2 = 0 .
Methods Substitution (solve one equation for a variable) and elimination (equalise coefficients and add or subtract).
Ratio test a 1 / a 2 ≠ b 1 / b 2 : one solution. All three ratios equal: infinitely many. First two equal, third different: none.
Parallel lines Equal slopes and different intercepts never meet.
Check Always substitute the answer back into both original equations.

Chapter 13: Two Variables, One Line 13.1 Linear Equations in Two Variables and the Standard Form Ganita Manjari · Class 9
13.1

Linear Equations in Two Variables and the Standard Form

Key Idea
If Radha buys x kg of mangoes at ₹60 and y kg of bananas at ₹50 and pays ₹280, then 60 x + 50 y = 280 : both sides are the same total cost. Standard form: a x + b y + c = 0 , where a , b , c are real and a and b are not both zero .

Coefficients may be fractions: multiply by the LCM to clear them. ¼x + (3/5)y − ½ = 0 times 20 gives 5x + 12y − 10 = 0.

An equation in one variable is a special case: 4x + 7 = 0 is 4x + 0y + 7 = 0 and 3y = 5 is 0x + 3y − 5 = 0.

Move all terms to one side before reading a, b, c.

Example 1
Write each in standard form and give a, b, c: (i) 5x + 2y = 2.7 (ii) x/2 − 4 = (3/2)y (iii) 4 = 1.5x − 1.3y (iv) 3y = 5.
Solution. (i) 5x + 2y − 2.7 = 0.
a = 5
b = 2
c = −2.7.
(ii) x/2 − (3/2)y − 4 = 0.
a = ½
b = −3/2
c = −4.
(Multiplying by 2: x − 3y − 8 = 0.)
(iii) 1.5x − 1.3y − 4 = 0.
a = 1.5
b = −1.3
c = −4.
(iv) 0x + 3y − 5 = 0.
a = 0
b = 3
c = −5.
Example 2
Clear the fractions in x/3 + y/4 = 1 and write the standard form.
Solution. The LCM of 3 and 4 is 12.
12 × (x/3 + y/4) = 12 × 1.
4x + 3y = 12.
4x + 3y − 12 = 0.
a = 4
b = 3
c = −12.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 184 of 215
Chapter 13: Two Variables, One Line 13.2 Solutions and the Infinite Solution Set Ganita Manjari · Class 9
13.2

Solutions and the Infinite Solution Set

Key Idea
A solution of a x + b y + c = 0 is an ordered pair ( u , v ) that makes LHS = RHS when x = u , y = v . Every linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions: write y in terms of x and every real x gives a y .

For 3x + 2y = 12: (2, 3) and (4, 0) are solutions; (1, 3) is not, since 3 + 6 = 9 ≠ 12.

Origin condition: the line passes through (0, 0) iff c = 0. Then x = 0 is the y-axis and y = 0 the x-axis.

Equivalent equations: multiplying every term by k ≠ 0 does not change the solutions.

Example 3
Is (1, 9/2) a solution of 3x + 2y = 12? Is (4, 1)?
Solution. For (1, 9/2): 3(1) + 2(9/2) = 3 + 9 = 12.
This equals the RHS, so it is a solution.
For (4, 1): 3(4) + 2(1) = 14.
14 ≠ 12, so it is not a solution.
Example 4
If (−3, 4) is a solution of both 3ax + 4y = −2 and 2x + by = 14, find a and b.
Solution. Put x = −3, y = 4 in the first equation.
3a(−3) + 4(4) = −2.
−9a + 16 = −2.
−9a = −18.
a = 2.
Put x = −3, y = 4 in the second equation.
2(−3) + b(4) = 14.
4b = 20.
b = 5.
Example 5
Write y in terms of x for 3x + 2y = 12 and find three solutions.
Solution. 2y = 12 − 3x.
y = 6 − (3/2)x.
x = 0: y = 6, so (0, 6).
x = 2: y = 3, so (2, 3).
x = 4: y = 0, so (4, 0).
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 185 of 215
Chapter 13: Two Variables, One Line 13.3 Graphing a Linear Equation Ganita Manjari · Class 9
13.3

Graphing a Linear Equation

Key Idea
The graph of a linear equation in two variables is always a straight line . Point on the line ⇒ solution. Solution ⇒ point on the line. Intercept method: put x = 0 for the y -intercept, y = 0 for the x -intercept, then join the two points.

If c = 0 the line passes through the origin: find a second point by choosing a convenient x.

Two points are enough to draw a line; a third is a useful check.

A point not on the line does not satisfy the equation.

Example 6
Draw the graph of 2x + y = 7 using the intercepts.
Solution. Put x = 0: y = 7, so A(0, 7).
Put y = 0: 2x = 7, so x = 3.5 and B(3.5, 0).
Join A and B and extend.
Other solutions on the line: (1, 5), (2, 3), (3, 1), (4, −1).
Example 7
Graph (i) 4x + 3y = 12 and (ii) 2x + 5y = 0.
Solution. (i) x = 0: y = 4, so (0, 4).
y = 0: x = 3, so (3, 0).
The line passes through (0, 4) and (3, 0).
(ii) c = 0, so the line passes through (0, 0).
Put x = 5: 10 + 5y = 0, so y = −2 and (5, −2) is a second point.
Join (0, 0) and (5, −2).
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 186 of 215
Chapter 13: Two Variables, One Line 13.4 Slope and the Slope-Intercept Form y = mx + d Ganita Manjari · Class 9
13.4

Slope and the Slope-Intercept Form y = mx + d

Key Idea
Slope m = rise ÷ run = ( y 2 − y 1 )/( x 2 − x 1 ) . It does not depend on the order of the two points. In y = m x + d : m is the slope and d the y -intercept. From a x + b y + c = 0 with b ≠ 0 : y = −( a / b ) x − c / b , so m = − a / b and the y -intercept is − c / b .

Why m is the slope: points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) on y = mx + d satisfy y1 = mx1 + d and y2 = mx2 + d. Subtracting, y2 − y1 = m(x2 − x1), so (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1) = m.

Parallel lines: lines with equal slopes and different intercepts never meet. If they met at (x0, y0), then mx0 + d1 = mx0 + d2, so d1 = d2, a contradiction.

Rank steepness by comparing the ratios rise/run.

Example 8
Find the slope of the line through A(−1, 0), B(1, 2), C(4, 5).
Solution. Use B and C: m = (5 − 2)/(4 − 1).
= 3/3.
= 1.
Check with A and B: (2 − 0)/(1 − (−1)) = 2/2 = 1.
Example 9
Show that the slope of the line through A(−4, 5) and B(−1, 2) does not depend on the order of the points.
Solution. From A to B: m = (2 − 5)/(−1 − (−4)).
= −3/3.
= −1.
From B to A: m = (5 − 2)/(−4 − (−1)).
= 3/(−3).
= −1.
Both orders give −1.
Example 10
Find the slope and y-intercept of 5x + y = 3 and of 2x − 3y + 6 = 0.
Solution. 5x + y = 3 gives y = −5x + 3.
Slope = −5, y-intercept = 3.
2x − 3y + 6 = 0 gives 3y = 2x + 6.
y = (2/3)x + 2.
Slope = 2/3, y-intercept = 2.
Example 11
A ramp rises 3 m over a run of 12 m. Find its slope and the rise for a run of 20 m at the same slope.
Solution. Slope = 3/12 = 1/4.
Rise for a run of 20 m = 1/4 × 20.
= 5 m.

Chapter 13: Two Variables, One Line 13.5 Pairs of Linear Equations: Modelling Real Situations Ganita Manjari · Class 9
13.5

Pairs of Linear Equations: Modelling Real Situations

Key Idea
When two unknowns satisfy two conditions at once we get a pair of linear equations : a 1 x + b 1 y + c 1 = 0 and a 2 x + b 2 y + c 2 = 0 . Steps: name the unknowns, translate each condition into an equation, solve , check .
Example 12
Rakesh says: “Two numbers have sum 25 and difference 11.” Frame and solve the pair.
Solution. Let the numbers be x and y.
x + y = 25 … (1)
x − y = 11 … (2)
Add: 2x = 36, so x = 18.
Then y = 25 − 18 = 7.
Check: 18 − 7 = 11.
Example 13
Group A pays ₹600 for 2 adult and 3 child tickets; Group B pays ₹700 for 3 adult and 2 child tickets. Frame the pair.
Solution. Let an adult ticket cost ₹x and a child ticket ₹y.
Group A: 2x + 3y = 600.
Group B: 3x + 2y = 700.
SJMaths Learning Series For concepts, ncert solutions, test visit at www.sjmaths.com Page 188 of 215
Chapter 13: Two Variables, One Line 13.6 Solving by Substitution and by Elimination Ganita Manjari · Class 9
13.6

Solving by Substitution and by Elimination

Key Idea
Substitution: express one variable from one equation, substitute into the other. Elimination: multiply to make the coefficient of one variable equal in size, then add or subtract to eliminate it. Always check in both original equations.
Example 14
Solve 7x − 15y = 2 and x + 2y = 3 by substitution.
Solution. From the second equation: x = 3 − 2y … (3)
Substitute (3) in the first: 7(3 − 2y) − 15y = 2.
21 − 14y − 15y = 2.
−29y = −19.
y = 19/29.
x = 3 − 2(19/29).
= (87 − 38)/29.
= 49/29.
Example 15
Two angles of a triangle are x° and y° with y = 4x and the third angle is 50°. Find x and y.
Solution. Angle sum: x + y + 50 = 180.
x + 4x = 130.
5x = 130.
x = 26.
y = 4 × 26
= 104.
Example 16
Incomes of two people are in the ratio 9 : 7, their expenditures in the ratio 4 : 3, and each saves ₹2000 per month. Find the incomes.
Solution. Let incomes be 9x and 7x, expenditures 4y and 3y.
9x − 4y = 2000 … (1)
7x − 3y = 2000 … (2)
Multiply (1) by 3: 27x − 12y = 6000 … (3)
Multiply (2) by 4: 28x − 12y = 8000 … (4)
Subtract (3) from (4): x = 2000.
Put in (1): 18000 − 4y = 2000.
4y = 16000, so y = 4000.
Incomes: 9 × 2000 = ₹18000 and 7 × 2000 = ₹14000.
Example 17
The sum of a two-digit number and its reverse is 66, and its digits differ by 2. Find the number.
Solution. Let the number be 10x + y
its reverse is 10y + x.
(10x + y) + (10y + x) = 66.
11(x + y) = 66.
x + y = 6 … (1)
x − y = 2 … (2)
Add (1) and (2): 2x = 8, so x = 4.
y = 2.
The number is 42 (or 24).
Example 18
Solve 2x + 3y = 13 and 5x − 3y = 8 by elimination.
Solution. The y coefficients are +3 and −3, so add.
7x = 21.
x = 3.
Put in the first equation: 6 + 3y = 13.
3y = 7, so y = 7/3.
Check in the second: 5(3) − 3(7/3) = 15 − 7 = 8.

Chapter 13: Two Variables, One Line 13.7 Consistency and the Ratio Rules Ganita Manjari · Class 9
13.7

Consistency and the Ratio Rules

Coefficient ratios Lines Solutions Type
a 1 / a 2 ≠ b 1 / b 2 intersecting exactly one consistent, independent
a 1 / a 2 = b 1 / b 2 = c 1 / c 2 coincident infinitely many consistent, dependent
a 1 / a 2 = b 1 / b 2 ≠ c 1 / c 2 parallel none inconsistent

In elimination, an identity 0 = 0 means infinitely many solutions; a contradiction 0 = k (k ≠ 0) means none.

To get a pair of the wanted type from ax + by + c = 0: change the constant (parallel), multiply by a number (coincident), or alter the ratio of a to b (intersecting).

Example 19
Solve graphically x + 3y = 6 and 2x − 3y = 12.
Solution. Line 1: (0, 2) and (6, 0).
Line 2: (0, −4) and (3, −2).
The lines cross at (6, 0).
Ratio check: a1/a2 = 1/2 and b1/b2 = 3/(−3) = −1.
The ratios differ, so there is one solution: x = 6, y = 0.
Example 20
Classify x + 2y − 4 = 0 and 2x + 4y − 12 = 0.
Solution. a1/a2 = 1/2.
b1/b2 = 2/4
= 1/2.
c1/c2 = −4/(−12)
= 1/3.
The first two ratios are equal and the third differs.
The lines are parallel and there is no solution.
Example 21
Romila buys 2 erasers and 3 sheets for ₹9; Sonali buys 4 erasers and 6 sheets for ₹18. Are the prices determined?
Solution. 2x + 3y = 9 and 4x + 6y = 18.
a1/a2 = 2/4
= 1/2.
b1/b2 = 3/6
= 1/2.
c1/c2 = 9/18
= 1/2.
All three ratios are equal: the lines coincide.
Infinitely many price pairs fit, so the prices are not determined.
Example 22
Find k so that kx + 3y = 6 and 2x + 6y = 9 have no solution.
Solution. No solution needs a1/a2 = b1/b2 ≠ c1/c2.
b1/b2 = 3/6
= 1/2.
a1/a2 = k/2
= 1/2, so k = 1.
c1/c2 = 6/9
= 2/3.
2/3 ≠ 1/2, so the condition holds.
k = 1.

Chapter 13: Two Variables, One Line 13.8 A Pinch of History: Mahāvīrāchārya’s Problem Ganita Manjari · Class 9
13.8

A Pinch of History: Mahāvīrāchārya’s Problem

Babylonia (c. 2000 BCE): clay-tablet problems on areas and sums of two unknown lengths.

China (c. 200 BCE): the Jiuzhang Suanshu used counting rods in columns (fangcheng), a method equivalent to elimination.

India (c. 500 to 850 CE): Āryabhaṭa and Brahmagupta gave rules for linear problems in several unknowns; Mahāvīrāchārya (c. 850 CE) posed the citron problem below.

Example 23
Mahāvīrāchārya’s problem: 9 citrons and 7 fragrant wood-apples cost 107; 7 citrons and 9 wood-apples cost 101. Find each price.
Solution. Let a citron cost x and a wood-apple y.
9x + 7y = 107 … (1)
7x + 9y = 101 … (2)
The coefficients of x and y are interchanged.
Add: 16x + 16y = 208, so x + y = 13 … (3)
Subtract (2) from (1): 2x − 2y = 6, so x − y = 3 … (4)
Add (3) and (4): 2x = 16, so x = 8.
y = 13 − 8
= 5.
A citron costs 8 and a wood-apple costs 5.

Chapter 14: Surface Area & Volume 14.1 Cuboids and Cubes Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Key Idea
Scaling by k : lengths × k , areas × k 2 , volumes × k 3 . Surface area of a solid is the total area of its faces; volume is the space it fills. Use π = 22/7 unless a question says otherwise.
14.1

Cuboids and Cubes

Key Idea
Total surface area (TSA) of a cuboid = 2( l w + w h + h l ) . Lateral surface area (four walls) = 2 h ( l + w ) . Volume = l w h . Cube: TSA = 6 a 2 , volume = a 3 , diagonal = a √3 .

Joining two solids hides the glued faces, so the total surface area decreases. Cutting a solid exposes two new faces, so the area increases.

Surface area is in square units, volume in cubic units; 1 m³ = 1000 litres.

Example 1
The volume of a cube is 64 cm³. Find its edge and total surface area.
Solution. a3 = 64.
a = 4 cm.
TSA = 6a2.
= 6 × 16.
= 96 cm².
Example 2
A cuboid is 8 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm. Find its TSA, lateral surface area and volume.
Solution. TSA = 2(8 × 5 + 5 × 4 + 4 × 8).
= 2(40 + 20 + 32).
= 184 cm².
Lateral area = 2 × 4 × (8 + 5).
= 104 cm².
Volume = 8 × 5 × 4.
= 160 cm³.
Example 3
Two cubes of edge 5 cm are joined face to face to make a cuboid. Find its TSA and compare with the two separate cubes.
Solution. The cuboid is 10 cm × 5 cm × 5 cm.
TSA = 2(50 + 25 + 50).
= 250 cm².
Two separate cubes: 2 × 6 × 25 = 300 cm².
The area falls by 2 × 25 = 50 cm², the two hidden faces.
Example 4
A cuboid 10 cm × 6 cm × 4 cm is cut into two equal halves along its length. By how much does the total surface area increase?
Solution. The cutting plane is a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle.
Two new faces are exposed.
Increase = 2 × 6 × 4.
= 48 cm².

Chapter 14: Surface Area & Volume 14.2 Cylinders Ganita Manjari · Class 9
Example 5
How many cubes of edge 2 cm fit in a box 10 cm × 8 cm × 6 cm?
Solution. Volume of the box = 10 × 8 × 6 = 480 cm³.
Volume of one cube = 23 = 8 cm³.
Number of cubes = 480/8.
= 60.
Check along the edges: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.
14.2

Cylinders

Key Idea
Curved surface area = 2π r h (the unrolled rectangle). Total surface area = 2π r h + 2π r 2 = 2π r ( r + h ) . Volume = π r 2 h (area of the base × height).

If the top is open, subtract one circle: TSA = 2πrh + πr2.

A pipe or roller makes a cylinder whose curved surface is what touches the ground or wall.

Doubling r multiplies the volume by 4; doubling h multiplies it by 2.

Example 6
A cylinder has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Find its curved surface area, total surface area and volume.
Solution. CSA = 2πrh = 2 × 22/7 × 7 × 10 = 440 cm².
Area of two circles = 2πr2 = 2 × 22/7 × 49 = 308 cm².
TSA = 440 + 308 = 748 cm².
Volume = πr2h = 22/7 × 49 × 10.
= 1540 cm³.
Example 7
A water tank is a cylinder of diameter 4 m and height 5 m. Find its capacity in litres (use π = 3.1416).
Solution. Radius = 2 m.
Volume = π × 22 × 5.
= 20π.
≈ 62.83 m³.
1 m³ = 1000 litres.
Capacity ≈ 62830 litres.
Example 8
A garden roller has radius 35 cm and length 1.2 m. How much ground does it cover in one revolution?
Solution. Radius = 0.35 m.
Area per revolution = curved surface area.
= 2πrh.
= 2 × 22/7 × 0.35 × 1.2.
= 2.64 m².
Example 9
A cylindrical can is open at the top, radius 5 cm and height 12 cm. Find the sheet of metal needed (use π = 3.14).
Solution. Area needed = curved surface + one base.
= 2πrh + πr2.
= 2 × 3.14 × 5 × 12 + 3.14 × 25.
= 376.8 + 78.5.
= 455.3 cm².

Chapter 14: Surface Area & Volume 14.3 Cones Ganita Manjari · Class 9
14.3

Cones

Key Idea
Slant height l = √( h 2 + r 2 ) . Curved surface area = π r l (sector of radius l and arc 2π r ). Total surface area = π r ( r + l ) . Volume = ⅓π r 2 h : exactly one-third of the cylinder with the same base and height.

To find r from a sector: arc length of sector = circumference of cone base.

Similar cones: lengths in ratio k give volumes in ratio k3.

Example 10
A cone has radius 6 cm and height 8 cm. Find l, the curved surface area and the volume (use π = 3.14).
Solution. l = √(82 + 62).
= √100.
= 10 cm.
CSA = πrl = 3.14 × 6 × 10.
= 188.4 cm².
Volume = ⅓πr2h = ⅓ × 3.14 × 36 × 8.
= 301.44 cm³.
Example 11
A conical cap has radius 7 cm and slant height 25 cm. Find its height and volume.
Solution. h = √(252 − 72).
= √(625 − 49).
= √576.
= 24 cm.
Volume = ⅓ × 22/7 × 49 × 24.
= 1232 cm³.
Example 12
A sector of radius 10 cm and angle 216° is bent into a cone. Find the base radius, height and volume.
Solution. Arc length of the sector = 216/360 × 2π × 10.
= 12π cm.
This is the base circumference: 2πr = 12π.
r = 6 cm.
Slant height l = 10 cm.
h = √(100 − 36)
= 8 cm.
Volume = ⅓π × 36 × 8.
= 96π.
≈ 301.6 cm³.

Chapter 14: Surface Area & Volume 14.4 Pyramids Ganita Manjari · Class 9
14.4

Pyramids

Key Idea
Volume of a pyramid = ⅓ × (area of base) × (height). The lateral faces are triangles. For a square pyramid with base side a and height h : slant height s = √( h 2 + ( a /2) 2 ) , lateral area = 4 × ½ a s = 2 a s .

A pyramid is one-third of the prism with the same base and height, just as a cone is one-third of a cylinder.

The height is perpendicular to the base; the slant height lies along a lateral face.

Example 13
A square pyramid has base side 6 cm and height 4 cm. Find its volume, slant height, lateral area and total surface area.
Solution. Base area = 6 × 6 = 36 cm².
Volume = ⅓ × 36 × 4.
= 48 cm³.
Slant height s = √(42 + 32).
= √25.
= 5 cm.
Lateral area = 2as = 2 × 6 × 5 = 60 cm².
TSA = 60 + 36 = 96 cm².
Example 14
A pyramid has volume 90 cm³ and a rectangular base 6 cm × 5 cm. Find its height.
Solution. Base area = 30 cm².
⅓ × 30 × h = 90.
10h = 90.
h = 9 cm.

Chapter 14: Surface Area & Volume 14.5 Spheres and Archimedes’ Discovery Ganita Manjari · Class 9
14.5

Spheres and Archimedes’ Discovery

Key Idea
Surface area of a sphere = 4π r 2 (four times the area of a great circle). Volume = 4/3 π r 3 . Archimedes: a sphere has the same surface area as the curved surface of its circumscribing cylinder ( 2π r × 2 r = 4π r 2 ), and two-thirds of its volume.
Example 15
Find the surface area and volume of a sphere of radius 7 cm.
Solution. Surface area = 4πr2.
= 4 × 22/7 × 49.
= 616 cm².
Volume = 4/3 × 22/7 × 343.
= 4312/3.
≈ 1437.33 cm³.
Example 16
If the radius of a sphere is doubled, how do its surface area and volume change?
Solution. New area = 4π(2r)2.
= 16πr2.
This is 4 times the old area.
New volume = 4/3 π (2r)3.
= 32/3 πr3.
This is 8 times the old volume.
Example 17
A solid sphere of radius 3 cm is melted and recast into small spheres of radius 1 cm. How many are made?
Solution. Volume of the big sphere = 4/3 π × 27 = 36π.
Volume of one small sphere = 4/3 π × 1 = 4π/3.
Number = 36π ÷ (4π/3).
= 36 × 3/4.
= 27.
Example 18
A hemispherical bowl has radius 7 cm. Find its total outer surface area (with the lid) and capacity.
Solution. Curved surface = 2πr2 = 2 × 22/7 × 49 = 308 cm².
Flat lid = πr2 = 154 cm².
TSA = 3πr2 = 462 cm².
Volume = 2/3 πr3 = 2/3 × 22/7 × 343.
= 15092/21.
≈ 718.67 cm³.

Chapter 14: Surface Area & Volume 14.6 Composite Solids, Recasting and Displacement Ganita Manjari · Class 9
14.6

Composite Solids, Recasting and Displacement

Key Idea
Add volumes of parts that are joined; subtract for hollows. Melting and recasting preserves volume , not surface area. A solid dropped in water displaces its own volume : the water level rises by (volume of solid) ÷ (base area of the container).
Example 19
An ice-cream cone has a hemisphere of radius 3 cm on a cone of height 12 cm and the same radius. Find the total volume.
Solution. Cone: ⅓πr2h = ⅓π × 9 × 12 = 36π.
Hemisphere: 2/3 πr3 = 2/3 π × 27 = 18π.
Total = 36π + 18π.
= 54π.
≈ 169.65 cm³.
Example 20
A solid cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 8 cm is melted into spheres of radius 1 cm. How many spheres?
Solution. Volume of the cylinder = π × 9 × 8 = 72π.
Volume of one sphere = 4π/3.
Number = 72π ÷ (4π/3).
= 72 × 3/4.
= 54.
Example 21
A marble of radius 1 cm is dropped into a cylindrical glass of radius 5 cm containing water. By how much does the water level rise?
Solution. Volume of the marble = 4π/3.
Base area of the glass = 25π.
Rise = (4π/3) ÷ 25π.
= 4/75.
≈ 0.053 cm.

Chapter 14: Surface Area & Volume 14.7 Estimation, Scaling and Guesstimates Ganita Manjari · Class 9
14.7

Estimation, Scaling and Guesstimates

Key Idea
Scaling by k multiplies lengths by k , areas by k 2 and volumes by k 3 . Surface area ÷ volume: for a sphere = 3/ r . Small objects have a large surface-area-to-volume ratio, which is why small drops cool or dry quickly.

Guesstimate: round to easy numbers, compute, and judge whether the answer is reasonable.

Circumference trick: adding length L to a circle’s circumference adds L/(2π) to its radius, whatever the radius.

Example 22
A model of a car is made at 1 : 10 scale. How do its surface area and volume compare with the real car?
Solution. Lengths are 1/10.
Areas are (1/10)2 = 1/100.
Volumes are (1/10)3 = 1/1000.
The model needs 1/100 of the paint and holds 1/1000 of the volume.
Example 23
The radius of a sphere is r. Find the ratio surface area ÷ volume, and compare for r = 1 and r = 10.
Solution. Ratio = 4πr2/(4/3 πr3).
= 3/r.
For r = 1: ratio = 3.
For r = 10: ratio = 0.3.
The small sphere has ten times the area per unit volume.
Example 24
A rope is wound once round the equator of the Earth and then lengthened by 1 m and raised evenly above the ground. Find the gap.
Solution. Original circumference = 2πR.
New circumference = 2πR + 1 = 2π(R + h).
2πh = 1.
h = 1/(2π).
≈ 0.159 m.
The gap does not depend on R.

Chapter 2: Linear Polynomials 2.2 Linear Polynomials as Functions Ganita Manjari · Class 9
2.2

Linear Polynomials as Functions

Key Idea
A linear polynomial has degree 1: a x + b with a ≠ 0 . Each extra unit of x changes the value by the same fixed amount a . As a function , f ( x ) = a x + b is an input–output machine: multiply the input by a , then add b .

The value of P(x) at x = k is P(k): replace x by k.

A linear polynomial has exactly one zero: ax + b = 0 gives x = −b/a.

Word problems: let a letter stand for the unknown, write an equation from the story, solve it, then check it against the story.

Example 4
Find the value of 5x − 3 at x = 0, −1 and 2.
Solution. x = 0: 5(0) − 3 = −3.
x = −1: 5(−1) − 3 = −8.
x = 2: 5(2) − 3 = 7.
Example 5
Find the zero of 4x − 10.
Solution. Set 4x − 10 = 0: x = 10/4 = 5/2.
Check: 4(5/2) − 10 = 0.
Example 6
Salil’s mother is three times as old as Salil. In 5 years their ages add up to 70. Find their present ages.
Solution. Salil’s age x
his mother’s 3x.
In 5 years: (x + 5) + (3x + 5) = 70, so 4x = 60 and x = 15.
Salil is 15 and his mother is 45.
Example 7
Two integers are in the ratio 2 : 5 and differ by 63. Find them.
Solution. Let them be 2x and 5x: 5x − 2x = 63, so x = 21.
The integers are 42 and 105.
Example 8
Ruby has ₹2 and ₹5 coins worth ₹88. She has three times as many ₹2 coins as ₹5 coins. How many of each?
Solution. ₹5 coins: x
₹2 coins: 3x.
5x + 2(3x) = 88, so 11x = 88 and x = 8.
She has 8 five-rupee coins and 24 two-rupee coins.
Example 9
A rectangle has perimeter 24 cm and length 3 cm more than twice its width. Find its sides.
Solution. Width w, length 2w + 3.
Half the perimeter: (2w + 3) + w = 12, so w = 3.
Length = 9 cm.
The sides are 9 cm and 3 cm.
